d_babylon.c: Roman tower of the Babylon fortress in Old Cairo, the district where Egyptian tradition places the Holy Family’s refuge. The fortress itself is later than Jesus’ day.
d_babylon.d: Roman tower in the Old Cairo district, tied to the Holy Family’s tradition.

d_banias.c: Pan’s cave and its shrine niches at Banias, ancient Caesarea Philippi, a pagan holy place when Peter confessed Jesus here.
d_banias.d: A pagan shrine cave at Caesarea Philippi.

d_bethesda.c: The excavated Pools of Bethesda beside St. Anne’s Church, Jerusalem: twin pools matching John 5’s “five porticoes”.
d_bethesda.d: Twin pools in Jerusalem matching John’s five porticoes.

d_bethsaida.c: Excavated ruins at et-Tell, identified by most scholars as Bethsaida.
d_bethsaida.d: Excavated ruins of Bethsaida on the lake’s north shore.

d_boat.c: The “Jesus Boat”: a 1st-century fishing boat found in the lake mud near Magdala (Ginosar) in 1986.
d_boat.d: A 1st-century fishing boat found in the lake mud.

d_caiaphas.c: Ossuary inscribed for “Joseph son of Caiaphas”, found in a Jerusalem tomb in 1990 and widely thought to be the high priest’s (Israel Museum).
d_caiaphas.d: A bone box inscribed for “Joseph son of Caiaphas”.

d_capsyn.c: Capernaum’s white-limestone synagogue (4th–5th c. AD). Black basalt foundations beneath it may belong to the 1st-century synagogue where Jesus taught.
d_capsyn.d: White-limestone synagogue over the likely 1st-century one.

d_chorazin.c: Carved basalt lintels from Chorazin’s synagogue (4th–6th c. AD), a town Jesus rebuked.
d_chorazin.d: Carved basalt from the synagogue of Chorazin.

d_denarius.c: A silver denarius of Emperor Tiberius, traditionally called the “tribute penny” of Mark 12:13–17.
d_denarius.d: The silver denarius of Tiberius Caesar, the coin of the tribute question.

d_emmaus.c: Emmaus-Nicopolis (Imwas), one of several candidate sites for Luke’s Emmaus.
d_emmaus.d: One candidate site for Luke’s Emmaus.

d_gallicantu.c: Rock-cut pit beneath St. Peter in Gallicantu, on the slope where tradition places Caiaphas’s house.
d_gallicantu.n: Pit at St. Peter in Gallicantu
d_gallicantu.d: A rock-cut pit on the slope where tradition puts Caiaphas’s house.

d_gamla.c: The synagogue at Gamla in the Golan, one of the few synagogues known from Jesus’ own century.
d_gamla.d: A 1st-century synagogue from a town on the Golan, near Galilee.

d_heelbone.c: A heel bone still pierced by an iron nail, from a man crucified in Jerusalem in the 1st century AD (Israel Museum).
d_heelbone.d: The only known remains of a crucified man from 1st-century Jerusalem.

d_herodium.c: Herodium, Herod the Great’s fortress-palace on a man-made hill just south of Jerusalem and east of Bethlehem.
d_herodium.d: Herod the Great’s fortress-palace by Bethlehem.

d_herodmosaic.c: Mosaic floor from Herod the Great’s palace at Herodium, south of Bethlehem.
d_herodmosaic.d: A mosaic floor from Herod’s palace at Herodium.

d_herodtomb.c: Herod’s Family Tomb in Jerusalem, with its round rolling-stone door: the same kind of tomb the Gospels describe for Jesus’ burial.
d_herodtomb.d: A Jerusalem tomb of Jesus’ day with a round rolling-stone door.

d_hezekiah.c: Hezekiah’s Tunnel emerges at the Pool of Siloam, carrying water from the Gihon Spring (2 Kings 20).
d_hezekiah.d: The water tunnel that empties into the Pool of Siloam.

d_hezir.c: The rock-cut Bnei Hezir tomb in the Kidron Valley, an example of the monumental Jerusalem tombs of the Second Temple period.
d_hezir.d: A rock-cut Jerusalem family tomb carved around Jesus’ day.

d_hippos.c: Hippos (Sussita), a Decapolis city on the hill above the Sea of Galilee’s east shore.
d_hippos.d: A Decapolis city above the lake’s east shore.

d_hulda.c: The Huldah Gates in the Temple Mount’s southern wall, the main entrances pilgrims used.
d_hulda.d: The sealed southern gates into the Temple Mount.

d_isaiah.c: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (about 125–100 BC), the kind of scroll Jesus unrolls in the Nazareth synagogue (Luke 4).
d_isaiah.d: A complete Isaiah scroll from about 100 BC, found at Qumran.

d_jerichopal.c: Opus reticulatum stonework from Herod’s winter palace at Jericho, the oasis city Jesus passes through on the road up to Jerusalem.
d_jerichopal.d: Diamond-pattern Roman stonework from Herod’s winter palace at Jericho.

d_lithos.c: Large stone pavement near the Antonia site, long linked to Pilate’s “Stone Pavement” (John 19:13). Many scholars now date it to Hadrian’s forum.
d_lithos.d: A large paved court long linked to Pilate’s trial.

d_machaerus.c: Herod’s hilltop fortress Machaerus east of the Dead Sea, where Josephus places John the Baptist’s imprisonment.
d_machaerus.d: Herod’s hilltop fortress where John was held.

d_magboat.c: A boat depicted in a mosaic at Magdala, a first-century fishing town on the Sea of Galilee.
d_magboat.d: A boat in a mosaic from Magdala, a Galilean fishing town.

d_magstone.c: The Magdala Stone, an ornately carved block from the Magdala synagogue, a Temple-themed relief from Jesus’ time.
d_magstone.d: A carved stone from the Magdala synagogue.

d_magsyn.c: The 1st-century synagogue uncovered at Magdala (Migdal) on the Sea of Galilee.

d_model.c: Scale model of Jerusalem in the late Second Temple period, built from archaeological and written evidence (Israel Museum).
d_model.d: A scale model of Jerusalem and Herod’s Temple, built from the digs.

d_nativityfloor.c: Mosaic floor of Constantine’s basilica, uncovered under the Church of the Nativity in 1934.
d_nativityfloor.d: A 4th-century mosaic floor under the Church of the Nativity.

d_nazvillage.c: Nazareth Village, a re-created first-century village built on an excavated Galilean farm.
d_nazvillage.d: A re-created 1st-century village on an excavated farm in Nazareth.

d_ossuaries.c: First-century Jerusalem ossuaries (bone boxes), one inscribed “Jesus son of Joseph”: a very common pair of names then.
d_ossuaries.d: 1st-century bone boxes from Jerusalem tombs. “Jesus son of Joseph” was a common name.

d_peterhouse.c: Remains of a 1st-century house beneath the modern church at Capernaum, venerated since early Christian times as Peter’s house.
d_peterhouse.d: A 1st-century house at Capernaum, honored as Peter’s home.

d_pilate.c: The Pilate Stone, a 1st-century inscription naming “Pontius Pilatus, prefect of Judea”, found at Caesarea.
d_pilate.d: A stone naming Pontius Pilate, found at Caesarea.

d_pilatecoin.c: A bronze coin minted in Judea under Pontius Pilate.
d_pilatecoin.d: A bronze coin struck under Pontius Pilate in Judea.

d_pilatepalace.c: The courtyard of Herod’s palace at Caesarea, used as the Roman governor’s residence in Pilate’s time.
d_pilatepalace.d: The courtyard of the Roman governor’s palace at Caesarea.

d_pilgrim.c: The stepped Pilgrimage Road in the City of David, the street pilgrims climbed from the Pool of Siloam to the Temple.
d_pilgrim.d: The stepped street pilgrims climbed from Siloam to the Temple.

d_prutah.c: A small bronze prutah of the type used in Judea in Jesus’ day, like the two “mites” the widow gave (Mark 12).
d_prutah.d: The tiny bronze coin of the widow’s two “mites”.

d_qumran.c: Caves at Qumran above the Dead Sea in the Judean Wilderness, where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found. A desert community here practised daily immersion in John’s day.
d_qumran.d: Desert caves above the Dead Sea where the Dead Sea Scrolls were hidden.

d_robinson.c: Robinson’s Arch, the stair remains at the southwest corner of Herod’s Temple Mount.
d_robinson.d: Stair remains at the Temple Mount’s southwest corner.

d_samaria.c: The colonnaded street of Sebaste, Herod’s rebuilt city of Samaria.
d_samaria.d: The columned street of Herod’s city of Sebaste in Samaria.
d_samaria.a: OSU Special Collections & Archives, public domain

d_scytho.c: Roman theater at Scythopolis (Beth Shean), the one Decapolis city west of the Jordan.
d_scytho.d: A Roman theater in Scythopolis, the one Decapolis city west of the Jordan.

d_shekel.c: A silver shekel from the Second Temple period, the kind of coin that moved through the Temple treasury.
d_shekel.d: Silver shekel of the Second Temple period.

d_siloam.c: The Pool of Siloam in the City of David, a stepped pool of Jesus’ day.
d_siloam.d: A stepped pool in the City of David from Jesus’ day.

d_tabgha.c: The loaves-and-fish mosaic at Tabgha’s Church of the Multiplication (Byzantine, 5th c.).
d_tabgha.d: The loaves-and-fish mosaic at Tabgha, 5th century.

d_tell.c: Tell es-Sultan, mound of Old Testament Jericho. Jesus’ Jericho was the nearby Herodian oasis city.
d_tell.d: The mound of Old Testament Jericho.

d_theodotus.c: The Theodotus inscription, a Greek dedication by a synagogue builder in 1st-century Jerusalem.
d_theodotus.d: A Greek stone naming the builder of a Jerusalem synagogue.

d_towerdavid.c: The Citadel, built on the foundations of Herod’s palace towers, a candidate for the Roman governor’s praetorium.

d_trumpet.c: Stone from the Temple Mount’s southwest corner, carved in Hebrew “to the place of trumpeting”, thrown down when Jerusalem fell in AD 70.
d_trumpet.d: A stone fallen from the Temple’s corner, carved “to the place of trumpeting”.

d_tyre.c: Roman-era columns at the Al Mina excavation site in Tyre, Phoenicia.

d_warning.c: The Temple warning stone, which bars foreigners from the inner courts on pain of death (Istanbul Archaeology Museums).
d_warning.d: The stone barring foreigners from the inner Temple courts.

d_west.c: Herodian stones of the Temple Mount’s western retaining wall, Jerusalem.
d_west.d: Herodian masonry of the Temple Mount’s western wall.

n_abuserga.c: Abu Serga in Old Cairo, a church built over a crypt that Coptic tradition links to the Holy Family’s stay.

n_akeldama.c: Akeldama, the traditional Field of Blood, in the Hinnom Valley.

n_ascen.c: The Edicule of the Ascension on the Mount of Olives.

n_beat.c: The Church of the Beatitudes above the Sea of Galilee.

n_beatview.c: Capernaum seen from the Mount of Beatitudes.

n_beth.c: The Church of the Nativity, Bethlehem.

n_cana.c: Kafr Kanna, the village traditionally identified with Cana of Galilee.

n_cana2.c: The Franciscan Wedding Church at Kafr Kanna.

n_cenacle.c: The Cenacle on Mount Zion, a Crusader-era hall traditionally venerated as the Upper Room.

n_dominus.c: The Dominus Flevit chapel on the Mount of Olives.

n_gadara.c: Gadara (Umm Qais), Jordan, the Decapolis city named in Matthew’s account of the demoniacs.

n_gal.c: The Sea of Galilee from the Mount of Beatitudes.

n_gardentomb.c: The Garden Tomb, a rock-cut tomb honored by many Protestants as an alternative site for the burial.

n_gerizim.c: Mount Gerizim from Mount Ebal, the Samaritans’ holy mountain near Sychar.

n_gethchurch.c: Gethsemane at the foot of the Mount of Olives.

n_gethtrees.c: Ancient olive trees in the Garden of Gethsemane.

n_ginosar.c: The Plain of Gennesaret (Ginosar) on the Sea of Galilee’s northwest shore.

n_golgotha.c: The traditional site of Golgotha inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

n_hermon.c: Snow-capped Mount Hermon, north of Caesarea Philippi.

n_hinnom.c: The Hinnom Valley south of Jerusalem’s Old City.

n_holysep.c: The aedicule over the traditional tomb of Jesus, Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

n_jacob.c: Jacob’s Well at Sychar (Nablus), inside the Greek Orthodox church.

n_jerus.c: Aerial view of the Temple Mount and the City of David ridge, Jerusalem.

n_lazarus.c: The entrance to the traditional tomb of Lazarus at Bethany (al-Eizariya).

n_maghtas.c: Al-Maghtas in Jordan, a traditional baptism site on the east bank of the Jordan, with excavated churches and pools.

n_manger.c: The Grotto of the Nativity beneath the Church of the Nativity, Bethlehem.

n_nain.c: Nain (Nein) in the Jezreel Valley foothills, Galilee.

n_nazareth.c: Nazareth’s old city and the Basilica of the Annunciation.

n_nazgrotto.c: The Venerated Grotto inside the Basilica of the Annunciation, Nazareth.

n_primacy.c: The Church of the Primacy of St. Peter on the shore at Tabgha.

n_qasr.c: Qasr al-Yahud on the Jordan, a traditional baptism site near Jericho.

n_shep.c: The Shepherds’ Field chapel, Beit Sahour, near Bethlehem.

n_tabor.c: The Church of the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor.

n_taybeh.c: Taybeh, the village usually identified with Ephraim.

n_temptmon.c: The Monastery of the Temptation, clinging to the cliff above Jericho.

n_viador.c: The Via Dolorosa, the traditional route to Golgotha, in Jerusalem’s Old City.

n_visit.c: The Church of the Visitation, Ein Karem.

n_wadi.c: Wadi Qelt in the Judean Desert, along the ancient Jerusalem–Jericho road.

n_wadi2.c: Ein Maboa spring in Wadi Qelt, on the road down to Jericho.

n_zacch.c: The sycamore-fig of Jericho, the kind of tree Zacchaeus climbed.

ro_nero_aureus.c: A gold aureus struck in AD 54 for the new emperor Nero, who was then a teenager.
ro_nero_aureus.d: A gold aureus struck in AD 54 for the new emperor Nero, who was then a teenager.

ro_macellum.c: The market hall of Pompeii, where meat was sold, some of it from pagan sacrifices. Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8 and 10 deal with the question of whether Christians could eat such food.
ro_macellum.d: The market hall of Pompeii, where meat was sold, some of it from pagan sacrifices. Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8 and 10 deal with the question of whether Christians could eat such food.

ro_tarraco.c: The Roman amphitheatre at Tarragona (ancient Tarraco), the capital of the Roman province in eastern Spain. The Bible does not say whether Paul reached Spain (Romans 15:24, 28).
ro_tarraco.d: The Roman amphitheatre at Tarragona (ancient Tarraco), the capital of the Roman province in eastern Spain. The Bible does not say whether Paul reached Spain (Romans 15:24, 28).

ro_circus.c: The remains of the Roman circus at Tarragona, the chief city of Roman Spain on the coast road from Gaul.
ro_circus.d: The remains of the Roman circus at Tarragona, the chief city of Roman Spain on the coast road from Gaul.

ro_salona.c: Ruins of Salona near Split in Croatia, capital of the Roman province of Dalmatia (Illyricum). Romans 15:19 says Paul preached as far as Illyricum, but does not say where.
ro_salona.d: Ruins of Salona near Split in Croatia, capital of the Roman province of Dalmatia (Illyricum). Romans 15:19 says Paul preached as far as Illyricum, but does not say where.
ro_salona.a: Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, CC BY 2.0

ro_kechries.c: The site of ancient Cenchreae, the eastern harbor of Corinth, where Phoebe served the church (Romans 16:1-2). Much of the harbor now lies under the sea.
ro_kechries.d: The site of ancient Cenchreae, the eastern harbor of Corinth, where Phoebe served the church (Romans 16:1-2). Much of the harbor now lies under the sea.

ro_santa_prisca.c: The church of Santa Prisca on the Aventine in Rome, built in the 5th century. A late tradition links the spot with Prisca and Aquila (Romans 16:3-5); no first-century proof of that has been found.
ro_santa_prisca.d: The church of Santa Prisca on the Aventine in Rome, built in the 5th century. A late tradition links the spot with Prisca and Aquila (Romans 16:3-5); no first-century proof of that has been found.

ro_domitilla.c: A gallery of the catacomb of Domitilla in Rome. The catacombs date from about AD 200 on, long after Paul, but they hold some of the earliest Christian burials in the city.
ro_domitilla.d: A gallery of the catacomb of Domitilla in Rome. The catacombs date from about AD 200 on, long after Paul, but they hold some of the earliest Christian burials in the city.

ro_ammias.f: Epitaph of Ammias, with inscriptions in Greek and in a semitic language and an engraved representation of the menorah.jpg
ro_ammias.c: A Jewish epitaph from Rome with Greek and Hebrew writing and a menorah (Capitoline Museums). Such burials, from about the 2nd to the 4th century, show the Jewish communities of Rome.
ro_ammias.d: A Jewish epitaph from Rome with Greek and Hebrew writing and a menorah (Capitoline Museums). Such burials, from about the 2nd to the 4th century, show the Jewish communities of Rome.

ro_priscilla.f: Consecrated Virgin, praying with Orans position, wearing dalmatic, tunic, and veil, from the Catacomb of Priscilla, 3rd century AD cropped.jpg
ro_priscilla.c: A woman at prayer, painted in the Catacomb of Priscilla in Rome in the 3rd century.
ro_priscilla.d: A woman at prayer, painted in the Catacomb of Priscilla in Rome in the 3rd century.
ro_priscilla.a: Painting from the 3rd century, photographed by Joseph Wilpert, public domain

ro_mamre_old.c: A photograph from about 1900 of the tree then shown as Abraham's Oak at Hebron.
ro_mamre_old.d: A photograph from about 1900 of the tree then shown as Abraham's Oak at Hebron.
ro_mamre_old.a: Matson Collection, Library of Congress, public domain

ro_potter.f: Penteskouphia tablet - potters at a kiln (Berlin Antikensammlung F 811).jpg
ro_potter.c: A clay plaque from Penteskouphia, near Corinth, showing potters at a kiln (about the 6th century BC). It is Greek, not Judean, but it shows the craft behind Paul's picture of the potter and the clay (Romans 9:21).
ro_potter.n: Potters at work, Corinthian clay plaque
ro_potter.d: A clay plaque from Penteskouphia, near Corinth, showing potters at a kiln (about the 6th century BC). It is Greek, not Judean, but it shows the craft behind Paul's picture of the potter and the clay (Romans 9:21).
ro_potter.a: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, Antikensammlung, CC BY-SA 4.0

ro_slave_collar.f: Inscribed bronze slave collar (Rome MNR 65043; CIL XV 7194).jpg
ro_slave_collar.c: An inscribed bronze collar of a runaway slave, Museo Nazionale Romano, Rome. Such collars date mostly to the 4th century, about 300 years after Romans, but they show the world of slavery that Paul's words about slaves and masters came from.
ro_slave_collar.d: An inscribed bronze collar of a runaway slave, Museo Nazionale Romano, Rome. Such collars date mostly to the 4th century, about 300 years after Romans, but they show the world of slavery that Paul's words about slaves and masters came from.

ro_alexamenos.c: A scratched drawing from the Palatine Hill in Rome (about AD 200) that mocks a Christian as worshiping a crucified man with a donkey's head. It is more than a century after Romans and shows how the message of the cross was mocked.
ro_alexamenos.d: A scratched drawing from the Palatine Hill in Rome (about AD 200) that mocks a Christian as worshiping a crucified man with a donkey's head. It is more than a century after Romans and shows how the message of the cross was mocked.

ro_claudius.f: Bust of the Roman Emperor Claudius, 37-64 CE. Marble. From Acerra near Formia, Italy. Altes Museum, Berlin.jpg
ro_claudius.c: A marble bust of the emperor Claudius (ruled AD 41-54), who according to Suetonius expelled Jews from Rome. Acts 18:2 says Claudius ordered all Jews to leave Rome, and that Aquila and Priscilla came to Corinth.
ro_claudius.n: Bust of Claudius, Altes Museum, Berlin
ro_claudius.d: A marble bust of the emperor Claudius (ruled AD 41-54), who according to Suetonius expelled Jews from Rome. Acts 18:2 says Claudius ordered all Jews to leave Rome, and that Aquila and Priscilla came to Corinth.
ro_claudius.a: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin, CC BY-SA 4.0

ro_helena.f: Tombs of the kings, Jerusalem, Holy Land-LCCN2002725016.jpg
ro_helena.c: An early photograph of the Tomb of the Kings in Jerusalem, which most scholars identify as the tomb of Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism of the mid-1st century AD. The identification is not certain.
ro_helena.d: An early photograph of the Tomb of the Kings in Jerusalem, which most scholars identify as the tomb of Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism of the mid-1st century AD. The identification is not certain.

ro_ephesus_harbor.c: The Harbor Street of Ephesus, which ran from the theater to the harbor. A customs law of AD 62 for the province of Asia was found near the harbor.
ro_ephesus_harbor.d: The Harbor Street of Ephesus, which ran from the theater to the harbor. A customs law of AD 62 for the province of Asia was found near the harbor.

ro_sinai.c: Jebel Musa in the Sinai, the traditional Mount Sinai (Horeb). The exact site is not certain.
ro_sinai.d: Jebel Musa in the Sinai, the traditional Mount Sinai (Horeb). The exact site is not certain.

co_elgreco.f: El Greco - Saint Peter and Saint Paul - Google Art Project.jpg
co_elgreco.c: Saint Peter and Saint Paul, by El Greco (about 1590-1600). In 1 Corinthians 1:12 some in Corinth said "I follow Paul" and others "I follow Cephas", which is Peter.

co_raphael.f: V&A - Raphael, St Paul Preaching in Athens (1515).jpg
co_raphael.c: Saint Paul Preaching in Athens, Raphael's design for a tapestry (1515). Paul came to Corinth from Athens (Acts 17:22 to 18:1) and tells the Corinthians he did not come with lofty words of wisdom (1 Corinthians 2:1-5).

co_reaper.f: Vincent van Gogh - Wheatfield with a reaper - Google Art Project.jpg
co_reaper.c: Wheatfield with a Reaper, by Vincent van Gogh (September 1889). Paul calls the church "God's field": one plants, another waters, and God gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6-9).

co_gladiator_relief.f: Carved relief of a Roman gladiator found at Ephesus, Ephesus Museum, Turkey (16654984954).jpg
co_gladiator_relief.c: A carved relief of a gladiator found at Ephesus (Ephesus Museum, Turkey). Fights in the arena were a common public show in Roman cities. Paul says God has put the apostles on display "as men sentenced to death" (1 Corinthians 4:9) and speaks of fighting "beasts at Ephesus" (15:32).
co_gladiator_relief.d: A carved relief of a gladiator found at Ephesus (Ephesus Museum, Turkey). Fights in the arena were a common public show in Roman cities. Paul says God has put the apostles on display "as men sentenced to death" (1 Corinthians 4:9) and speaks of fighting "beasts at Ephesus" (15:32).

co_ghent.c: The Ghent Altarpiece, by Jan van Eyck (finished 1432), with the Adoration of the Lamb in the center. Paul writes "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Corinthians 5:7).

co_michelangelo.c: The Last Judgment, by Michelangelo (1536-41), in the Sistine Chapel. Paul asks, "Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?" (1 Corinthians 6:2).

co_arnolfini.c: The Arnolfini Portrait, by Jan van Eyck (1434), a married couple in their home. It comes from a different time and place, but it is a picture of the marriage Paul writes about in 1 Corinthians 7.

co_kylix.c: A Greek red-figure drinking cup with a symposium scene, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. Such cups were made centuries before Paul, but dinner parties with wine and couches were part of social life in Corinth, the setting of 1 Corinthians 8 and 10.
co_kylix.a: Mark Landon, CC BY 4.0 (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston)

co_runners.c: A Greek prize vase with a foot race, made about 530-520 BC (British Museum). Paul uses runners and boxers in the games as a picture of discipline (1 Corinthians 9:24-27).
co_runners.a: Attributed to the Euphiletos Painter (about 530-520 BC), British Museum

co_poussin.f: Nicolas Poussin - The Adoration of the Golden Calf - WGA18293.jpg
co_poussin.c: The Adoration of the Golden Calf, by Nicolas Poussin (about 1634). Paul recalls Israel's idolatry at Sinai as a warning for the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 10:6-7).

co_leonardo.f: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) - The Last Supper (1495-1498).jpg
co_leonardo.c: The Last Supper, by Leonardo da Vinci (1495-98). Paul passes on what he "received from the Lord" about that night (1 Corinthians 11:23-26).

co_pentecost.c: Pentecost, by El Greco (about 1600). Paul says the gifts differ but come from one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:4-11).

co_sarto.f: La Charité - Andrea del Sarto - Musée du Louvre Peintures INV 712.jpg
co_sarto.c: Charity, by Andrea del Sarto (1518). The Greek word for love in 1 Corinthians 13 is agape, which older English Bibles translated "charity".

co_babel.f: Pieter Bruegel the Elder - The Tower of Babel (Vienna) - Google Art Project - edited.jpg
co_babel.c: The Tower of Babel, by Pieter Bruegel the Elder (1563). The scattering of languages in Genesis 11 is the background to Paul's talk of tongues that no one understands (1 Corinthians 14:10-11).

co_isenheim.c: The Resurrection, a panel of the Isenheim Altarpiece by Matthias Grünewald (1512-16). Paul gives the creed he received: Christ died, was buried and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

co_rembrandt.f: Saint Paul at his Writing-Desk, by Rembrandt.jpg
co_rembrandt.c: Saint Paul at his Writing Desk, by Rembrandt (about 1629-30). At the end of the letter Paul adds a greeting "in my own hand" (1 Corinthians 16:21).

co_rubens.f: Peter Paul Rubens - Raising of the Cross - 1610.jpg
co_rubens.c: The Raising of the Cross, by Peter Paul Rubens (about 1610). "We preach Christ crucified," says Paul, a message that was foolishness to Greeks (1 Corinthians 1:23).

co_acro.c: Acrocorinth, the great rock above Corinth, with the ruins of the ancient city below. Rome destroyed the Greek city in 146 BC and refounded it as a colony in 44 BC, so Paul wrote to a Roman city.
co_acro.d: Acrocorinth, the great rock above Corinth, with the ruins of the ancient city below. Rome destroyed the Greek city in 146 BC and refounded it as a colony in 44 BC, so Paul wrote to a Roman city.

co_delphi.c: Ruins in the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi, home of the most famous Greek oracle. Paul does not mention Delphi, but the Greek world he wrote to prized wisdom and inspired speech (1 Corinthians 1:22; 2:4).
co_delphi.d: Ruins in the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi, home of the most famous Greek oracle. Paul does not mention Delphi, but the Greek world he wrote to prized wisdom and inspired speech (1 Corinthians 1:22; 2:4).

co_lechaion.c: The Lechaion Road at Corinth, the paved street that led from the forum north to the harbor at Lechaion. The paving that survives is Roman, but not all of it dates from Paul's time.
co_lechaion.d: The Lechaion Road at Corinth, the paved street that led from the forum north to the harbor at Lechaion. The paving that survives is Roman, but not all of it dates from Paul's time.

co_shops.f: The west shops in the Roman forum of Corinth on 6 April 2019.jpg
co_shops.c: The row of shops on the west side of the Roman forum at Corinth. Paul worked as a tentmaker in the city (Acts 18:3), but nothing marks the shop where he worked.
co_shops.d: The row of shops on the west side of the Roman forum at Corinth. Paul worked as a tentmaker in the city (Acts 18:3), but nothing marks the shop where he worked.

co_peirene.f: The Fountain of Peirene in ancient Corinth on 6 April 2019.jpg
co_peirene.c: The Fountain of Peirene at Corinth, a famous spring beside the forum. What stands today is mostly Roman and later rebuilding.
co_peirene.d: The Fountain of Peirene at Corinth, a famous spring beside the forum. What stands today is mostly Roman and later rebuilding.

co_theater.c: The theater at Corinth, first built in the Greek period and rebuilt in Roman times, so the stonework that stands today is a mixture of periods. The Erastus pavement was found beside it.
co_theater.d: The theater at Corinth, first built in the Greek period and rebuilt in Roman times, so the stonework that stands today is a mixture of periods. The Erastus pavement was found beside it.

co_votive.f: Votive terracotta objects, 4th century BC, AM Corinthos, 202795.jpg
co_votive.c: Votive offerings in clay, including an eye and ears (4th century BC), in the Archaeological Museum of Ancient Corinth. Such offerings were left at healing sanctuaries, among them the Asklepieion at Corinth. They are older than Paul and are not mentioned in the letter.
co_votive.d: Votive offerings in clay, including an eye and ears (4th century BC), in the Archaeological Museum of Ancient Corinth. Such offerings were left at healing sanctuaries, among them the Asklepieion at Corinth. They are older than Paul and are not mentioned in the letter.

co_curse.f: Lead curse tablets, 3rd century BC, AM of Nemea, 201807.jpg
co_curse.c: Two rolled lead curse tablets from Nemea, near Corinth, dated to the 3rd century BC. Similar tablets were found at Corinth itself. They show how common curses were in the Greek world Paul wrote to.
co_curse.d: Two rolled lead curse tablets from Nemea, near Corinth, dated to the 3rd century BC. Similar tablets were found at Corinth itself. They show how common curses were in the Greek world Paul wrote to.

co_isthmia.c: The ruins of the Temple of Poseidon at Isthmia, near Corinth, where the Isthmian Games were held every two years. Paul does not name the games, but his picture of the race would speak to anyone from Corinth (1 Corinthians 9:24-27).
co_isthmia.d: The ruins of the Temple of Poseidon at Isthmia, near Corinth, where the Isthmian Games were held every two years. Paul does not name the games, but his picture of the race would speak to anyone from Corinth (1 Corinthians 9:24-27).

co_delphi_stadium.c: The stadium at Delphi, where the Pythian Games were held. The stone seating seen today was added in the 2nd century AD, after Paul. The Isthmian Games near Corinth held a similar contest.
co_delphi_stadium.d: The stadium at Delphi, where the Pythian Games were held. The stone seating seen today was added in the 2nd century AD, after Paul. The Isthmian Games near Corinth held a similar contest.

co_delphi_wall.c: The polygonal wall below the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, covered with inscriptions. Many record slaves "sold" to Apollo to win their freedom, language that parallels "you were bought with a price" (1 Corinthians 6:20; 7:23), though Paul does not mention the custom.
co_delphi_wall.d: The polygonal wall below the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, covered with inscriptions. Many record slaves "sold" to Apollo to win their freedom, language that parallels "you were bought with a price" (1 Corinthians 6:20; 7:23), though Paul does not mention the custom.

co_triclinium.f: Fresco showing guests at a banquet, from the House of the Triclinium in Pompeii, AD 40-79, National Archaeological Museum of Naples (49197773156).jpg
co_triclinium.c: A fresco of a dinner party from the House of the Triclinium at Pompeii (AD 40-79, National Archaeological Museum, Naples). Guests recline on couches while slaves serve them, much like the meals in Corinth where some ate and drank while others went hungry (1 Corinthians 11:20-22).
co_triclinium.d: A fresco of a dinner party from the House of the Triclinium at Pompeii (AD 40-79, National Archaeological Museum, Naples). Guests recline on couches while slaves serve them, much like the meals in Corinth where some ate and drank while others went hungry (1 Corinthians 11:20-22).

co_mirror_box.f: Greek Bronze Mirror Box, Corinth, 350-325 BC (28221243421).jpg
co_mirror_box.c: A Greek bronze mirror box from Corinth (350-325 BC), now in the Louvre. Corinth was known for its bronze, and metal mirrors gave only a dim image, as in "now we see in a mirror dimly" (1 Corinthians 13:12).
co_mirror_box.n: Bronze mirror box from Corinth, Louvre
co_mirror_box.d: A Greek bronze mirror box from Corinth (350-325 BC), now in the Louvre. Corinth was known for its bronze, and metal mirrors gave only a dim image, as in "now we see in a mirror dimly" (1 Corinthians 13:12).

co_vaticanus.c: A 19th-century photograph of 1 Corinthians 13 in Codex Vaticanus, a Greek Bible written in the 4th century.
co_vaticanus.d: A 19th-century photograph of 1 Corinthians 13 in Codex Vaticanus, a Greek Bible written in the 4th century.

co_p46.c: A folio of Papyrus 46, a codex of Paul's letters usually dated to about AD 200, though some scholars place it earlier. This page carries 2 Corinthians 11:33 to 12:9, but the same codex holds 1 Corinthians.
co_p46.d: A folio of Papyrus 46, a codex of Paul's letters usually dated to about AD 200, though some scholars place it earlier. This page carries 2 Corinthians 11:33 to 12:9, but the same codex holds 1 Corinthians.

co_oxy932.f: P. Oxy. VI 932 private letter on papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, written in a Greek hand of the second century AD.jpg
co_oxy932.c: A private letter on papyrus from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, written in the 2nd century AD, after Paul's time. Letters like it had a greeting, a message and a farewell, as 1 Corinthians does.
co_oxy932.d: A private letter on papyrus from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, written in the 2nd century AD, after Paul's time. Letters like it had a greeting, a message and a farewell, as 1 Corinthians does.
co_oxy932.a: Spurlock Museum, University of Illinois, public domain

co_marriage.f: Marble sarcophagus fragment- marriage scene MET DP276799.jpg
co_marriage.c: A marble sarcophagus fragment with a marriage scene, from the early 3rd century AD, long after Paul. The joined right hands were a standard sign of Roman marriage.
co_marriage.d: A marble sarcophagus fragment with a marriage scene, from the early 3rd century AD, long after Paul. The joined right hands were a standard sign of Roman marriage.
co_marriage.a: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0

co_veiled.f: Limestone statue of a veiled female votary MET DT241323.jpg
co_veiled.c: A limestone statue of a veiled woman from Cyprus (1st century BC). Veils and head coverings were common in the ancient world, though customs varied from place to place (see 1 Corinthians 11:2-16).
co_veiled.d: A limestone statue of a veiled woman from Cyprus (1st century BC). Veils and head coverings were common in the ancient world, though customs varied from place to place (see 1 Corinthians 11:2-16).
co_veiled.a: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0

co_thresh.f: Galilee trip. Saffourieh (near Nazareth). Saforis (Sepphoris). General view of the Saffourie(h) threshing floors below the village, threshing board drawn by horse LOC matpc.20758.jpg
co_thresh.c: Threshing floors below the village of Saffuriyeh, near Nazareth, photographed in the early 1900s, with a threshing board drawn by a horse. Paul quotes the law about not muzzling an ox that treads out the grain (1 Corinthians 9:9, from Deuteronomy 25:4).
co_thresh.d: Threshing floors below the village of Saffuriyeh, near Nazareth, photographed in the early 1900s, with a threshing board drawn by a horse. Paul quotes the law about not muzzling an ox that treads out the grain (1 Corinthians 9:9, from Deuteronomy 25:4).
co_thresh.a: Matson Collection, Library of Congress, public domain

tc_samaritan.f: Vincent van Gogh - The Good Samaritan, 1890 - Google Art Project.jpg
tc_samaritan.c: The Good Samaritan, painted by Vincent van Gogh in 1890 after Delacroix. Paul calls God "the God of all comfort" who comforts us so that we can comfort others (2 Corinthians 1:3-4). The painting shows one man caring for a wounded stranger; Paul does not mention the Samaritan.
tc_samaritan.a: Vincent van Gogh (1890), after Eugène Delacroix

tc_prodigal.f: Rembrandt Harmensz. van Rijn - The Return of the Prodigal Son.jpg
tc_prodigal.c: The Return of the Prodigal Son, by Rembrandt (about 1668). Paul asks the church to forgive the man who caused pain, to comfort him, and to reaffirm their love for him (2 Corinthians 2:7-8). The painting shows Jesus' parable in Luke 15, not Paul's story, but it pictures a welcome back.

tc_moses.f: Rembrandt - Moses with the Ten Commandments - Google Art Project.jpg
tc_moses.c: Moses with the Ten Commandments, by Rembrandt (1659). Paul speaks of the glory on the face of Moses, of the veil he wore, and of a veil that lies over the minds of those who read the old covenant (2 Corinthians 3:7-16).

tc_honthorst.f: Gerard van Honthorst - Adoration of the Shepherds (1622).jpg
tc_honthorst.c: Adoration of the Shepherds, by Gerard van Honthorst (1622), lit by the light that comes from the child. Paul says God, who first said "Let light shine out of darkness," has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

tc_grunewald.c: The Crucifixion, from the Isenheim Altarpiece by Matthias Grünewald (1512-16). Paul says the love of Christ compels him, because one died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14-15).

tc_bonheur.f: Rosa Bonheur - Ploughing in Nevers - Google Art Project.jpg
tc_bonheur.c: Ploughing in the Nivernais, by Rosa Bonheur (1849), with teams of yoked oxen. Paul writes "Do not be yoked together with unbelievers" (2 Corinthians 6:14). Many scholars hear an echo of Deuteronomy 22:10, which forbids ploughing with an ox and a donkey together.

tc_repent.f: Georges de La Tour - Saint Peter Repentant - 1951.454 - Cleveland Museum of Art.jpg
tc_repent.c: Saint Peter Repentant, by Georges de La Tour (about 1645). Paul writes that godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10). The painting shows Peter after he denied Jesus (Luke 22:62), not a scene from Paul's letter.
tc_repent.a: Georges de La Tour (about 1645), Cleveland Museum of Art

tc_manna.f: La Manne - Nicolas Poussin - Musée du Louvre Peintures INV 7275.jpg
tc_manna.c: The Gathering of the Manna, by Nicolas Poussin (1637-39). Paul quotes the manna story of Exodus 16 to teach fair sharing between the churches: the one who gathered much had nothing left over, and the one who gathered little had no lack (2 Corinthians 8:15).

tc_sower.f: Vincent van Gogh - Le Semeur dans un champ de blé au soleil couchant (1888).jpg
tc_sower.c: The Sower with Setting Sun, by Vincent van Gogh (1888). Paul writes that whoever sows generously will reap generously, and that God supplies seed to the sower (2 Corinthians 9:6-10).

tc_fouquet.f: Jean Fouquet. La Prise de Jéricho par Josué (enluminure, détails).jpg
tc_fouquet.c: The fall of the walls of Jericho, a manuscript painting by Jean Fouquet (15th century). Paul says his weapons "have divine power to demolish strongholds" (2 Corinthians 10:4). Paul does not mention Jericho; the picture shows the best-known story of God bringing down a stronghold.

tc_fall.f: Michelangelo, Fall and Expulsion from Garden of Eden 00.jpg
tc_fall.c: The Fall and Expulsion from the Garden of Eden, by Michelangelo (1509-10), in the Sistine Chapel. Paul fears that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, the minds of the Corinthians may be led astray from devotion to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:3).

tc_ecstasy.f: Nicolas Poussin - Le Ravissement de saint Paul, 1650 (vers).jpg
tc_ecstasy.c: The Ecstasy of Saint Paul, by Nicolas Poussin (about 1649-50). Paul writes of a man "in Christ" who was caught up to the third heaven and to Paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2-4). The painter shows Paul lifted by angels, but Paul himself describes no scene and says the man heard things that cannot be told.

tc_rublev.f: Andrey Rublev - Св. Троица - Google Art Project.jpg
tc_rublev.c: The Trinity, an icon by Andrei Rublev (early 15th century). Paul ends the letter with the blessing of "the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit" (2 Corinthians 13:14). Rublev painted the icon around the three visitors who came to Abraham (Genesis 18).

tc_rode.f: Paulus wird in Damaskus von seinen Schülern gerettet.jpg
tc_rode.c: Paul Is Rescued by His Pupils in Damascus, an engraving by Bernhard Rode (1783), showing the disciples lowering Paul from the wall in a basket (Acts 9:23-25; 2 Corinthians 11:32-33).

tc_jars.c: Storage jars of the type used for the Dead Sea Scrolls, on display at Qumran. Paul says the gospel is a treasure that he and his team carry "in jars of clay" (2 Corinthians 4:7). These jars belonged to the Dead Sea community in Judea, not to Paul's world.
tc_jars.d: Storage jars of the type used for the Dead Sea Scrolls, on display at Qumran. Paul says the gospel is a treasure that he and his team carry "in jars of clay" (2 Corinthians 4:7). These jars belonged to the Dead Sea community in Judea, not to Paul's world.

tc_tent.c: A Bedouin camp at Wadi Rum in Jordan, with a tent of woven cloth. Paul compares the body to "an earthly tent" and the resurrection body to a building from God (2 Corinthians 5:1). Acts 18:3 says Paul and his friends made tents, but exactly what their tents were made of is not known.
tc_tent.d: A Bedouin camp at Wadi Rum in Jordan, with a tent of woven cloth. Paul compares the body to "an earthly tent" and the resurrection body to a building from God (2 Corinthians 5:1). Acts 18:3 says Paul and his friends made tents, but exactly what their tents were made of is not known.

tc_bab_kisan.c: Bab Kisan in the wall of Damascus, now a Greek Catholic chapel of St. Paul. By tradition it is where the disciples lowered Paul in a basket (Acts 9:25; 2 Corinthians 11:32-33). The wall seen today is medieval over older foundations, and the exact spot is not known.
tc_bab_kisan.d: Bab Kisan in the wall of Damascus, now a Greek Catholic chapel of St. Paul. By tradition it is where the disciples lowered Paul in a basket (Acts 9:25; 2 Corinthians 11:32-33). The wall seen today is medieval over older foundations, and the exact spot is not known.

tc_masada_ramp.f: The Roman siege ramp seen from the hilltop, Masada (15444361849).jpg
tc_masada_ramp.c: The Roman siege ramp at Masada, seen from the hilltop. Paul writes that his weapons "have divine power to demolish strongholds" (2 Corinthians 10:4). The siege was about AD 73, after Paul's death, but it shows how armies took a fortress.
tc_masada_ramp.d: The Roman siege ramp at Masada, seen from the hilltop. Paul writes that his weapons "have divine power to demolish strongholds" (2 Corinthians 10:4). The siege was about AD 73, after Paul's death, but it shows how armies took a fortress.

tc_hezekiah_seal.c: A clay seal impression (bulla) of Hezekiah, king of Judah, in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem, on loan from a private collection. It is not the one found in the Ophel excavation in 2009, and it is centuries older than Paul. A seal showed who owned something, and Paul says God put his seal on believers (2 Corinthians 1:22).
tc_hezekiah_seal.d: A clay seal impression (bulla) of Hezekiah, king of Judah, in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem, on loan from a private collection. It is not the one found in the Ophel excavation in 2009, and it is centuries older than Paul. A seal showed who owned something, and Paul says God put his seal on believers (2 Corinthians 1:22).

tc_titus_triumph.f: Reliëf van de Boog van Titus voorstellend Titus op een zegekar die gekroond wordt door de Overwinning Rome. Triomfboog van Titus. (titel op object), RP-F-00-4176.jpg
tc_titus_triumph.c: Titus riding in a triumphal chariot, crowned by Victory, on a relief of the Arch of Titus in Rome (photographed about 1875-1900, Rijksmuseum). Paul writes that God "always leads us in triumphal procession in Christ" (2 Corinthians 2:14). The arch was built after Paul's death to mark the triumph of AD 71.
tc_titus_triumph.n: Titus in his chariot, Arch of Titus
tc_titus_triumph.d: Titus riding in a triumphal chariot, crowned by Victory, on a relief of the Arch of Titus in Rome (photographed about 1875-1900, Rijksmuseum). Paul writes that God "always leads us in triumphal procession in Christ" (2 Corinthians 2:14). The arch was built after Paul's death to mark the triumph of AD 71.

tc_res_gestae.f: The Temple of Augustus and Rome with the Res Gestae Divi Augusti ("Deeds of the Divine Augustus") inscribed on the walls of the cella, Ancyra, Ankara (Turkey) (26068591006).jpg
tc_res_gestae.c: The Temple of Augustus and Rome at Ankara, with the Res Gestae, the emperor's own account of his deeds, inscribed on its walls. Paul writes "we are ambassadors for Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:20). The inscription is a copy made soon after Augustus died in AD 14, decades before Paul wrote.
tc_res_gestae.d: The Temple of Augustus and Rome at Ankara, with the Res Gestae, the emperor's own account of his deeds, inscribed on its walls. Paul writes "we are ambassadors for Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:20). The inscription is a copy made soon after Augustus died in AD 14, decades before Paul wrote.

tc_songs.c: A fragment of the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice (4Q403) from Qumran, copied in the mid-1st century BC. The songs describe angels worshiping in a heavenly temple. Paul tells of a man caught up to the third heaven and to Paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2-4). The songs do not use those words, and nothing says Paul knew them.
tc_songs.d: A fragment of the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice (4Q403) from Qumran, copied in the mid-1st century BC. The songs describe angels worshiping in a heavenly temple. Paul tells of a man caught up to the third heaven and to Paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2-4). The songs do not use those words, and nothing says Paul knew them.
tc_songs.a: Dead Sea Scrolls fragment, public domain

tc_aretas_coin.f: Coin of Aretas IV and Shaqilath.jpg
tc_aretas_coin.c: A bronze coin of the Nabataean king Aretas IV and his queen Shaqilat (9 BC to AD 40). Paul says the governor under King Aretas guarded Damascus to seize him (2 Corinthians 11:32).
tc_aretas_coin.n: Coin of Aretas IV and Shaqilat
tc_aretas_coin.d: A bronze coin of the Nabataean king Aretas IV and his queen Shaqilat (9 BC to AD 40). Paul says the governor under King Aretas guarded Damascus to seize him (2 Corinthians 11:32).

tc_petra.c: The Treasury (Al-Khazneh) at Petra in Jordan, the capital of the Nabataean kingdom ruled by Aretas IV. It is often dated to the reign of Aretas or a little earlier, but its purpose is debated.
tc_petra.d: The Treasury (Al-Khazneh) at Petra in Jordan, the capital of the Nabataean kingdom ruled by Aretas IV. It is often dated to the reign of Aretas or a little earlier, but its purpose is debated.

tc_isis_ship.c: A Roman fresco of a merchant ship named the Isis Giminiana, now in the Vatican Museums (about AD 200-250). Paul says he was shipwrecked three times before he wrote 2 Corinthians (11:25). The painting is about 150 years later than Paul and shows a cargo ship of the kind he knew, not his own.
tc_isis_ship.d: A Roman fresco of a merchant ship named the Isis Giminiana, now in the Vatican Museums (about AD 200-250). Paul says he was shipwrecked three times before he wrote 2 Corinthians (11:25). The painting is about 150 years later than Paul and shows a cargo ship of the kind he knew, not his own.

ga_conv.f: Conversion of Saul, from Michelangelo's fresco in the Pauline Chapel at the Vatican MET DP844274.jpg
ga_conv.c: The Conversion of Saul, an engraving by Nicolas Beatrizet (about 1545) after Michelangelo's fresco in the Pauline Chapel at the Vatican. Paul says that God was pleased to reveal his Son to him, and that he had once tried to destroy the church (Galatians 1:13-16). Acts 9 tells the story of the road to Damascus; Galatians does not.
ga_conv.a: Nicolas Beatrizet after Michelangelo (about 1545), Metropolitan Museum of Art

ga_embrace.f: Angelos Akotantos (active 1436-1450) - Icon of The Embrace of the Apostles Peter and Paul - WA1982.192 - Ashmolean Museum.jpg
ga_embrace.c: The Embrace of the Apostles Peter and Paul, an icon by Angelos Akotantos (active 1436-1450), in the Ashmolean Museum. Paul says James, Cephas and John agreed to a partnership with him and Barnabas by a handshake (Galatians 2:9). Later in the same chapter he opposes Peter to his face at Antioch (2:11-14).

ga_velazquez.f: Diego Velázquez - Christ on the Cross - WGA24389.jpg
ga_velazquez.c: Christ on the Cross, by Diego Velázquez (about 1632), in the Prado. Paul tells the Galatians that Jesus Christ was set before their eyes as the crucified one (Galatians 3:1), and that on the cross he took the law's curse on himself (3:13).

ga_guercino.c: Abraham Casting Out Hagar and Ishmael, by Guercino (1657), in the Brera Gallery in Milan. In Galatians 4:21-31 Paul reads the story of Hagar and Sarah as a picture of two covenants, and he ends with the command to drive out the slave woman and her son (4:30, quoting Genesis 21:10).

ga_basket.c: Basket of Fruit, by Caravaggio (about 1599), in the Ambrosiana in Milan. Paul sets the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit, which he lists as love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:19-23).

ga_gleaners.c: The Gleaners, by Jean-François Millet (1857), in the Musée d'Orsay. Paul tells the Galatians not to grow weary in doing good, because in due time they will reap if they do not give up, and to do good to everyone, above all to the household of faith (Galatians 6:9-10). The law of Moses left the edges of the field for the poor to glean (Leviticus 19:9-10).

ga_gaul.f: The Dying Gaul, second-century AD Roman copy of a third-century BC Hellenistic bronze, Capitoline Museums (11340686655).jpg
ga_gaul.c: The Dying Gaul, a Roman copy of a Hellenistic bronze, in the Capitoline Museums in Rome. The original is usually thought to have honored a victory over the Galatians, the Celtic people who crossed into Anatolia in the 3rd century BC and gave their name to the region Paul writes to (Galatians 1:2).
ga_gaul.d: The Dying Gaul, a Roman copy of a Hellenistic bronze, in the Capitoline Museums in Rome. The original is usually thought to have honored a victory over the Galatians, the Celtic people who crossed into Anatolia in the 3rd century BC and gave their name to the region Paul writes to (Galatians 1:2).

ga_warrior.c: A terracotta figurine of a Galatian warrior with a dagger and a shield, made at Myrina about 150-100 BC and now in the Louvre. Greek artists often showed Galatians as fierce Celtic fighters. Paul's letter says nothing about their appearance; it speaks of their quick turn from the gospel he preached (Galatians 1:6).
ga_warrior.d: A terracotta figurine of a Galatian warrior with a dagger and a shield, made at Myrina about 150-100 BC and now in the Louvre. Greek artists often showed Galatians as fierce Celtic fighters. Paul's letter says nothing about their appearance; it speaks of their quick turn from the gospel he preached (Galatians 1:6).

ga_hegra.c: Rock-cut tombs at Hegra (Mada'in Salih) in northwest Saudi Arabia, a great city of the Nabataean kingdom. Paul says that after his call he went away into "Arabia" (Galatians 1:17), a name that in his day covered the Nabataean lands. He does not say where he went or why, so this is only a picture of the region.
ga_hegra.d: Rock-cut tombs at Hegra (Mada'in Salih) in northwest Saudi Arabia, a great city of the Nabataean kingdom. Paul says that after his call he went away into "Arabia" (Galatians 1:17), a name that in his day covered the Nabataean lands. He does not say where he went or why, so this is only a picture of the region.

ga_antioch_cave.f: Antakya Church of St. Peter interior general ın 2019 06.jpg
ga_antioch_cave.c: Inside the Cave Church of St. Peter at Antakya, ancient Syrian Antioch, a grotto that tradition ties to the first Christians of the city. The tradition is late and cannot be proved. Paul describes his open quarrel with Peter at Antioch in Galatians 2:11-14.
ga_antioch_cave.n: Cave Church of St. Peter, Antakya
ga_antioch_cave.d: Inside the Cave Church of St. Peter at Antakya, ancient Syrian Antioch, a grotto that tradition ties to the first Christians of the city. The tradition is late and cannot be proved. Paul describes his open quarrel with Peter at Antioch in Galatians 2:11-14.

ga_mosaic.f: The Megalopsychia Hunt of Antioch mosaic, late 5th century AD, found in the village of Yakto near Daphne, Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya, Turke - 50735694481.jpg
ga_mosaic.c: Part of the Megalopsychia Hunt mosaic from Yakto, near Daphne, a suburb of Antioch, now in the Hatay Archaeology Museum in Antakya. It dates from the late 5th century AD, long after Paul, but it shows the wealth of the city where Jewish and Gentile believers shared meals until the men from James arrived (Galatians 2:11-14).
ga_mosaic.d: Part of the Megalopsychia Hunt mosaic from Yakto, near Daphne, a suburb of Antioch, now in the Hatay Archaeology Museum in Antakya. It dates from the late 5th century AD, long after Paul, but it shows the wealth of the city where Jewish and Gentile believers shared meals until the men from James arrived (Galatians 2:11-14).

ga_douris.f: School cup by Douris Antikensammlung Berlin.jpg
ga_douris.c: School scenes on an Athenian red-figure drinking cup by the painter Douris (about 480 BC), now in Berlin. Boys have lessons in music and reading while older men look on. Greek households often sent a trusted slave, a paidagogos, with a boy to school, and Paul uses that figure for the law, a guardian that held the child until Christ came (Galatians 3:24-25).
ga_douris.d: School scenes on an Athenian red-figure drinking cup by the painter Douris (about 480 BC), now in Berlin. Boys have lessons in music and reading while older men look on. Greek households often sent a trusted slave, a paidagogos, with a boy to school, and Paul uses that figure for the law, a guardian that held the child until Christ came (Galatians 3:24-25).

ga_pesher.f: The Commentary on Habakkuk Scroll (1QpHab) Written in Hebrew - Google Art Project.jpg
ga_pesher.c: The Habakkuk Commentary (1QpHab), found at Qumran in Cave 1 and copied about the end of the 1st century BC, now in the Shrine of the Book in Jerusalem. It explains Habakkuk 2:4, the verse Paul quotes in Galatians 3:11, as being about people who keep the law and stay loyal to the community's Teacher.
ga_pesher.d: The Habakkuk Commentary (1QpHab), found at Qumran in Cave 1 and copied about the end of the 1st century BC, now in the Shrine of the Book in Jerusalem. It explains Habakkuk 2:4, the verse Paul quotes in Galatians 3:11, as being about people who keep the law and stay loyal to the community's Teacher.
ga_pesher.a: Dead Sea Scrolls, Israel Museum, public domain

ga_lystra_coin.f: Monnaie - Bronze, Lystra, Lycaonie, Auguste - btv1b8516625b (1 of 2).jpg
ga_lystra_coin.c: A bronze coin of Lystra from the reign of Augustus, who made it a Roman colony about 25 BC, in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Acts 14 places Paul at Lystra, where the crowd called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes. Whether Lystra was one of the "churches of Galatia" (Galatians 1:2) depends on the south Galatian view.
ga_lystra_coin.d: A bronze coin of Lystra from the reign of Augustus, who made it a Roman colony about 25 BC, in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Acts 14 places Paul at Lystra, where the crowd called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes. Whether Lystra was one of the "churches of Galatia" (Galatians 1:2) depends on the south Galatian view.
ga_lystra_coin.a: Bibliothèque nationale de France, public domain

ep_pantocrator.c: Christ Pantocrator, a sixth-century icon at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai, one of the oldest surviving icons of Christ. In Ephesians 1:20-23 Paul says God seated Christ at His right hand, far above every rule and authority, and made Him head over all things for the church.
ep_pantocrator.a: Unknown artist (6th century), Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai

ep_anastasis.c: The Anastasis fresco in the Chora Church in Istanbul, painted about 1320. Christ pulls Adam and Eve out of their tombs. In Ephesians 2:4-6 Paul says God made us alive together with Christ and raised us up with Him.

ep_ascension.f: Rembrandt The Ascension 1636 Oil on canvas Alte Pinakothek Munich Germany.jpg
ep_ascension.c: The Ascension, by Rembrandt (1636), in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich, one of the paintings of his Passion cycle. In Ephesians 4:8-10 Paul says that Christ "ascended on high" and gave gifts to His people.

ep_durer.f: Albrecht Dürer, Knight, Death and Devil, 1513, NGA 6637.jpg
ep_durer.c: Knight, Death and the Devil, an engraving by Albrecht Dürer (1513). Many art historians read the armored rider as a Christian soldier who keeps going in spite of fear. Paul's call to put on the full armor of God (Ephesians 6:10-18) is one of the texts behind that picture.
ep_durer.a: Albrecht Dürer (1513), National Gallery of Art, Washington

ep_terrace.c: The Terrace Houses on the hillside at Ephesus, a group of wealthy Roman homes with mosaics and painted walls. They show the kind of household, with family, servants and slaves, that Ephesians 5:21-6:9 speaks to.
ep_terrace.d: The Terrace Houses on the hillside at Ephesus, a group of wealthy Roman homes with mosaics and painted walls. They show the kind of household, with family, servants and slaves, that Ephesians 5:21-6:9 speaks to.

ep_laodicea.c: The colonnaded Syria Street at Laodicea on the Lycus, a wealthy city in the same valley as Colossae. Paul mentions Laodicea in Colossians 4:15-16, and some scholars think "the letter from Laodicea" was Ephesians.
ep_laodicea.d: The colonnaded Syria Street at Laodicea on the Lycus, a wealthy city in the same valley as Colossae. Paul mentions Laodicea in Colossians 4:15-16, and some scholars think "the letter from Laodicea" was Ephesians.

ep_colossae.c: The site of Colossae near Denizli in southwestern Turkey. It was a small town beside the larger cities of Laodicea and Hierapolis, and most of it has never been excavated. Onesimus, the slave in Paul's letter to Philemon, belonged to a household here (Colossians 4:9).
ep_colossae.d: The site of Colossae near Denizli in southwestern Turkey. It was a small town beside the larger cities of Laodicea and Hierapolis, and most of it has never been excavated. Onesimus, the slave in Paul's letter to Philemon, belonged to a household here (Colossians 4:9).

ep_pompeii.f: Pompeii columned atrium with impluvium House of the Ceii Pompeii (circa 2005).jpg
ep_pompeii.c: The columned atrium and rainwater pool (impluvium) of the House of the Ceii at Pompeii, the town buried by Vesuvius in AD 79. A Roman household like this included the owner's family, slaves and freed people, the setting of Ephesians 5:21-6:9.
ep_pompeii.n: Atrium of the House of the Ceii, Pompeii
ep_pompeii.d: The columned atrium and rainwater pool (impluvium) of the House of the Ceii at Pompeii, the town buried by Vesuvius in AD 79. A Roman household like this included the owner's family, slaves and freed people, the setting of Ephesians 5:21-6:9.

ep_castra.c: Part of the brick wall of the Castra Praetoria, the barracks of the Praetorian Guard in Rome, built under the emperor Tiberius about AD 23. In Philippians 1:13 Paul says the whole palace guard knew he was in chains for Christ.
ep_castra.n: Wall of the Praetorian camp, Rome
ep_castra.d: Part of the brick wall of the Castra Praetoria, the barracks of the Praetorian Guard in Rome, built under the emperor Tiberius about AD 23. In Philippians 1:13 Paul says the whole palace guard knew he was in chains for Christ.

ep_lorica.c: Remains and a modern reconstruction of lorica segmentata, the segmented plate armor of Roman legionaries, from the Corbridge hoard in northern England. Paul lists a soldier's gear in Ephesians 6:14-17 but does not name a type of armor; plate armor like this came into use in his time.
ep_lorica.d: Remains and a modern reconstruction of lorica segmentata, the segmented plate armor of Roman legionaries, from the Corbridge hoard in northern England. Paul lists a soldier's gear in Ephesians 6:14-17 but does not name a type of armor; plate armor like this came into use in his time.

ph_prison.f: 1627 Rembrandt Paulus im Gefängnis Staatsgalerie Stuttgart anagoria.JPG
ph_prison.c: Paul in Prison, by Rembrandt (1627), in the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart. It is an imagined scene. In Philippians 1:7 and 1:13 Paul says he is in chains, and in 1:12-14 he says his imprisonment has helped spread the gospel.

ph_cross.f: Diego Velázquez - Christ on the Cross - WGA24389.jpg
ph_cross.c: Christ on the Cross, by Diego Velázquez (about 1632), in the Prado. In Philippians 2:8 Paul says that Christ became obedient to death, even death on a cross.

ph_runners.c: A Greek prize vase with a foot race, made about 530-520 BC (British Museum). In Philippians 3:13-14 Paul pictures himself as a runner who forgets what is behind and strains toward the prize.
ph_runners.a: Attributed to the Euphiletos Painter (about 530-520 BC), British Museum

ph_writing.f: Valentin de Boulogne - Saint Paul Writing His Epistles - BF.1991.4 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg
ph_writing.c: Saint Paul Writing His Epistles, by Valentin de Boulogne (about 1618-20). Philippians is a thank-you letter, and in chapter 4 Paul thanks the church for its gift and tells them to bring everything to God in prayer.
ph_writing.a: Valentin de Boulogne (c. 1618-20), Museum of Fine Arts, Boston

ph_exalted.c: Christ Pantocrator, a sixth-century icon at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai. Philippians 2:9-11 says God exalted Christ and gave him the name above every name, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.
ph_exalted.a: Unknown artist (6th century), Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai

ph_theater.c: The ancient theater of Philippi, cut into the hillside below the acropolis. It goes back to the Macedonian city and was reworked in Roman times, so it shows both layers of the colony Paul's readers lived in.
ph_theater.d: The ancient theater of Philippi, cut into the hillside below the acropolis. It goes back to the Macedonian city and was reworked in Roman times, so it shows both layers of the colony Paul's readers lived in.

ph_latin.f: Latin inscriptions found in the Forum, Philippi (7272469500).jpg
ph_latin.c: Latin inscriptions found in the forum of Philippi. One is the epitaph of Gaius Julius Maximus, a town councillor of Philippi (CIL III 7339); it mentions the deified Antoninus Pius, so it is later than Paul. Texts like these show how much Philippi took pride in Roman rank and office.
ph_latin.n: Latin inscriptions from the forum of Philippi
ph_latin.d: Latin inscriptions found in the forum of Philippi. One is the epitaph of Gaius Julius Maximus, a town councillor of Philippi (CIL III 7339); it mentions the deified Antoninus Pius, so it is later than Paul. Texts like these show how much Philippi took pride in Roman rank and office.

ph_praetorians.f: The Praetorians Relief from the Arch of Claudius, once part of the Arch of Claudius erected in 51 AD to commemorate the conquest of Britain, Louvre Lens, France (26917568745).jpg
ph_praetorians.c: A relief of soldiers of the Praetorian Guard, from the Arch of Claudius in Rome (AD 51), now in the Louvre. In Philippians 1:13 Paul says his imprisonment became known to the whole palace guard, a word that could point to the emperor's guard or to a governor's residence.
ph_praetorians.n: Praetorian relief from the Arch of Claudius
ph_praetorians.d: A relief of soldiers of the Praetorian Guard, from the Arch of Claudius in Rome (AD 51), now in the Louvre. In Philippians 1:13 Paul says his imprisonment became known to the whole palace guard, a word that could point to the emperor's guard or to a governor's residence.

ph_columbarium.f: Interieur van het columbarium van de Vigna Codini Columbaria Tomb of “The officers of Ceasar's household” (titel op object), RP-F-2001-7-164-2.jpg
ph_columbarium.c: A heliogravure of the interior of a columbarium (a tomb with niches for urns) at the Vigna Codini in Rome, about 1867-77. The print is titled for the tomb of "the officers of Caesar's household". Philippians 4:22 sends greetings from the household of Caesar.
ph_columbarium.n: Columbarium at the Vigna Codini, Rome
ph_columbarium.d: A heliogravure of the interior of a columbarium (a tomb with niches for urns) at the Vigna Codini in Rome, about 1867-77. The print is titled for the tomb of "the officers of Caesar's household". Philippians 4:22 sends greetings from the household of Caesar.

ph_libation.c: An Athenian red-figure cup by the painter Macron in the Louvre, showing a libation, the pouring out of wine to the gods. In Philippians 2:17 Paul pictures his life as poured out like a drink offering over the Philippians' sacrifice of faith.
ph_libation.n: Greek cup with a libation scene (Louvre)
ph_libation.d: An Athenian red-figure cup by the painter Macron in the Louvre, showing a libation, the pouring out of wine to the gods. In Philippians 2:17 Paul pictures his life as poured out like a drink offering over the Philippians' sacrifice of faith.

cl_pantocrator.c: Christ Pantocrator, a sixth-century icon at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai. Colossians 1:15-20 calls Christ the image of the invisible God, the one through whom and for whom all things were made.
cl_pantocrator.a: Unknown artist (6th century), Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai

cl_prison.f: 1627 Rembrandt Paulus im Gefängnis Staatsgalerie Stuttgart anagoria.JPG
cl_prison.c: Paul in Prison, by Rembrandt (1627), in the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart. It is an imagined scene. In Colossians 4:3 and 4:18 Paul says he is in chains, but the letter does not say where.

cl_cross.f: Diego Velázquez - Christ on the Cross - WGA24389.jpg
cl_cross.c: Christ on the Cross, by Diego Velázquez (about 1632), in the Prado. Colossians 2:14 says God took the record of debt against us and nailed it to the cross.

cl_risen.c: The Resurrection, a panel of the Isenheim Altarpiece by Matthias Grünewald (1512-16). Colossians 3:1 says that since you have been raised with Christ, you are to strive for the things above, and the chapter goes on to say what that means for daily life.

cl_pen.f: Saint Paul at his Writing-Desk, by Rembrandt.jpg
cl_pen.c: Saint Paul at his Writing Desk, by Rembrandt (about 1629-30). In Colossians 4:18 Paul adds a greeting in his own hand and asks the church to remember his chains.

cl_colossae.c: Another view of the mound of Colossae near Denizli, Turkey (2020). The town was small and has hardly been dug. Paul says Epaphras "is one of you" (Colossians 4:12), and 1:2 addresses the church here.
cl_colossae.d: Another view of the mound of Colossae near Denizli, Turkey (2020). The town was small and has hardly been dug. Paul says Epaphras "is one of you" (Colossians 4:12), and 1:2 addresses the church here.

cl_pamukkale.f: The hot springs and travertines, terraces of carbonate minerals left by the flowing water, Hierapolis, Phrygia, Turkey (32481236792).jpg
cl_pamukkale.c: The hot springs and white travertine terraces at Hierapolis (modern Pamukkale), across the valley from Laodicea. Paul says Epaphras worked hard for the believers here (Colossians 4:13).
cl_pamukkale.n: Hot springs and travertine terraces, Hierapolis
cl_pamukkale.d: The hot springs and white travertine terraces at Hierapolis (modern Pamukkale), across the valley from Laodicea. Paul says Epaphras worked hard for the believers here (Colossians 4:13).

cl_plutonium.f: The Plutonium (Pluto's Gate), a sacred cave believed to be an entrance to the underworld and the oldest local sanctuary, Hierapolis, Phrygia, Turkey (31528582034).jpg
cl_plutonium.c: The Plutonium, a cave at Hierapolis that ancient writers said was an entrance to the underworld. Strabo says its vapor was fatal to anyone who entered except the eunuch priests of Cybele (Geography 13.4.14).
cl_plutonium.d: The Plutonium, a cave at Hierapolis that ancient writers said was an entrance to the underworld. Strabo says its vapor was fatal to anyone who entered except the eunuch priests of Cybele (Geography 13.4.14).

cl_apollo.f: The Temple of Apollo built in the 3rd century AD using stone blocks from the older temple, Hierapolis, Phrygia, Turkey (32332234786).jpg
cl_apollo.c: The Temple of Apollo at Hierapolis. What stands was built in the 3rd century AD from blocks of an older temple, so it is later than Paul, but it marks the old sanctuary of the city.
cl_apollo.d: The Temple of Apollo at Hierapolis. What stands was built in the 3rd century AD from blocks of an older temple, so it is later than Paul, but it marks the old sanctuary of the city.

cl_necropolis.c: A sarcophagus in the necropolis of Hierapolis. Tomb inscriptions here, mostly of the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD, name trade guilds such as dyers and weavers and mention Jewish festivals. They are later than Paul but come from the same valley.
cl_necropolis.n: Sarcophagus in the necropolis of Hierapolis
cl_necropolis.d: A sarcophagus in the necropolis of Hierapolis. Tomb inscriptions here, mostly of the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD, name trade guilds such as dyers and weavers and mention Jewish festivals. They are later than Paul but come from the same valley.

cl_stadium.c: The stadium at Laodicea on the Lycus, the large city in the valley about 9 miles (15 km) from Colossae. Most of what stands was built after Paul's time. Colossians 2:1 and 4:13-16 name the church here.
cl_stadium.d: The stadium at Laodicea on the Lycus, the large city in the valley about 9 miles (15 km) from Colossae. Most of what stands was built after Paul's time. Colossians 2:1 and 4:13-16 name the church here.

cl_laod_fountain.c: A monumental fountain at the corner of Syria Street and Stadium Street in Laodicea, dedicated to the emperor Caracalla (AD 212-217), long after Paul. Laodicea had no good spring of its own and brought its water in by pipe.
cl_laod_fountain.d: A monumental fountain at the corner of Syria Street and Stadium Street in Laodicea, dedicated to the emperor Caracalla (AD 212-217), long after Paul. Laodicea had no good spring of its own and brought its water in by pipe.

cl_chonae.c: Archangel Michael and the monk Archippus at Chonae, an Orthodox icon of the first half of the 12th century. The story comes from Chonai, the town that grew up near Colossae, more than a thousand years after Paul. The monk shares a name with the Archippus of Colossians 4:17, but the link is only the name.

cl_ephesus_prison.f: The prison of Saint Paul in Ephesus, according to tradition - Bruyn Cornelis De - 1714.jpg
cl_ephesus_prison.c: The so-called Prison of Paul at Ephesus, drawn by Cornelis de Bruyn and published in 1714. The tower is a later tradition. The letters say only that Paul was in chains (Colossians 4:3, 4:18), not where.

th_galerius.f: Thessaloniki Arch of Galerius from the west.jpg
th_galerius.c: The Arch of Galerius, built about AD 300 across the main east-west street of Thessaloniki, on the line of the Via Egnatia. It is some 250 years later than Paul, but Amphipolis and Apollonia (Acts 17:1) lay on the same road.
th_galerius.d: The Arch of Galerius, built about AD 300 across the main east-west street of Thessaloniki, on the line of the Via Egnatia. It is some 250 years later than Paul, but Amphipolis and Apollonia (Acts 17:1) lay on the same road.

th_rotunda.f: Thessaloniki Saint George Rotunda from the Arch of Galerius.jpg
th_rotunda.c: The Rotunda, a round Roman building put up under Galerius about AD 300 and later used as a church and a mosque, seen from the Arch of Galerius. Like the arch, it is far later than Paul. Little of the first-century city is visible under modern Thessaloniki.
th_rotunda.d: The Rotunda, a round Roman building put up under Galerius about AD 300 and later used as a church and a mosque, seen from the Arch of Galerius. Like the arch, it is far later than Paul. Little of the first-century city is visible under modern Thessaloniki.

th_milestones.f: Roman milliaria - Archaeological Museum, Thessaloniki. Photo by Giovanni Dall'Orto, Apr 17 2024.jpg
th_milestones.c: Roman milestones in the courtyard of the Archaeological Museum of Thessaloniki. Roman roads such as the Via Egnatia, which ran through Thessalonica, were marked with stones like these.
th_milestones.d: Roman milestones in the courtyard of the Archaeological Museum of Thessaloniki. Roman roads such as the Via Egnatia, which ran through Thessalonica, were marked with stones like these.

th_aphrodeisia.f: Thessaloniki Archaeological Museum Funerary relief of Aphrodeisia.jpg
th_aphrodeisia.c: A funerary relief for a woman named Aphrodeisia, found in Thessaloniki and dated to the late 1st century BC or early 1st century AD, so about Paul's time. First Thessalonians 4:13 was written to people who buried their own dead in a city like this.
th_aphrodeisia.d: A funerary relief for a woman named Aphrodeisia, found in Thessaloniki and dated to the late 1st century BC or early 1st century AD, so about Paul's time. First Thessalonians 4:13 was written to people who buried their own dead in a city like this.

th_stoa.c: The Stoa of Attalos, a long colonnade on the east side of the Athenian Agora, built in the 2nd century BC and rebuilt in the 1950s. Acts 17:17 says Paul reasoned in the marketplace every day while he waited in Athens, and in 1 Thessalonians 3:1 he says he was left behind there alone.
th_stoa.d: The Stoa of Attalos, a long colonnade on the east side of the Athenian Agora, built in the 2nd century BC and rebuilt in the 1950s. Acts 17:17 says Paul reasoned in the marketplace every day while he waited in Athens, and in 1 Thessalonians 3:1 he says he was left behind there alone.

th_caligula.f: Cuirassed bust of Caligula, found in Rome, AD 37-41, Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, Copenhagen (13192017765) cropped.jpg
th_caligula.c: A cuirassed bust of the emperor Caligula (ruled AD 37-41), now in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek. About AD 40 he ordered a statue of himself set up in the Jerusalem Temple, and his death in AD 41 stopped it (Josephus, Antiquities 18). Some readers think this memory lies behind 2 Thessalonians 2:4. Paul does not mention him.
th_caligula.d: A cuirassed bust of the emperor Caligula (ruled AD 37-41), now in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek. About AD 40 he ordered a statue of himself set up in the Jerusalem Temple, and his death in AD 41 stopped it (Josephus, Antiquities 18). Some readers think this memory lies behind 2 Thessalonians 2:4. Paul does not mention him.

th_antiochus.c: A silver tetradrachm of Antiochus IV (ruled 175-164 BC), struck at Antioch. His coins call him Theos Epiphanes, "God Manifest". In 167 BC he set up an altar to Zeus in the Jerusalem Temple, the "abomination of desolation" of Daniel 11:31. Paul's words in 2 Thessalonians 2:4 resemble Daniel 11:36-37, but he does not name Antiochus.
th_antiochus.d: A silver tetradrachm of Antiochus IV (ruled 175-164 BC), struck at Antioch. His coins call him Theos Epiphanes, "God Manifest". In 167 BC he set up an altar to Zeus in the Jerusalem Temple, the "abomination of desolation" of Daniel 11:31. Paul's words in 2 Thessalonians 2:4 resemble Daniel 11:36-37, but he does not name Antiochus.

th_ara_pacis.c: The Ara Pacis Augustae, the Altar of Augustan Peace, dedicated in Rome in 9 BC. It shows how the empire presented itself as the giver of peace. Whether "peace and security" in 1 Thessalonians 5:3 echoes that message, or the prophets' warnings about false peace (Jeremiah 6:14), is debated.
th_ara_pacis.d: The Ara Pacis Augustae, the Altar of Augustan Peace, dedicated in Rome in 9 BC. It shows how the empire presented itself as the giver of peace. Whether "peace and security" in 1 Thessalonians 5:3 echoes that message, or the prophets' warnings about false peace (Jeremiah 6:14), is debated.

th_temple_model.c: A model of Herod's Temple in the Holyland Model of Jerusalem, now at the Israel Museum. Second Thessalonians 2:4 speaks of the man of lawlessness taking his seat "in the temple of God". Readers differ on whether that means the Jerusalem Temple, the church, or something else.
th_temple_model.d: A model of Herod's Temple in the Holyland Model of Jerusalem, now at the Israel Museum. Second Thessalonians 2:4 speaks of the man of lawlessness taking his seat "in the temple of God". Readers differ on whether that means the Jerusalem Temple, the church, or something else.

th_hallaton.c: A Roman cavalry helmet of the 1st century AD, found with the Hallaton treasure in Leicestershire, England. Paul pictures "the hope of salvation" as a helmet (1 Thessalonians 5:8).
th_hallaton.d: A Roman cavalry helmet of the 1st century AD, found with the Hallaton treasure in Leicestershire, England. Paul pictures "the hope of salvation" as a helmet (1 Thessalonians 5:8).

th_hypnos.f: Euphronios - ARV 14 extra - Hypnos and Thanatos carrying the body of Sarpedon - warriors arming - Cerveteri MAN - 01.jpg
th_hypnos.c: An Athenian red-figure vase of the late 6th century BC, attributed to Euphronios, now at Cerveteri. Sleep (Hypnos) and Death (Thanatos) carry off the dead warrior Sarpedon. Greeks spoke of sleep and death as brothers. Paul's "fall asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:13-15) comes with the promise of waking.
th_hypnos.d: An Athenian red-figure vase of the late 6th century BC, attributed to Euphronios, now at Cerveteri. Sleep (Hypnos) and Death (Thanatos) carry off the dead warrior Sarpedon. Greeks spoke of sleep and death as brothers. Paul's "fall asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:13-15) comes with the promise of waking.

th_resurrection.f: Luca Signorelli - Resurrection of the Flesh - WGA21214.jpg
th_resurrection.c: The Resurrection of the Flesh, a fresco by Luca Signorelli in Orvieto Cathedral (about 1500). First Thessalonians 4:16 says "the dead in Christ will rise first."

th_antichrist.f: Luca Signorelli - Sermon and Deeds of the Antichrist - WGA21202.jpg
th_antichrist.c: The Sermon and Deeds of the Antichrist, a fresco by Luca Signorelli in Orvieto Cathedral (about 1500). Later Christians linked "the man of lawlessness" (2 Thessalonians 2:3) with the figure called Antichrist, but Paul does not use that name here, and readers disagree about whom he means.

th_lystra.f: Monnaie - Bronze, Lystra, Lycaonie, Auguste - btv1b8516625b (1 of 2).jpg
th_lystra.c: A bronze coin of Lystra from the reign of Augustus, who made it a Roman colony about 25 BC, in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Acts 16:1-3 places Timothy at Lystra, and Paul took him along. In 1 Thessalonians 3:2 Paul calls him "our brother and God's coworker" and sends him to the church.
th_lystra.d: A bronze coin of Lystra from the reign of Augustus, who made it a Roman colony about 25 BC, in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Acts 16:1-3 places Timothy at Lystra, and Paul took him along. In 1 Thessalonians 3:2 Paul calls him "our brother and God's coworker" and sends him to the church.
th_lystra.a: Bibliothèque nationale de France, public domain

th_shops.f: The west shops in the Roman forum of Corinth on 6 April 2019.jpg
th_shops.c: The row of shops on the west side of the Roman forum at Corinth. Paul says he worked "night and day" among the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8). Acts 18:3 says he worked as a tentmaker in Corinth, but nothing marks his shop.
th_shops.d: The row of shops on the west side of the Roman forum at Corinth. Paul says he worked "night and day" among the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8). Acts 18:3 says he worked as a tentmaker in Corinth, but nothing marks his shop.

th_potter.f: Penteskouphia tablet - potters at a kiln (Berlin Antikensammlung F 811).jpg
th_potter.c: A clay plaque from Penteskouphia, near Corinth, showing potters at a kiln (about the 6th century BC). It is older than Paul, but it shows the hand trades of a Greek city, the world of the work Paul describes in 1 Thessalonians 2:9 and 4:11.
th_potter.n: Potters at work, Corinthian clay plaque
th_potter.d: A clay plaque from Penteskouphia, near Corinth, showing potters at a kiln (about the 6th century BC). It is older than Paul, but it shows the hand trades of a Greek city, the world of the work Paul describes in 1 Thessalonians 2:9 and 4:11.
th_potter.a: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, Antikensammlung, CC BY-SA 4.0

th_papyrus.f: P. Oxy. VI 932 private letter on papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, written in a Greek hand of the second century AD.jpg
th_papyrus.c: A private letter on papyrus from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, written in the 2nd century AD, after Paul's time. Letters of the period opened with the sender, the reader and a greeting, as 1 Thessalonians 1:1 does: "Paul, Silvanus and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians."
