th_papyrus.d: A private letter on papyrus from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, written in the 2nd century AD, after Paul's time. Letters of the period opened with the sender, the reader and a greeting, as 1 Thessalonians 1:1 does: "Paul, Silvanus and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians."
th_papyrus.a: Spurlock Museum, University of Illinois, public domain

th_bema.c: The bema, a raised platform in Corinth's forum where officials judged cases. Acts 18:5 says Silas and Timothy rejoined Paul in Corinth, and in 1 Thessalonians 3:6 Paul says Timothy had just come back with good news. Most readers think the letter was written there soon after.
th_bema.d: The bema, a raised platform in Corinth's forum where officials judged cases. Acts 18:5 says Silas and Timothy rejoined Paul in Corinth, and in 1 Thessalonians 3:6 Paul says Timothy had just come back with good news. Most readers think the letter was written there soon after.

th_lorica.c: Remains and a modern reconstruction of lorica segmentata, the segmented plate armor of Roman legionaries, from the Corbridge hoard in northern England. Paul pictures faith and love as a breastplate (1 Thessalonians 5:8). Plate armor like this came into use in his time.
th_lorica.d: Remains and a modern reconstruction of lorica segmentata, the segmented plate armor of Roman legionaries, from the Corbridge hoard in northern England. Paul pictures faith and love as a breastplate (1 Thessalonians 5:8). Plate armor like this came into use in his time.

th_claudius.f: Bust of the Roman Emperor Claudius, 37-64 CE. Marble. From Acerra near Formia, Italy. Altes Museum, Berlin.jpg
th_claudius.c: A marble bust of the emperor Claudius (ruled AD 41-54), emperor when Paul wrote these letters. Some early readers thought the restrainer of 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7 was Roman rule. Others proposed the preaching of the gospel, the Spirit or an angel. Paul does not say.
th_claudius.n: Bust of Claudius, Altes Museum, Berlin
th_claudius.d: A marble bust of the emperor Claudius (ruled AD 41-54), emperor when Paul wrote these letters. Some early readers thought the restrainer of 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7 was Roman rule. Others proposed the preaching of the gospel, the Spirit or an angel. Paul does not say.
th_claudius.a: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin, CC BY-SA 4.0

th_columbarium.f: Interieur van het columbarium van de Vigna Codini Columbaria Tomb of “The officers of Ceasar's household” (titel op object), RP-F-2001-7-164-2.jpg
th_columbarium.c: A heliogravure of the interior of a columbarium, a Roman tomb with niches for urns, at the Vigna Codini (about 1867-77). Many in the Roman world ended with a niche and a short inscription. Paul does not want the Thessalonians to grieve "as the rest do who have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
th_columbarium.n: Columbarium at the Vigna Codini, Rome
th_columbarium.d: A heliogravure of the interior of a columbarium, a Roman tomb with niches for urns, at the Vigna Codini (about 1867-77). Many in the Roman world ended with a niche and a short inscription. Paul does not want the Thessalonians to grieve "as the rest do who have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

th_domitilla.c: A gallery of the catacomb of Domitilla in Rome. The catacombs date from about AD 200 on, long after Paul, but their burial inscriptions often say "in peace" and speak of the dead as sleeping, as 1 Thessalonians 4 does.
th_domitilla.d: A gallery of the catacomb of Domitilla in Rome. The catacombs date from about AD 200 on, long after Paul, but their burial inscriptions often say "in peace" and speak of the dead as sleeping, as 1 Thessalonians 4 does.

th_trumpet.c: A stone from the southwest corner of the Temple Mount carved in Hebrew "to the place of trumpeting." Priests sounded trumpets at the Temple. Paul says the Lord will come down with "the trumpet of God" (1 Thessalonians 4:16), a picture drawn from Exodus 19:16 and Isaiah 27:13.
th_trumpet.d: A stone from the southwest corner of the Temple Mount carved in Hebrew "to the place of trumpeting." Priests sounded trumpets at the Temple. Paul says the Lord will come down with "the trumpet of God" (1 Thessalonians 4:16), a picture drawn from Exodus 19:16 and Isaiah 27:13.

th_writing.f: Valentin de Boulogne - Saint Paul Writing His Epistles - BF.1991.4 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg
th_writing.c: Saint Paul Writing His Epistles, by Valentin de Boulogne (about 1618-20). First Thessalonians opens with three names, "Paul, Silvanus and Timothy" (1:1), and is probably the earliest of Paul's letters that survive.
th_writing.a: Valentin de Boulogne (c. 1618-20), Museum of Fine Arts, Boston

th_desk.f: Saint Paul at his Writing-Desk, by Rembrandt.jpg
th_desk.c: Saint Paul at his Writing Desk, by Rembrandt (about 1629-30). In 2 Thessalonians 3:17 Paul says, "I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand," and calls it the sign in every letter of his.

th_lydia.f: Paulus bekeert de vrouwen van Filippi Handelingen van de apostelen (serietitel) Acta Apostolorum (serietitel), RP-P-OB-6565.jpg
th_lydia.c: Paul speaks to the women at Philippi (Acts 16:13-15), from a 16th-century print series on Acts. In 1 Thessalonians 2:2 Paul recalls that he had "suffered and been mistreated in Philippi" before he came to Thessalonica.
th_lydia.a: Print series on Acts (16th c.), Rijksmuseum, CC0

th_athens.f: V&A - Raphael, St Paul Preaching in Athens (1515).jpg
th_athens.c: St Paul Preaching in Athens, Raphael's 1515 cartoon for a tapestry. First Thessalonians 3:1 says Paul was "left behind at Athens alone" and sent Timothy to Thessalonica from there.

th_sarto.f: La Charité - Andrea del Sarto - Musée du Louvre Peintures INV 712.jpg
th_sarto.c: Charity, by Andrea del Sarto (1518), a woman with children. In 1 Thessalonians 2:7 Paul says, "we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children."

th_arnolfini.c: The Arnolfini Portrait, by Jan van Eyck (1434), a married couple in their home. It comes from a different time and place. First Thessalonians 4:3-8 asks believers to live in holiness and honor in sexual matters and not to wrong a brother.

th_bonheur.f: Rosa Bonheur - Ploughing in Nevers - Google Art Project.jpg
th_bonheur.c: Ploughing in the Nivernais, by Rosa Bonheur (1849). Paul tells the Thessalonians to "work with your hands" and to behave properly toward outsiders (1 Thessalonians 4:11-12).

th_michelangelo.c: The Last Judgment, by Michelangelo (1536-41), in the Sistine Chapel. First Thessalonians 5:2 says the day of the Lord comes "like a thief in the night," and 2 Thessalonians 1:7-10 pictures the Lord Jesus revealed from heaven. Michelangelo's scene blends many biblical passages.

th_ascension.f: Rembrandt The Ascension 1636 Oil on canvas Alte Pinakothek Munich Germany.jpg
th_ascension.c: The Ascension, by Rembrandt (1636), in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich. Second Thessalonians 1:7 says the Lord Jesus will be revealed "from heaven with His mighty angels." In Acts 1:11 the angels say He will come in the same way He went.

th_rublev.f: Andrey Rublev - Св. Троица - Google Art Project.jpg
th_rublev.c: The Trinity, an icon by Andrei Rublev (early 15th century). First Thessalonians closes with commands to rejoice, pray and not quench the Spirit (5:16-19), and a blessing: "May the God of peace Himself sanctify you" (5:23).

th_anastasis.c: The Anastasis fresco in the Chora Church in Istanbul, painted about 1320. Christ pulls Adam and Eve out of their tombs. First Thessalonians 4:14 rests the hope of the dead on Jesus' own death and rising.

ti_durer.f: Albrecht Dürer, Adam and Eve, 1504, NGA 6610.jpg
ti_durer.c: Adam and Eve, an engraving by Albrecht Dürer (1504). First Timothy 2:13-14 points back to Adam being formed first and to Eve being deceived. How Paul uses that in 2:12-15 is one of the most debated questions in the letter.
ti_durer.a: Albrecht Dürer (1504), National Gallery of Art, Washington

ti_celsus.c: The façade of the Library of Celsus at Ephesus, built in the early 2nd century AD, decades after Paul's time. It shows the wealth and pride of the city where, according to 1 Timothy 1:3, Paul asked Timothy to stay on.
ti_celsus.d: The façade of the Library of Celsus at Ephesus, built in the early 2nd century AD, decades after Paul's time. It shows the wealth and pride of the city where, according to 1 Timothy 1:3, Paul asked Timothy to stay on.

ti_plancia.f: Statue of Plancia Magna, a great benefactress of Perge, 2nd century AD, Antalya Museum, Turkey.jpg
ti_plancia.c: A statue of Plancia Magna, a wealthy woman of Perge who paid for public buildings in the 2nd century AD, in the Antalya Museum. Perge is not Ephesus and she lived after Paul, but she shows that women in the cities of Asia Minor could hold civic honors and fund public works. That is part of the background scholars raise for 1 Timothy 2:9-10 and 5:10.
ti_plancia.d: A statue of Plancia Magna, a wealthy woman of Perge who paid for public buildings in the 2nd century AD, in the Antalya Museum. Perge is not Ephesus and she lived after Paul, but she shows that women in the cities of Asia Minor could hold civic honors and fund public works. That is part of the background scholars raise for 1 Timothy 2:9-10 and 5:10.

ti_flavian.f: Portrait bust of a woman with Flavian hairstyle, Apollonia, Albania.jpg
ti_flavian.c: A marble portrait of a Roman woman with the tall, built-up hairstyle of the Flavian period (about AD 70-100), found at Apollonia in Albania. It is a little later than Paul, but it shows the kind of elaborate hairdo that fits the "braided hair" of 1 Timothy 2:9.
ti_flavian.n: Roman woman with a tall hairstyle
ti_flavian.d: A marble portrait of a Roman woman with the tall, built-up hairstyle of the Flavian period (about AD 70-100), found at Apollonia in Albania. It is a little later than Paul, but it shows the kind of elaborate hairdo that fits the "braided hair" of 1 Timothy 2:9.

ti_dura_plan.c: A plan of the house church at Dura-Europos in Syria, a private house remodeled for Christian use in the AD 230s. It is nearly two centuries after 1 Timothy, but it shows how an ordinary household could become a meeting place, in the world of the "household of God" (3:15).
ti_dura_plan.n: Plan of the house church at Dura-Europos
ti_dura_plan.d: A plan of the house church at Dura-Europos in Syria, a private house remodeled for Christian use in the AD 230s. It is nearly two centuries after 1 Timothy, but it shows how an ordinary household could become a meeting place, in the world of the "household of God" (3:15).

ti_anna.f: Rembrandt The Prophetess Anna in the Temple.jpg
ti_anna.c: The Prophetess Anna, by Rembrandt (17th century). Luke 2:36-37 describes Anna, an elderly widow who stayed in the temple worshiping night and day. First Timothy 5:5 describes a widow left alone who sets her hope on God and continues night and day in prayer.

ti_bible.c: Still Life with Open Bible, by Vincent van Gogh (1885). First Timothy 4:13 tells Timothy to give his attention to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation and to teaching. The painting is from the Netherlands, long after Paul, but it shows the book at the center of a community's life.
ti_bible.a: Vincent van Gogh (1885), Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam

ti_richfool.f: Rembrandt - The Parable of the Rich Fool.jpg
ti_richfool.c: The Parable of the Rich Fool, by Rembrandt (1627): an old man checks his money by candlelight (Luke 12:16-21). First Timothy 6:9-10 warns about the desire to be rich, and 6:17-19 tells the rich not to put their hope in wealth.

ti_timlois.c: Timothy and Lois, by Willem Drost (about 1650), in the Hermitage. Second Timothy 1:5 names Timothy's grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice as the source of his faith, and 1 Timothy 1:2 calls him Paul's "true child in the faith."

ti_lawrence.c: Saint Lawrence Distributing Alms, a fresco by Fra Angelico (1447-49). Lawrence was a deacon of Rome who died in AD 258, long after Paul, and later Christians remembered deacons for caring for the poor. First Timothy 3:8-13 names the character deacons must have but does not list their duties.

ti_sin12.c: A page of Codex Sinaiticus, a Greek Bible copied in the 4th century AD, with 1 Timothy 1:1-2:12. It is one of the oldest surviving copies of the letter.
ti_sin12.d: A page of Codex Sinaiticus, a Greek Bible copied in the 4th century AD, with 1 Timothy 1:1-2:12. It is one of the oldest surviving copies of the letter.

ti_sin69.f: End of 1 Timothy and beginning of 2 Timothy in Sinaiticus.jpg
ti_sin69.c: The end of 1 Timothy (6:9-21) and the start of 2 Timothy in Codex Sinaiticus. The scribes wrote in capital letters with no gaps between words, so a reader had to know a text well to read it aloud, as Timothy is told to do in 4:13.
ti_sin69.n: End of 1 Timothy in Codex Sinaiticus
ti_sin69.d: The end of 1 Timothy (6:9-21) and the start of 2 Timothy in Codex Sinaiticus. The scribes wrote in capital letters with no gaps between words, so a reader had to know a text well to read it aloud, as Timothy is told to do in 4:13.

ti_sin316.c: The lines of Codex Sinaiticus that contain 1 Timothy 3:16, "the mystery of godliness." Many scholars think the verse quotes an early Christian hymn. Manuscripts differ on its opening word ("who," "God" or "which").
ti_sin316.d: The lines of Codex Sinaiticus that contain 1 Timothy 3:16, "the mystery of godliness." Many scholars think the verse quotes an early Christian hymn. Manuscripts differ on its opening word ("who," "God" or "which").

ti_pliny.c: A statue of Pliny the Younger on the façade of Como cathedral, carved in the late 15th century. About AD 112, as governor of Bithynia, Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan that Christians sang a hymn to Christ as to a god (Letters 10.96). It is a later witness to the kind of hymn singing many see behind 1 Timothy 3:16.
ti_pliny.n: Statue of Pliny the Younger, Como
ti_pliny.d: A statue of Pliny the Younger on the façade of Como cathedral, carved in the late 15th century. About AD 112, as governor of Bithynia, Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan that Christians sang a hymn to Christ as to a god (Letters 10.96). It is a later witness to the kind of hymn singing many see behind 1 Timothy 3:16.

ti_augustus.c: The Augustus of Prima Porta, a marble statue of the first emperor (ruled 27 BC-AD 14), found near Rome. His marriage laws of 18 BC and AD 9 rewarded marriage and children and pressed widows to marry again. Some scholars see them behind 1 Timothy 5:11-14, where Paul urges younger widows to marry.
ti_augustus.d: The Augustus of Prima Porta, a marble statue of the first emperor (ruled 27 BC-AD 14), found near Rome. His marriage laws of 18 BC and AD 9 rewarded marriage and children and pressed widows to marry again. Some scholars see them behind 1 Timothy 5:11-14, where Paul urges younger widows to marry.

ti_amphorae.f: Roman amphorae for wine with stamps.jpg
ti_amphorae.c: Roman wine amphorae with makers' stamps, in the Historical Museum in Bratislava. Wine was an ordinary drink of the Mediterranean world, usually mixed with water. In 1 Timothy 5:23 Paul tells Timothy to stop drinking only water and to use a little wine for his stomach and frequent illnesses.
ti_amphorae.d: Roman wine amphorae with makers' stamps, in the Historical Museum in Bratislava. Wine was an ordinary drink of the Mediterranean world, usually mixed with water. In 1 Timothy 5:23 Paul tells Timothy to stop drinking only water and to use a little wine for his stomach and frequent illnesses.

ti_stadium.c: The ancient stadium at Ephesus, where athletic contests were held in the Roman period. Paul uses training as a picture in 1 Timothy 4:7-8: physical training is of some value, but godliness is valuable in every way.
ti_stadium.d: The ancient stadium at Ephesus, where athletic contests were held in the Roman period. Paul uses training as a picture in 1 Timothy 4:7-8: physical training is of some value, but godliness is valuable in every way.

ti_onesimos.f: Funerary relief from the monument of Onessimos and his family (8726699040).jpg
ti_onesimos.c: A funerary relief of the Roman period for Onesimos, a slave who managed the household of Aelius Menogenes, an official in the province of Macedonia, shown with his family. It shows that a slave could hold a position of trust in a Roman household. First Timothy 6:1-2 speaks to slaves and to masters who are believers.
ti_onesimos.n: Relief of Onesimos, a slave household manager
ti_onesimos.d: A funerary relief of the Roman period for Onesimos, a slave who managed the household of Aelius Menogenes, an official in the province of Macedonia, shown with his family. It shows that a slave could hold a position of trust in a Roman household. First Timothy 6:1-2 speaks to slaves and to masters who are believers.

ti_eph_theatre.c: The Great Theater at Ephesus, which held some 24,000 people. Acts 19:29-41 tells of the riot there, and 1 Timothy 1:3 says Paul left Timothy at Ephesus to deal with false teaching.
ti_eph_theatre.d: The Great Theater at Ephesus, which held some 24,000 people. Acts 19:29-41 tells of the riot there, and 1 Timothy 1:3 says Paul left Timothy at Ephesus to deal with false teaching.

ti_artemis_temple.c: The single reconstructed column of the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the great temples of the ancient world. The church that 1 Timothy 1:3 places at Ephesus lived in a city where Artemis was the chief goddess (Acts 19:27-28). The letter calls the church the "pillar and foundation of the truth" (3:15).
ti_artemis_temple.d: The single reconstructed column of the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the great temples of the ancient world. The church that 1 Timothy 1:3 places at Ephesus lived in a city where Artemis was the chief goddess (Acts 19:27-28). The letter calls the church the "pillar and foundation of the truth" (3:15).

ti_artemis_statue.f: Artemis of Ephesus statue Ephesus Museum 2024.jpeg
ti_artemis_statue.c: A statue of Artemis of Ephesus in the Ephesus Museum, with the rows of rounded shapes on her chest that scholars still explain in different ways. Some suggest her cult shaped the problems behind 1 Timothy 2:9-15, but the letter never names her, so that remains a suggestion.
ti_artemis_statue.d: A statue of Artemis of Ephesus in the Ephesus Museum, with the rows of rounded shapes on her chest that scholars still explain in different ways. Some suggest her cult shaped the problems behind 1 Timothy 2:9-15, but the letter never names her, so that remains a suggestion.

ti_terrace.c: The Terrace Houses on the hillside at Ephesus, wealthy Roman homes with mosaics and painted walls. Most of what survives is from the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD, later than Paul, but they show how the rich lived. First Timothy 6:17-19 speaks to those who are rich in the present age.
ti_terrace.d: The Terrace Houses on the hillside at Ephesus, wealthy Roman homes with mosaics and painted walls. Most of what survives is from the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD, later than Paul, but they show how the rich lived. First Timothy 6:17-19 speaks to those who are rich in the present age.

ti_harbor.c: The Harbor Street of Ephesus, which ran from the theater to the harbor and carried the traffic of one of the busiest cities of Roman Asia. Its surviving colonnades are mostly later than Paul. First Timothy 6:5-10 warns against treating godliness as a way to make money.
ti_harbor.d: The Harbor Street of Ephesus, which ran from the theater to the harbor and carried the traffic of one of the busiest cities of Roman Asia. Its surviving colonnades are mostly later than Paul. First Timothy 6:5-10 warns against treating godliness as a way to make money.

ti_slave_collar.f: Inscribed bronze slave collar (Rome MNR 65043; CIL XV 7194).jpg
ti_slave_collar.c: An inscribed bronze collar of a runaway slave, Museo Nazionale Romano, Rome. Such collars date mostly to the 4th century, well after Paul, but they show the legal power masters held over slaves, the world that 1 Timothy 6:1-2 speaks into.
ti_slave_collar.d: An inscribed bronze collar of a runaway slave, Museo Nazionale Romano, Rome. Such collars date mostly to the 4th century, well after Paul, but they show the legal power masters held over slaves, the world that 1 Timothy 6:1-2 speaks into.

ti_delphi_wall.c: The polygonal wall below the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, covered with inscriptions. Many record slaves "sold" to Apollo to win their freedom. It shows how formal and public freeing a slave could be, the setting for 1 Timothy 6:1-2, which says nothing about freeing slaves.
ti_delphi_wall.d: The polygonal wall below the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, covered with inscriptions. Many record slaves "sold" to Apollo to win their freedom. It shows how formal and public freeing a slave could be, the setting for 1 Timothy 6:1-2, which says nothing about freeing slaves.

ti_pilate.c: The Pilate Stone, a 1st-century inscription naming Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judea, found at Caesarea. First Timothy 6:13 says Christ Jesus gave His good confession before Pontius Pilate.
ti_pilate.d: The Pilate Stone, a 1st-century inscription naming Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judea, found at Caesarea. First Timothy 6:13 says Christ Jesus gave His good confession before Pontius Pilate.

ti_pilatecoin.c: A bronze coin minted in Judea under Pontius Pilate, who governed from about AD 26 to 36. His name in 1 Timothy 6:13 dates the "good confession" to a real governor in a real year.
ti_pilatecoin.d: A bronze coin minted in Judea under Pontius Pilate, who governed from about AD 26 to 36. His name in 1 Timothy 6:13 dates the "good confession" to a real governor in a real year.

ti_nero_aureus.f: MBALyon2018 - Expo Claude - Aureus de Neron 54 ap J-C.jpg
ti_nero_aureus.c: A gold aureus struck in AD 54 for the new emperor Nero. If Paul wrote 1 Timothy near the end of his life, Nero (ruled AD 54-68) was the "king" for whom 1 Timothy 2:1-2 asks believers to pray.
ti_nero_aureus.d: A gold aureus struck in AD 54 for the new emperor Nero. If Paul wrote 1 Timothy near the end of his life, Nero (ruled AD 54-68) was the "king" for whom 1 Timothy 2:1-2 asks believers to pray.

ti_priene.c: The Priene inscription (about 9 BC), which calls the birthday of Augustus the beginning of good news for the world. Rulers were also called "savior." First Timothy calls God our Savior (1:1; 2:3; 4:10).
ti_priene.d: The Priene inscription (about 9 BC), which calls the birthday of Augustus the beginning of good news for the world. Rulers were also called "savior." First Timothy calls God our Savior (1:1; 2:3; 4:10).

ti_lystra_coin.f: Monnaie - Bronze, Lystra, Lycaonie, Auguste - btv1b8516625b (1 of 2).jpg
ti_lystra_coin.c: A bronze coin of Lystra from the reign of Augustus, who made it a Roman colony about 25 BC. Acts 16:1-3 places Timothy at Lystra, and 1 Timothy 4:12 asks that no one despise his youth.
ti_lystra_coin.d: A bronze coin of Lystra from the reign of Augustus, who made it a Roman colony about 25 BC. Acts 16:1-3 places Timothy at Lystra, and 1 Timothy 4:12 asks that no one despise his youth.
ti_lystra_coin.a: Bibliothèque nationale de France, public domain

ti_philippi.c: The forum of Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia (Acts 16:12). First Timothy 1:3 says Paul went on to Macedonia after leaving Timothy at Ephesus. The letter does not name the city, so Philippi is only a pin on the map.
ti_philippi.d: The forum of Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia (Acts 16:12). First Timothy 1:3 says Paul went on to Macedonia after leaving Timothy at Ephesus. The letter does not name the city, so Philippi is only a pin on the map.

ti_straight.f: Damascus Straight Street and East Gate 8193.jpg
ti_straight.c: The main east-west street of Roman Damascus, the "Street called Straight" of Acts 9:11, with the Roman east gate. In 1 Timothy 1:12-16 Paul looks back on his turn from blasphemer and persecutor to apostle, the event Acts 9 places near Damascus.
ti_straight.d: The main east-west street of Roman Damascus, the "Street called Straight" of Acts 9:11, with the Roman east gate. In 1 Timothy 1:12-16 Paul looks back on his turn from blasphemer and persecutor to apostle, the event Acts 9 places near Damascus.

ti_miletus.c: The theater at Miletus, the port where Paul met the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:17-38) and called them overseers (20:28). The present Roman theater is later than Paul. First Timothy 3 and 5:17-22 deal with the same kind of leaders.
ti_miletus.d: The theater at Miletus, the port where Paul met the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:17-38) and called them overseers (20:28). The present Roman theater is later than Paul. First Timothy 3 and 5:17-22 deal with the same kind of leaders.

ti_orans.f: Consecrated Virgin, praying with Orans position, wearing dalmatic, tunic, and veil, from the Catacomb of Priscilla, 3rd century AD cropped.jpg
ti_orans.c: A woman at prayer with arms raised, painted in the Catacomb of Priscilla in Rome in the 3rd century. Standing with raised hands was the usual way to pray, the posture behind "lifting up holy hands" in 1 Timothy 2:8.
ti_orans.n: Woman at prayer, Catacomb of Priscilla
ti_orans.d: A woman at prayer with arms raised, painted in the Catacomb of Priscilla in Rome in the 3rd century. Standing with raised hands was the usual way to pray, the posture behind "lifting up holy hands" in 1 Timothy 2:8.
ti_orans.a: Painting from the 3rd century, photographed by Joseph Wilpert, public domain

ti_isaiah.c: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (about 125-100 BC). Scripture was read aloud to groups from scrolls like this. First Timothy 4:13 tells Timothy to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture.
ti_isaiah.d: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (about 125-100 BC). Scripture was read aloud to groups from scrolls like this. First Timothy 4:13 tells Timothy to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture.

ti_runners.c: A Greek prize vase with a foot race, made about 530-520 BC (British Museum). Athletic training was a common picture of discipline, and Paul uses it in 1 Timothy 4:7-8.
ti_runners.d: A Greek prize vase with a foot race, made about 530-520 BC (British Museum). Athletic training was a common picture of discipline, and Paul uses it in 1 Timothy 4:7-8.
ti_runners.a: Attributed to the Euphiletos Painter (about 530-520 BC), British Museum

ti_dura.f: Christ Healing the Paralytic - Dura-Europos circa 232.jpg
ti_dura.c: Christ healing the paralytic, painted in the baptistery of the house church at Dura-Europos in Syria in the 3rd century, before the city fell in AD 256. It is far later than 1 Timothy, but it shows a household remodeled for Christian worship.
ti_dura.d: Christ healing the paralytic, painted in the baptistery of the house church at Dura-Europos in Syria in the 3rd century, before the city fell in AD 256. It is far later than 1 Timothy, but it shows a household remodeled for Christian worship.
ti_dura.a: Yale University Art Gallery, public domain

ti_conv.c: The Conversion of Saint Paul, by Caravaggio (about 1600). In 1 Timothy 1:13-16 Paul recalls that he had been a blasphemer and persecutor and was shown mercy.
ti_conv.a: Caravaggio (c. 1600), Santa Maria del Popolo, Rome

ti_ephesus_preach.f: Eustache Le Sueur - The Preaching of St Paul at Ephesus - WGA12613.jpg
ti_ephesus_preach.c: The Preaching of Saint Paul at Ephesus, by Eustache Le Sueur (17th century). Acts 19 and 20 say Paul spent about three years in Ephesus, and 1 Timothy 1:3 says he asked Timothy to stay on there.

ti_writing.f: Valentin de Boulogne - Saint Paul Writing His Epistles - BF.1991.4 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg
ti_writing.c: Saint Paul Writing His Epistles, by Valentin de Boulogne (about 1618-20). First Timothy opens with Paul's name and title and is addressed to one person, Timothy, though it was meant to be read where he served too.
ti_writing.a: Valentin de Boulogne (c. 1618-20), Museum of Fine Arts, Boston

ti_lorica.c: Remains and a reconstruction of lorica segmentata, the segmented plate armor of Roman legionaries, which came into use in the 1st century AD. Paul calls on Timothy to fight "the good fight" (1:18; 6:12), a soldier's and an athlete's picture.
ti_lorica.d: Remains and a reconstruction of lorica segmentata, the segmented plate armor of Roman legionaries, which came into use in the 1st century AD. Paul calls on Timothy to fight "the good fight" (1:18; 6:12), a soldier's and an athlete's picture.

ti_shipwreck.f: Laurent de La Hyre's Saint Paul Shipwrecked on Malta.jpg
ti_shipwreck.c: Saint Paul Shipwrecked on Malta, by Laurent de La Hyre (17th century). Paul knew the sea (Acts 27; 2 Corinthians 11:25), and in 1 Timothy 1:19 he uses shipwreck as a picture of some who have wrecked their faith.

t2_timlois.c: Timothy and Lois, by Willem Drost (about 1650), in the Hermitage. It is an imagined scene. Second Timothy 1:5 names Timothy's grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice as the first in whom his sincere faith lived.

t2_prison.f: 1627 Rembrandt Paulus im Gefängnis Staatsgalerie Stuttgart anagoria.JPG
t2_prison.c: Paul in Prison, by Rembrandt (1627), in the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart. It is an imagined scene, but 2 Timothy speaks of Paul in chains (1:16; 2:9) and asks for a cloak, scrolls and parchments (4:13).

t2_writing.f: Valentin de Boulogne - Saint Paul Writing His Epistles - BF.1991.4 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg
t2_writing.c: Saint Paul Writing His Epistles, by Valentin de Boulogne (about 1618-20). Second Timothy opens with Paul's name and title and is addressed to one person, Timothy, whom he calls his beloved child (1:1-2).
t2_writing.a: Valentin de Boulogne (c. 1618-20), Museum of Fine Arts, Boston

t2_plough.f: Rosa Bonheur - Ploughing in Nevers - Google Art Project.jpg
t2_plough.c: Ploughing in the Nivernais, by Rosa Bonheur (1849). The third picture in 2 Timothy 2:3-6 is the hardworking farmer, who should be the first to receive a share of the crops.

t2_magicians.f: The Rods of Moses and the Magicians Turned into Serpents (5752932).jpg
t2_magicians.c: The rods of Moses and the magicians turned into serpents (Exodus 7:10-12), by Gerard Hoet (1728). Exodus does not name Pharaoh's magicians. Second Timothy 3:8 calls them Jannes and Jambres.

t2_nero.c: A portrait of the emperor Nero (ruled AD 54-68). Later Christian writers place Paul's death under Nero. Second Timothy does not name the emperor, but it shows Paul in chains and expecting to die (4:6-8).

t2_sin.f: End of 1 Timothy and beginning of 2 Timothy in Sinaiticus.jpg
t2_sin.c: The end of 1 Timothy and the opening of 2 Timothy in Codex Sinaiticus, a Greek Bible copied in the 4th century AD. Second Timothy begins like an ordinary letter, with the sender, the reader and a greeting (1:1-2).
t2_sin.n: The start of 2 Timothy in Codex Sinaiticus
t2_sin.d: The end of 1 Timothy and the opening of 2 Timothy in Codex Sinaiticus, a Greek Bible copied in the 4th century AD. Second Timothy begins like an ordinary letter, with the sender, the reader and a greeting (1:1-2).

t2_mamertine.c: The Mamertine Prison (Carcer Tullianum) in Rome. Later tradition, not the New Testament, says Peter and Paul were held here. Second Timothy speaks of Paul in chains (1:16; 2:9) but does not name the prison.
t2_mamertine.d: The Mamertine Prison (Carcer Tullianum) in Rome. Later tradition, not the New Testament, says Peter and Paul were held here. Second Timothy speaks of Paul in chains (1:16; 2:9) but does not name the prison.

t2_lystra_coin.f: Monnaie - Bronze, Lystra, Lycaonie, Auguste - btv1b8516625b (1 of 2).jpg
t2_lystra_coin.c: A bronze coin of Lystra from the reign of Augustus, who made it a Roman colony about 25 BC. Timothy was a disciple at Lystra (Acts 16:1-2), and 2 Timothy 3:11 recalls what Paul suffered there.
t2_lystra_coin.d: A bronze coin of Lystra from the reign of Augustus, who made it a Roman colony about 25 BC. Timothy was a disciple at Lystra (Acts 16:1-2), and 2 Timothy 3:11 recalls what Paul suffered there.
t2_lystra_coin.a: Bibliothèque nationale de France, public domain

t2_eph_theatre.c: The Great Theater at Ephesus, which held some 24,000 people. Acts 19:29-41 tells of the riot there. Second Timothy 1:18 says Onesiphorus served at Ephesus, and 4:12 says Paul sent Tychicus there.
t2_eph_theatre.d: The Great Theater at Ephesus, which held some 24,000 people. Acts 19:29-41 tells of the riot there. Second Timothy 1:18 says Onesiphorus served at Ephesus, and 4:12 says Paul sent Tychicus there.

t2_aureus.f: MBALyon2018 - Expo Claude - Aureus de Neron 54 ap J-C.jpg
t2_aureus.c: A gold aureus struck in AD 54 for the new emperor Nero (ruled AD 54-68). Christian tradition places Paul's death in Nero's reign; 2 Timothy does not name the emperor.
t2_aureus.d: A gold aureus struck in AD 54 for the new emperor Nero (ruled AD 54-68). Christian tradition places Paul's death in Nero's reign; 2 Timothy does not name the emperor.

t2_lorica.c: Remains and a reconstruction of lorica segmentata, the segmented plate armor of Roman legionaries, which came into use in the 1st century AD. Paul asks Timothy to endure hardship like a good soldier (2 Timothy 2:3).
t2_lorica.d: Remains and a reconstruction of lorica segmentata, the segmented plate armor of Roman legionaries, which came into use in the 1st century AD. Paul asks Timothy to endure hardship like a good soldier (2 Timothy 2:3).

t2_diploma.c: A Roman bronze military diploma, about AD 149, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Diplomas like this were given to soldiers of auxiliary units and fleets on discharge and recorded a grant of Roman citizenship. This one is later than Paul. Second Timothy 2:4 says a soldier avoids civilian entanglements to please the one who enlisted him.
t2_diploma.d: A Roman bronze military diploma, about AD 149, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Diplomas like this were given to soldiers of auxiliary units and fleets on discharge and recorded a grant of Roman citizenship. This one is later than Paul. Second Timothy 2:4 says a soldier avoids civilian entanglements to please the one who enlisted him.
t2_diploma.a: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0

t2_runners.c: A Greek prize vase with a foot race, made about 530-520 BC (British Museum). Paul's athlete in 2 Timothy 2:5 is crowned only if he competes according to the rules.
t2_runners.d: A Greek prize vase with a foot race, made about 530-520 BC (British Museum). Paul's athlete in 2 Timothy 2:5 is crowned only if he competes according to the rules.
t2_runners.a: Attributed to the Euphiletos Painter (about 530-520 BC), British Museum

t2_stadium.c: The ancient stadium at Ephesus, where athletic contests were held in the Roman period. Paul uses the athlete (2 Timothy 2:5) and the finished race (4:7) as pictures of faithful service.
t2_stadium.d: The ancient stadium at Ephesus, where athletic contests were held in the Roman period. Paul uses the athlete (2 Timothy 2:5) and the finished race (4:7) as pictures of faithful service.

t2_terrace.c: The Terrace Houses on the hillside at Ephesus, wealthy Roman homes with mosaics and painted walls, mostly from the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD. Second Timothy 2:20 speaks of "a large house" with vessels of different kinds.
t2_terrace.d: The Terrace Houses on the hillside at Ephesus, wealthy Roman homes with mosaics and painted walls, mostly from the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD. Second Timothy 2:20 speaks of "a large house" with vessels of different kinds.

t2_silver.f: Roman Silver Treasure from Hildesheim, Germany (28702976576).jpg
t2_silver.c: Roman silver tableware from the Hildesheim Treasure, found in 1868 and now in the Altes Museum, Berlin. Second Timothy 2:20 says a large house has vessels of gold and silver as well as of wood and clay.
t2_silver.d: Roman silver tableware from the Hildesheim Treasure, found in 1868 and now in the Altes Museum, Berlin. Second Timothy 2:20 says a large house has vessels of gold and silver as well as of wood and clay.

t2_clay.f: Terra sigillata bowl, Roman, Italy or France, 1st century AD, terracotta - Spurlock Museum, UIUC - DSC05836.jpg
t2_clay.c: A Roman terra sigillata bowl of the 1st century AD, in the Spurlock Museum. This red-gloss pottery was common tableware. Second Timothy 2:20 says a large house has vessels of clay as well as of gold and silver.
t2_clay.d: A Roman terra sigillata bowl of the 1st century AD, in the Spurlock Museum. This red-gloss pottery was common tableware. Second Timothy 2:20 says a large house has vessels of clay as well as of gold and silver.

t2_pisidia.c: The theater at Pisidian Antioch near Yalvaç, Turkey. Second Timothy 3:11 names Antioch among the places where Paul was persecuted, and Acts 13:50 says he was driven out of the region.
t2_pisidia.d: The theater at Pisidian Antioch near Yalvaç, Turkey. Second Timothy 3:11 names Antioch among the places where Paul was persecuted, and Acts 13:50 says he was driven out of the region.

t2_konya.c: Konya in central Turkey, built over ancient Iconium, seen from the Seljuk Tower, with the Alaeddin Mosque on its hill. Second Timothy 3:11 names Iconium among the places where Paul suffered (Acts 14:1-6).
t2_konya.d: Konya in central Turkey, built over ancient Iconium, seen from the Seljuk Tower, with the Alaeddin Mosque on its hill. Second Timothy 3:11 names Iconium among the places where Paul suffered (Acts 14:1-6).

t2_kilistra.c: Kilistra, a rock-cut Byzantine town near the site of ancient Lystra in Turkey. At Lystra Paul was stoned and dragged out of the city (Acts 14:19), and he recalls it in 2 Timothy 3:11.
t2_kilistra.d: Kilistra, a rock-cut Byzantine town near the site of ancient Lystra in Turkey. At Lystra Paul was stoned and dragged out of the city (Acts 14:19), and he recalls it in 2 Timothy 3:11.

t2_isaiah.c: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (about 125-100 BC). Scripture was copied by hand on scrolls like this. Second Timothy 3:15-16 says Timothy has known the Holy Scriptures from infancy, and 4:13 asks for Paul's scrolls.
t2_isaiah.d: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (about 125-100 BC). Scripture was copied by hand on scrolls like this. Second Timothy 3:15-16 says Timothy has known the Holy Scriptures from infancy, and 4:13 asks for Paul's scrolls.

t2_basilica.f: Rome (IT), Sankt Paul vor den Mauern -- 2013 -- 3982.jpg
t2_basilica.c: The Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls in Rome, which tradition says stands over Paul's burial place. The first church here dates from the 4th century. Much of the present building was rebuilt after a fire in 1823. In 2 Timothy 4:6-8 Paul himself looks toward death.
t2_basilica.n: Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls, Rome
t2_basilica.d: The Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls in Rome, which tradition says stands over Paul's burial place. The first church here dates from the 4th century. Much of the present building was rebuilt after a fire in 1823. In 2 Timothy 4:6-8 Paul himself looks toward death.

t2_trefontane.c: The Tre Fontane Abbey south of Rome, where later tradition says Paul was beheaded. The New Testament does not describe his death, and the buildings here are medieval and later. In 2 Timothy 4:6 Paul says his departure is near.
t2_trefontane.d: The Tre Fontane Abbey south of Rome, where later tradition says Paul was beheaded. The New Testament does not describe his death, and the buildings here are medieval and later. In 2 Timothy 4:6 Paul says his departure is near.

t2_stylus.f: Replica of roman wax writing tablet with stylus.jpg
t2_stylus.c: A replica of a Roman wax writing tablet with a stylus. The sharp tip wrote and the flat end smoothed the wax. Paul's "parchments" (2 Timothy 4:13) were sheets of animal skin, but wax tablets were a common place for notes and drafts.
t2_stylus.n: Replica of a Roman wax writing tablet
t2_stylus.d: A replica of a Roman wax writing tablet with a stylus. The sharp tip wrote and the flat end smoothed the wax. Paul's "parchments" (2 Timothy 4:13) were sheets of animal skin, but wax tablets were a common place for notes and drafts.
t2_stylus.a: Peter van der Sluijs, CC BY-SA 3.0

t2_troas.c: Roman baths at Alexandria Troas, a later Roman building. In 2 Timothy 4:13 Paul asks Timothy to bring the cloak he left at Troas with Carpus.
t2_troas.d: Roman baths at Alexandria Troas, a later Roman building. In 2 Timothy 4:13 Paul asks Timothy to bring the cloak he left at Troas with Carpus.

t2_erastus.c: A paving stone at Corinth recording that Erastus laid the pavement at his own cost. Many link him to the Erastus of Romans 16:23. Second Timothy 4:20 says Erastus stayed at Corinth; the letter does not say whether this is the same man.
t2_erastus.d: A paving stone at Corinth recording that Erastus laid the pavement at his own cost. Many link him to the Erastus of Romans 16:23. Second Timothy 4:20 says Erastus stayed at Corinth; the letter does not say whether this is the same man.

t2_miletus.c: The theater at Miletus, the port where Paul met the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:17-38). Second Timothy 4:20 says Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus. The present Roman theater is later than Paul.
t2_miletus.d: The theater at Miletus, the port where Paul met the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:17-38). Second Timothy 4:20 says Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus. The present Roman theater is later than Paul.

t2_santaprisca.c: The church of Santa Prisca on the Aventine in Rome, built in the 5th century. A late tradition links the spot with Prisca and Aquila, greeted in 2 Timothy 4:19; no first-century proof of that has been found.
t2_santaprisca.d: The church of Santa Prisca on the Aventine in Rome, built in the 5th century. A late tradition links the spot with Prisca and Aquila, greeted in 2 Timothy 4:19; no first-century proof of that has been found.

t2_castra.c: Part of the brick wall of the Castra Praetoria, the barracks of the Praetorian Guard in Rome, built under the emperor Tiberius about AD 23. Second Timothy does not say who guarded Paul, but it speaks of his chains (1:16; 2:9).
t2_castra.n: Wall of the Praetorian camp, Rome
t2_castra.d: Part of the brick wall of the Castra Praetoria, the barracks of the Praetorian Guard in Rome, built under the emperor Tiberius about AD 23. Second Timothy does not say who guarded Paul, but it speaks of his chains (1:16; 2:9).

tt_epimenides.c: Epimenides, a half-legendary Cretan seer and poet of the 6th century BC, in an imagined portrait from Guillaume Rouillé's book of portraits (1553). Later writers connect the saying about Cretans with him. Paul calls its author "one of their own prophets" (Titus 1:12) and does not give a name.

tt_pantocrator.c: Christ Pantocrator, a sixth-century icon at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai, one of the oldest surviving icons of Christ. Titus 2:11-14 says the grace of God has appeared and looks for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for us.
tt_pantocrator.a: Unknown artist (6th century), Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai

tt_piero.f: Piero della Francesca - Battesimo di Cristo (National Gallery, London).jpg
tt_piero.c: The Baptism of Christ, by Piero della Francesca (after 1451). Titus 3:5 says God saved us through "the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit." Many readers think of baptism here, though the verse does not use the word.
tt_piero.a: Piero della Francesca (after 1451), National Gallery, London

tt_headpiece.f: Vignette by Loutherbourg for the Macklin Bible 114 of 134. Bowyer Bible New Testament. Headpiece to Titus.gif
tt_headpiece.c: The head-piece to the epistle to Titus in the Macklin Bible (1800), designed by Philippe-Jacques de Loutherbourg: a crucifix over a fountain. It is an artist's picture of the washing and mercy in Titus 3:5.

tt_fresco.f: Fresco of Saints Titos and Kyrillos of Gortyna.jpg
tt_fresco.c: A fresco of Saints Titus and Cyril of Gortyn, painted between the 13th and 15th centuries. It shows how later Christians remembered Titus as a bishop of Crete. Tradition, not the New Testament, calls him the first bishop of the island.

tt_gortyn_basilica.c: The ruined church of Saint Titus at Gortyn in the Messara plain of Crete. It was a large cathedral built in the 6th century AD, about 500 years after Paul. Tradition, not the New Testament, links Titus with Gortyn. Titus 1:5 says Paul left him in Crete and does not name a town.
tt_gortyn_basilica.d: The ruined church of Saint Titus at Gortyn in the Messara plain of Crete. It was a large cathedral built in the 6th century AD, about 500 years after Paul. Tradition, not the New Testament, links Titus with Gortyn. Titus 1:5 says Paul left him in Crete and does not name a town.

tt_gortyn_odeon.f: Gortyn Odeion and Ayios Titos from acropolis (1992).jpg
tt_gortyn_odeon.c: Gortyn seen from the acropolis, with the Roman Odeion in the foreground and the church of Saint Titus behind it (looking southeast). Gortyn was the seat of the Roman governor of Crete. Titus 1:5 asks Titus to appoint elders in every town but names none.
tt_gortyn_odeon.n: The Odeion and Saint Titus from the acropolis, Gortyn
tt_gortyn_odeon.d: Gortyn seen from the acropolis, with the Roman Odeion in the foreground and the church of Saint Titus behind it (looking southeast). Gortyn was the seat of the Roman governor of Crete. Titus 1:5 asks Titus to appoint elders in every town but names none.

tt_gortyn_code.f: The Law Code of Gortyn dated to the early 5th century BC, Gortyn - 30501009556.jpg
tt_gortyn_code.c: Part of the Law Code of Gortyn, carved on stone in the early 5th century BC, about 500 years before Titus. The Roman Odeion at Gortyn was later built around it. Its rules on marriage, divorce, property, inheritance and slaves show how Cretans ordered family life long before the household duties of Titus 2:1-10.
tt_gortyn_code.d: Part of the Law Code of Gortyn, carved on stone in the early 5th century BC, about 500 years before Titus. The Roman Odeion at Gortyn was later built around it. Its rules on marriage, divorce, property, inheritance and slaves show how Cretans ordered family life long before the household duties of Titus 2:1-10.

tt_gortyn_code2.c: A detail of the Law Code of Gortyn. The lines run in alternate directions, left to right and then right to left, a style called boustrophedon ("as the ox turns"). It is in an old Cretan form of Greek, long before the Greek of the New Testament.
tt_gortyn_code2.n: Detail of the Law Code of Gortyn
tt_gortyn_code2.d: A detail of the Law Code of Gortyn. The lines run in alternate directions, left to right and then right to left, a style called boustrophedon ("as the ox turns"). It is in an old Cretan form of Greek, long before the Greek of the New Testament.

tt_knossos_throne.f: Throne of Minos at Knossos Palace.jpg
tt_knossos_throne.c: The so-called Throne of Minos in the throne room of the palace at Knossos, a Bronze Age palace more than a thousand years older than Paul. Knossos is the town tradition links with the poet Epimenides (Titus 1:12). In Paul's day it was a Roman colony, and the letter does not say that Titus went there.
tt_knossos_throne.d: The so-called Throne of Minos in the throne room of the palace at Knossos, a Bronze Age palace more than a thousand years older than Paul. Knossos is the town tradition links with the poet Epimenides (Titus 1:12). In Paul's day it was a Roman colony, and the letter does not say that Titus went there.

tt_matala.f: Beach and troglodytes at Matala, Crete, Greece.jpg
tt_matala.c: Caves cut into the sandstone cliffs at Matala on the south coast of Crete. Matala served as a port for Gortyn. Titus 1:5 shows that Paul and Titus worked on the island but does not say where they landed or which towns they reached.
tt_matala.d: Caves cut into the sandstone cliffs at Matala on the south coast of Crete. Matala served as a port for Gortyn. Titus 1:5 shows that Paul and Titus worked on the island but does not say where they landed or which towns they reached.

tt_kaloi.c: Kaloi Limenes (Fair Havens) on the south coast of Crete. Acts 27:8 says Paul's ship put in here on the way to Rome. That voyage is the only visit to Crete that Acts records. Titus 1:5 refers to a later time when Paul left Titus on the island.

tt_heraklion_titus.c: The front of the Church of Saint Titus in Heraklion, Crete. A church stood here from the 10th century. The present building dates mostly from the rebuilding after an earthquake in 1856. A reliquary said to hold the saint's skull, returned from Venice in 1966, is kept inside. The relic cannot be traced to the first century.
tt_heraklion_titus.d: The front of the Church of Saint Titus in Heraklion, Crete. A church stood here from the 10th century. The present building dates mostly from the rebuilding after an earthquake in 1856. A reliquary said to hold the saint's skull, returned from Venice in 1966, is kept inside. The relic cannot be traced to the first century.

tt_priene.c: The Priene inscription (about 9 BC), which honors the emperor Augustus with titles such as savior and calls his birthday the beginning of "good news" for the world. Titus uses "Savior" for both God and Jesus Christ (1:3-4; 2:10, 13; 3:4, 6), so the word was not used only of Christ in the Roman world.
tt_priene.d: The Priene inscription (about 9 BC), which honors the emperor Augustus with titles such as savior and calls his birthday the beginning of "good news" for the world. Titus uses "Savior" for both God and Jesus Christ (1:3-4; 2:10, 13; 3:4, 6), so the word was not used only of Christ in the Roman world.

tt_antiochus.c: A silver tetradrachm of Antiochus IV (ruled 175-164 BC), struck at Antioch. His coins call him Theos Epiphanes, "God Manifest." Titus 2:11 and 2:13 use the same family of Greek words for the grace of God that "has appeared" and the appearing of our great God and Savior, a word the Greek world used for the visit of a god or a ruler.
tt_antiochus.d: A silver tetradrachm of Antiochus IV (ruled 175-164 BC), struck at Antioch. His coins call him Theos Epiphanes, "God Manifest." Titus 2:11 and 2:13 use the same family of Greek words for the grace of God that "has appeared" and the appearing of our great God and Savior, a word the Greek world used for the visit of a god or a ruler.

tt_collar.f: Inscribed bronze slave collar (Rome MNR 65043; CIL XV 7194).jpg
tt_collar.c: An inscribed bronze collar of a runaway slave, Museo Nazionale Romano, Rome. Such collars date mostly to the 4th century, about 300 years after Paul, but they show the world of slavery that Titus 2:9-10 speaks into: slaves who are to be honest and to adorn the teaching.
tt_collar.d: An inscribed bronze collar of a runaway slave, Museo Nazionale Romano, Rome. Such collars date mostly to the 4th century, about 300 years after Paul, but they show the world of slavery that Titus 2:9-10 speaks into: slaves who are to be honest and to adorn the teaching.

tt_onesimos.f: Funerary relief from the monument of Onessimos and his family (8726699040).jpg
tt_onesimos.c: A funerary relief of the Roman period for Onesimos, a slave who managed the household of Aelius Menogenes, an official in the province of Macedonia, shown with his family. It shows that a slave could hold a position of trust in a Roman household. Titus 2:9-10 speaks to slaves in the churches of Crete.
tt_onesimos.n: Relief of Onesimos, a slave household manager
tt_onesimos.d: A funerary relief of the Roman period for Onesimos, a slave who managed the household of Aelius Menogenes, an official in the province of Macedonia, shown with his family. It shows that a slave could hold a position of trust in a Roman household. Titus 2:9-10 speaks to slaves in the churches of Crete.

tt_nic_theatre.c: The Roman theater at Nicopolis near Preveza in Epirus, western Greece, a city Augustus founded after his victory at Actium in 31 BC. Titus 3:12 asks Titus to come to Paul at Nicopolis. Several cities had that name, and the letter does not say which one Paul meant, but the one in Epirus is the usual guess.
tt_nic_theatre.d: The Roman theater at Nicopolis near Preveza in Epirus, western Greece, a city Augustus founded after his victory at Actium in 31 BC. Titus 3:12 asks Titus to come to Paul at Nicopolis. Several cities had that name, and the letter does not say which one Paul meant, but the one in Epirus is the usual guess.

tt_nic_odeon.c: The Roman Odeon at Nicopolis, a small roofed hall for concerts and readings. Nicopolis had games every four years and the city was large and busy. Paul says he has decided to winter there (Titus 3:12).
tt_nic_odeon.d: The Roman Odeon at Nicopolis, a small roofed hall for concerts and readings. Nicopolis had games every four years and the city was large and busy. Paul says he has decided to winter there (Titus 3:12).

tt_nic_aqueduct.c: Part of the Roman aqueduct that brought water to Nicopolis. The water came from springs at some distance, and long stretches of the channel survive. Paul's plan to winter at Nicopolis (Titus 3:12) fits a city with good public works, though the letter says nothing about the city.
tt_nic_aqueduct.d: Part of the Roman aqueduct that brought water to Nicopolis. The water came from springs at some distance, and long stretches of the channel survive. Paul's plan to winter at Nicopolis (Titus 3:12) fits a city with good public works, though the letter says nothing about the city.

tt_nic_actium.c: The terrace wall of Octavian's victory monument for the battle of Actium on the hill above Nicopolis. The wall has cuttings where the bronze rams of captured warships were fixed. Augustus founded Nicopolis, the City of Victory, to mark that victory in 31 BC.
tt_nic_actium.d: The terrace wall of Octavian's victory monument for the battle of Actium on the hill above Nicopolis. The wall has cuttings where the bronze rams of captured warships were fixed. Augustus founded Nicopolis, the City of Victory, to mark that victory in 31 BC.

tt_nic_plan.c: A plan of the ruins of Nicopolis, with the Roman South Gate, theater, Odeon, baths, cisterns and the later Byzantine walls and churches. The city was founded about 31-29 BC and was large. Titus 3:12 is the only mention of it in the New Testament, if this is the Nicopolis Paul meant.
tt_nic_plan.d: A plan of the ruins of Nicopolis, with the Roman South Gate, theater, Odeon, baths, cisterns and the later Byzantine walls and churches. The city was founded about 31-29 BC and was large. Titus 3:12 is the only mention of it in the New Testament, if this is the Nicopolis Paul meant.
tt_nic_plan.a: Marsyas (French original) and Redx360 (English), CC BY-SA 3.0

tt_dura.f: Christ Healing the Paralytic - Dura-Europos circa 232.jpg
tt_dura.c: Christ healing the paralytic, painted in the baptistery of the house church at Dura-Europos in Syria, in the 3rd century (before the city fell in AD 256). It is the oldest known Christian baptistery, long after Titus, but a picture of baptism as the early church practiced it. Titus 3:5 speaks of "the washing of new birth."
tt_dura.d: Christ healing the paralytic, painted in the baptistery of the house church at Dura-Europos in Syria, in the 3rd century (before the city fell in AD 256). It is the oldest known Christian baptistery, long after Titus, but a picture of baptism as the early church practiced it. Titus 3:5 speaks of "the washing of new birth."
tt_dura.a: Yale University Art Gallery, public domain

pm_p87_recto.f: Cologne, Uni Köln Ms Papyrus 12 recto Philemon 13-15.jpg
pm_p87_recto.c: Papyrus 87 (Cologne, Papyrus 12), the earliest known fragment of the letter to Philemon, usually dated to the late 2nd or early 3rd century, about 150 years after Paul. This side has Philemon 13-15, where Paul says he would have liked to keep Onesimus with him and suggests that Onesimus was parted from Philemon "for a while" so that Philemon might have him back for good.
pm_p87_recto.d: Papyrus 87 (Cologne, Papyrus 12), the earliest known fragment of the letter to Philemon, usually dated to the late 2nd or early 3rd century, about 150 years after Paul. This side has Philemon 13-15, where Paul says he would have liked to keep Onesimus with him and suggests that Onesimus was parted from Philemon "for a while" so that Philemon might have him back for good.
pm_p87_recto.a: Unknown author (late 2nd or early 3rd century), public domain

pm_p87_verso.f: Cologne, Uni Köln Ms Papyrus 12 verso Philemon 24-25.jpg
pm_p87_verso.c: The other side of Papyrus 87, with Philemon 24-25: the greetings from Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke, and the closing blessing. The letter survived because Christians copied and kept it, even though it is private and short.
pm_p87_verso.d: The other side of Papyrus 87, with Philemon 24-25: the greetings from Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke, and the closing blessing. The letter survived because Christians copied and kept it, even though it is private and short.
pm_p87_verso.a: Unknown author (late 2nd or early 3rd century), public domain

pm_zoninus.c: An iron slave collar with a bronze plate from Rome, dated to the 4th or 5th century AD, about 300 years or more after Paul. The inscription offers a gold coin to anyone who catches the wearer, a runaway, and brings him back to his owner Zoninus. Philemon 10-18 deals with a slave who is away from his owner.
pm_zoninus.d: An iron slave collar with a bronze plate from Rome, dated to the 4th or 5th century AD, about 300 years or more after Paul. The inscription offers a gold coin to anyone who catches the wearer, a runaway, and brings him back to his owner Zoninus. Philemon 10-18 deals with a slave who is away from his owner.

pm_smyrna.c: A marble relief from Smyrna (Izmir) in Asia Minor, about AD 200, showing slaves wearing collars. Smyrna was not far from Colossae. The relief shows how slaves in the region were marked and controlled, in the setting in which Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave" (Philemon 16).
pm_smyrna.n: Roman relief of collared slaves, Smyrna
pm_smyrna.d: A marble relief from Smyrna (Izmir) in Asia Minor, about AD 200, showing slaves wearing collars. Smyrna was not far from Colossae. The relief shows how slaves in the region were marked and controlled, in the setting in which Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave" (Philemon 16).

pm_stock.f: Iron ring for chaining Roman slaves to it (52786634823).jpg
pm_stock.c: An iron stock for punishment from the Gladiatorial Barracks at Pompeii, about the 1st century AD, in the Naples Archaeological Museum. It shows the kind of restraints used on slaves and prisoners in Paul's time. Paul calls himself a prisoner of Christ and says he is "in chains" (Philemon 1, 9, 10, 13).
pm_stock.d: An iron stock for punishment from the Gladiatorial Barracks at Pompeii, about the 1st century AD, in the Naples Archaeological Museum. It shows the kind of restraints used on slaves and prisoners in Paul's time. Paul calls himself a prisoner of Christ and says he is "in chains" (Philemon 1, 9, 10, 13).

pm_tabulae.c: A Roman fresco from Pompeii (now in Naples) showing wax writing tablets, scrolls and a bag of money. Debts and receipts were written on tablets and papyrus. In Philemon 18-19 Paul writes with his own hand that he will repay anything Onesimus owes.
pm_tabulae.d: A Roman fresco from Pompeii (now in Naples) showing wax writing tablets, scrolls and a bag of money. Debts and receipts were written on tablets and papyrus. In Philemon 18-19 Paul writes with his own hand that he will repay anything Onesimus owes.

pm_pliny_ms.f: Pliny the Younger, Letters, Biblioteca Malatestiana.jpg
pm_pliny_ms.c: The beginning of Pliny the Younger's letters in a 15th-century manuscript at Cesena, Italy. In Letter 9.21 Pliny asks a friend to forgive a freedman who had angered him. The letter was written about 45 years after Paul's and is often compared with Philemon.
pm_pliny_ms.d: The beginning of Pliny the Younger's letters in a 15th-century manuscript at Cesena, Italy. In Letter 9.21 Pliny asks a friend to forgive a freedman who had angered him. The letter was written about 45 years after Paul's and is often compared with Philemon.
pm_pliny_ms.a: Pliny the Younger (manuscript copy, 15th century), public domain

pm_onesimos.f: Funerary relief from the monument of Onessimos and his family (8726699040).jpg
pm_onesimos.c: A funerary relief of the Roman period for a slave named Onesimus who managed the household of Aelius Menogenes, an official in Macedonia, shown with his family. Onesimus was a common slave name. The relief is not about the Onesimus of Philemon, but it shows that a slave could hold a position of trust in a Roman household.
pm_onesimos.n: Relief of Onesimos, a slave household manager
pm_onesimos.d: A funerary relief of the Roman period for a slave named Onesimus who managed the household of Aelius Menogenes, an official in Macedonia, shown with his family. Onesimus was a common slave name. The relief is not about the Onesimus of Philemon, but it shows that a slave could hold a position of trust in a Roman household.

pm_onesimus_icon.c: An Orthodox icon of Saint Onesimus. Churches remember Onesimus, the slave of Philemon, as a saint. Early writers name a bishop of Ephesus called Onesimus (Ignatius, about AD 110), but whether he was the same man is unknown.

pm_col_view.c: The mound of Colossae in 2025, looking toward Mount Honaz. The buried theater lies just behind the photographer. Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, and the letter to Philemon is addressed to a man who most likely lived here.

pm_col_theatre.c: The theater of Colossae, almost completely buried, though its location is clear. Most of the Roman town has never been dug. The letter to Philemon greets the church that met in a house here (Philemon 2).
pm_col_theatre.d: The theater of Colossae, almost completely buried, though its location is clear. Most of the Roman town has never been dug. The letter to Philemon greets the church that met in a house here (Philemon 2).

pm_col_column.c: A column fragment half buried in the soil at Colossae in 2025. Few built remains of the town show above ground, which is why so little is known about its homes and its first Christians.
pm_col_column.d: A column fragment half buried in the soil at Colossae in 2025. Few built remains of the town show above ground, which is why so little is known about its homes and its first Christians.

pm_honaz.c: The town of Honaz at the foot of Mount Honaz, which rises 2,571 meters and is the highest mountain in the Aegean region of Turkey. The ruins of Colossae lie near Honaz in the Lycus Valley.
pm_honaz.n: Mount Honaz and the town of Honaz
pm_honaz.d: The town of Honaz at the foot of Mount Honaz, which rises 2,571 meters and is the highest mountain in the Aegean region of Turkey. The ruins of Colossae lie near Honaz in the Lycus Valley.

pm_dura_front.f: Doura Europos domus ecclesiae front from S.jpg
pm_dura_front.c: The front of the house church at Dura-Europos in Syria, a private house remodeled for Christian worship in the 230s, about 170 years after Philemon. Philemon 2 greets the church that met at Philemon's house, so Christians were meeting in homes long before they built churches.
pm_dura_front.d: The front of the house church at Dura-Europos in Syria, a private house remodeled for Christian worship in the 230s, about 170 years after Philemon. Philemon 2 greets the church that met at Philemon's house, so Christians were meeting in homes long before they built churches.

hb_vaticanus.c: A page of Codex Vaticanus, a Greek Bible copied in the 4th century and kept in the Vatican Library. It shows the end of 2 Thessalonians (3:11-18) and the opening of Hebrews (1:1-2:2). In this manuscript Hebrews follows 2 Thessalonians, among the letters of Paul, although the letter itself never names its author.
hb_vaticanus.d: A page of Codex Vaticanus, a Greek Bible copied in the 4th century and kept in the Vatican Library. It shows the end of 2 Thessalonians (3:11-18) and the opening of Hebrews (1:1-2:2). In this manuscript Hebrews follows 2 Thessalonians, among the letters of Paul, although the letter itself never names its author.

hb_p13_4.f: London, British Library Ms Inv. Nr. 1532v (Papyrus 13) Fragment 1 recto Hebrews 4,2-12.jpg
hb_p13_4.c: A piece of Papyrus 13, a roll found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and usually dated to the 3rd or early 4th century. Hebrews was copied on the back of an old roll that had a summary of Livy's Roman history on the front. This fragment has Hebrews 4:2-12, the passage about the promised rest and the word of God that is living and active.
hb_p13_4.d: A piece of Papyrus 13, a roll found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and usually dated to the 3rd or early 4th century. Hebrews was copied on the back of an old roll that had a summary of Livy's Roman history on the front. This fragment has Hebrews 4:2-12, the passage about the promised rest and the word of God that is living and active.
hb_p13_4.a: Unknown scribe (3rd or early 4th century), public domain

hb_p13_10.f: Papyrus PSI 1292 - Papyrus 13, P. Oxy. IV 657 - Epistle to the Hebrews 10,8–22 - Egyptian Museum, Cairo.jpg
hb_p13_10.c: Another piece of Papyrus 13, with Hebrews 10:8-22. The passage says that Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and invites the readers to draw near to God with a true heart, with hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed with pure water.
hb_p13_10.d: Another piece of Papyrus 13, with Hebrews 10:8-22. The passage says that Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and invites the readers to draw near to God with a true heart, with hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed with pure water.
hb_p13_10.a: Unknown scribe (3rd or early 4th century), public domain

hb_p126.f: Florence, Papyrological Institute "G. Vitelli" Ms PSI XV 1497 - PSI inv. 2176 (Papyrus 126) recto Heb 13, 12-13.jpg
hb_p126.c: Papyrus 126, a small 4th-century fragment now in Florence, with Hebrews 13:12-13: Jesus suffered outside the gate, so let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach.
hb_p126.d: Papyrus 126, a small 4th-century fragment now in Florence, with Hebrews 13:12-13: Jesus suffered outside the gate, so let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach.

hb_p46.c: Papyrus 46, a codex of Paul's letters usually dated to about AD 200, is the oldest large copy that includes Hebrews. In this manuscript Hebrews comes right after Romans. By the same time Christians were already debating who wrote it, and Origen later said that only God knows.
hb_p46.d: Papyrus 46, a codex of Paul's letters usually dated to about AD 200, is the oldest large copy that includes Hebrews. In this manuscript Hebrews comes right after Romans. By the same time Christians were already debating who wrote it, and Origen later said that only God knows.

hb_qumran11.c: The entrance of Cave 11 at Qumran by the Dead Sea. Among the scrolls found here in 1956 is a damaged Hebrew text (11Q13) that describes Melchizedek as a heavenly figure who frees captives and brings God's judgment at the end of days. Hebrews never refers to it, but it shows that Jews of the time were interested in Melchizedek.
hb_qumran11.d: The entrance of Cave 11 at Qumran by the Dead Sea. Among the scrolls found here in 1956 is a damaged Hebrew text (11Q13) that describes Melchizedek as a heavenly figure who frees captives and brings God's judgment at the end of days. Hebrews never refers to it, but it shows that Jews of the time were interested in Melchizedek.

hb_mikveh.c: A stepped cistern used for ritual washing at Qumran. Hebrews 9:10 speaks of special washings in the old system, and 10:22 speaks of bodies washed with pure water, language that would have been familiar to readers who knew Jewish purity customs.
hb_mikveh.d: A stepped cistern used for ritual washing at Qumran. Hebrews 9:10 speaks of special washings in the old system, and 10:22 speaks of bodies washed with pure water, language that would have been familiar to readers who knew Jewish purity customs.

hb_timna.c: A life-size modern model of the tabernacle at Timna Park in southern Israel, built from the description in Exodus. No remains of the original tent have been found. Hebrews 8-9 describes the tabernacle as a copy and shadow of heavenly things.

hb_ark.f: Timna Tabernacle inside Ark of the Covenant.jpg
hb_ark.c: A modern model of the ark of the covenant inside the Timna Park tabernacle replica. Hebrews 9:4 says the ark was covered with gold and lists what was in it: a golden jar of manna, Aaron's staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant.
hb_ark.n: Model of the ark of the covenant, Timna Park
hb_ark.d: A modern model of the ark of the covenant inside the Timna Park tabernacle replica. Hebrews 9:4 says the ark was covered with gold and lists what was in it: a golden jar of manna, Aaron's staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant.

hb_incense.c: A modern model of the golden altar of incense in the tabernacle replica at Timna Park. Hebrews 9:3-4 mentions the golden altar of incense in its description of the sanctuary behind the second curtain.
hb_incense.n: Model of the incense altar, Timna Park
hb_incense.d: A modern model of the golden altar of incense in the tabernacle replica at Timna Park. Hebrews 9:3-4 mentions the golden altar of incense in its description of the sanctuary behind the second curtain.

hb_showbread.c: A modern model of the table of the bread of the Presence in the Timna Park tabernacle replica. Hebrews 9:2 names the lampstand, the table and the bread of the Presence as the furnishings of the first room.
hb_showbread.n: Model of the table of showbread, Timna Park
hb_showbread.d: A modern model of the table of the bread of the Presence in the Timna Park tabernacle replica. Hebrews 9:2 names the lampstand, the table and the bread of the Presence as the furnishings of the first room.

hb_jericho.c: Tell es-Sultan, the mound of ancient Jericho. Hebrews 11:30 says the walls fell after the people had marched around them for seven days. Excavators have disagreed for decades about what the Late Bronze Age city looked like at the time of Joshua.
hb_jericho.d: Tell es-Sultan, the mound of ancient Jericho. Hebrews 11:30 says the walls fell after the people had marched around them for seven days. Excavators have disagreed for decades about what the Late Bronze Age city looked like at the time of Joshua.

hb_maccabees.f: The Martyrdom of the Seven Maccabee Brothers and their Mother MET DT275472.jpg
hb_maccabees.c: The martyrdom of the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother, in a stained-glass panel made in Antwerp about 1530 by Dirck Vellert. Many readers link Hebrews 11:35, "Others were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection," to the stories in 2 Maccabees 6-7, where Jews under Antiochus IV chose death over breaking the law.

hb_melch.f: Dieric Bouts - The Meeting of Abraham and Melchizedek - WGA03010.jpg
hb_melch.c: The meeting of Abraham and Melchizedek, painted by Dieric Bouts for a church in Leuven (Belgium). Genesis 14:18-20 says Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brought out bread and wine and blessed Abraham, who gave him a tenth. Hebrews 7:1-10 builds an argument on this short scene.

hb_scapegoat.f: William Holman Hunt - The Scapegoat - WGA11808.jpg
hb_scapegoat.c: "The Scapegoat" by William Holman Hunt, painted on the shore of the Dead Sea in 1854-55. On the Day of Atonement the high priest sent a live goat into the wilderness carrying the people's sins (Leviticus 16:20-22). Hebrews 9-10 refers to the yearly ritual to show that it had to be repeated, while Christ's offering did not. (The goat that was burned outside the camp, in Hebrews 13:11, was a different animal, the sin offering.)

hb_priest.f: Tissot Drawing 147 The costume of the high priest (Exodus 28 4) for Brunoff 137 Le costume du Grand-Prétre.jpg
hb_priest.c: The high priest's clothing from Exodus 28, as imagined by the French artist James Tissot in a pen-and-ink sketch of about 1900. It is a modern artist's picture, not an archaeological find. Hebrews 5:1-4 and 7:26-28 compare Jesus with the high priests of Israel, who were chosen from among men, were weak themselves, and had to offer sacrifices for their own sins too.

hb_gladius.c: A Roman short sword (gladius) from Germany of the Mainz type, with a blade sharp on both edges and a point. Hebrews 4:12 says that the word of God is "Sharper than any double-edged sword."
hb_gladius.d: A Roman short sword (gladius) from Germany of the Mainz type, with a blade sharp on both edges and a point. Hebrews 4:12 says that the word of God is "Sharper than any double-edged sword."

hb_anchor.c: A limestone anchor of the Hellenistic or Roman period, found off the coast near Paphos, Cyprus, and now in the Paphos museum. Iron-bound wooden stocks were fitted into the holes at the lower end. Anchors were a familiar sight in Mediterranean harbors. Hebrews 6:19 calls the hope we have "an anchor for the soul, firm and secure" that enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain.
hb_anchor.n: An ancient anchor from Paphos, Cyprus
hb_anchor.d: A limestone anchor of the Hellenistic or Roman period, found off the coast near Paphos, Cyprus, and now in the Paphos museum. Iron-bound wooden stocks were fitted into the holes at the lower end. Anchors were a familiar sight in Mediterranean harbors. Hebrews 6:19 calls the hope we have "an anchor for the soul, firm and secure" that enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain.

hb_zion.c: Dormition Abbey on the hill in Jerusalem now called Mount Zion, southwest of the Old City. In the Bible, Zion usually means the Temple hill or the city of David. In Hebrews 12:22 it means the heavenly city of the living God, to which believers have already come.

hb_isaac.c: "The Sacrifice of Isaac" by Caravaggio, painted about 1598. Hebrews 11:17-19 says Abraham offered up Isaac by faith, reasoning that God was able even to raise the dead.

hb_isaac_bless.f: Master of the Isaac Stories - Scenes from the Old Testament - Isaac Blessing Jacob - WGA14569.jpg
hb_isaac_bless.c: Isaac blessing Jacob, in a late 13th-century fresco at Assisi attributed to the Isaac Master. Hebrews 11:20 says that by faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau in matters regarding the future.

hb_cain.f: Cain leadeth abel to death tissot.jpg
hb_cain.c: Cain leads Abel out to the field, by James Tissot, about 1896-1902. Hebrews 11:4 says that by faith Abel offered a better sacrifice than Cain, and 12:24 says the blood of Jesus speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.

hb_dura_moses.f: Moses and Burning Bush Dura Europos.jpg
hb_dura_moses.c: A wall painting of Moses at the burning bush from the synagogue at Dura-Europos in Syria. Moses was held in the highest honor in Judaism, so Hebrews 3 begins by praising him as "faithful in all God's house" before saying that the Son is greater.
hb_dura_moses.n: Moses at the burning bush, Dura-Europos
hb_dura_moses.d: A wall painting of Moses at the burning bush from the synagogue at Dura-Europos in Syria. Moses was held in the highest honor in Judaism, so Hebrews 3 begins by praising him as "faithful in all God's house" before saying that the Son is greater.
hb_dura_moses.a: Unknown artist (3rd century AD), public domain

hb_h2.c: Papyrus 46, usually dated to about AD 200, is the oldest large copy that includes Hebrews, and so it carries chapter 2, where the Son is made like his brothers in every way (2:17). The manuscript is a book of leaves, a codex, and not a roll.
hb_h2.d: Papyrus 46, usually dated to about AD 200, is the oldest large copy that includes Hebrews, and so it carries chapter 2, where the Son is made like his brothers in every way (2:17). The manuscript is a book of leaves, a codex, and not a roll.

hb_h8.f: Carrying off the Menorah from the Temple in Jerusalem depicted on a frieze on the Arch of Titus in the Forum Romanum.JPG
hb_h8.c: Roman soldiers carry the temple menorah in a procession of spoils from Jerusalem, on the Arch of Titus in Rome, built soon after AD 81. Hebrews 8:13 says that what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear. After the temple fell in AD 70 the sacrifices it describes could no longer be offered.
hb_h8.d: Roman soldiers carry the temple menorah in a procession of spoils from Jerusalem, on the Arch of Titus in Rome, built soon after AD 81. Hebrews 8:13 says that what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear. After the temple fell in AD 70 the sacrifices it describes could no longer be offered.

hb_h12.c: The stadium at Ephesus. Footraces in stadiums watched by crowds were familiar across the Greek-speaking world, and Hebrews 12:1 pictures believers running a race with "a great cloud of witnesses" around them.
hb_h12.d: The stadium at Ephesus. Footraces in stadiums watched by crowds were familiar across the Greek-speaking world, and Hebrews 12:1 pictures believers running a race with "a great cloud of witnesses" around them.

hb_c1.c: The Temple Mount in Jerusalem from the air. The letter to the Hebrews is full of the language of the temple and its priests, though it never names Jerusalem as its destination.

hb_c2.c: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, built over the place that Christian tradition since the 4th century has marked as the site of the crucifixion and the tomb. Hebrews 2:9 says Jesus tasted death for everyone.

hb_c3.c: Jebel Musa ("Moses' mountain") in the southern Sinai, the traditional Mount Sinai. Hebrews 3 compares Jesus with Moses and recalls the generation that left Egypt under him but failed to enter the promised land.

hb_c4.c: The Western Wall of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. Hebrews 4:14-16 pictures believers coming to a throne of grace, an echo of the temple and the mercy seat, but with a high priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses.

hb_c5.c: Old olive trees at Gethsemane on the Mount of Olives. Hebrews 5:7 speaks of Jesus offering prayers "with loud cries and tears" in the days of his flesh. Many readers connect this with Gethsemane, though the letter does not name the place.

hb_c6.c: The site of Mamre near Hebron, where Abraham lived. Hebrews 6:13-18 recalls how God promised Abraham a blessing and swore by himself, because there was no one greater to swear by.

hb_c7.c: Jerusalem and the Temple Mount from the air. Many identify Salem, where Melchizedek was king, with Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2), so Hebrews 7 connects the priest-king with the city of the temple.

hb_c10.c: The Temple Mount in Jerusalem from the air. Hebrews 10 compares the repeated sacrifices of the temple with the single offering of Christ and then invites the readers to enter the holy places with confidence.

hb_c13.c: The traditional site of Golgotha inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. In the time of Jesus this place lay outside the city wall. Hebrews 13:12 says Jesus suffered outside the gate and calls believers to go out to him bearing his reproach.

jm_p23_15.c: One side of Papyrus 23, a leaf from a codex of the letter of James found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and dated to the 3rd century (now in the Spurlock Museum, University of Illinois). This side has James 1:15-18: desire gives birth to sin, and every good gift comes down from above. It shows that James was copied and read in Egypt by the 200s.
jm_p23_15.d: One side of Papyrus 23, a leaf from a codex of the letter of James found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and dated to the 3rd century (now in the Spurlock Museum, University of Illinois). This side has James 1:15-18: desire gives birth to sin, and every good gift comes down from above. It shows that James was copied and read in Egypt by the 200s.

jm_p23_10.c: The other side of Papyrus 23, with James 1:10-12. It holds the words about the rich person who will pass away like a flower of the field and the blessing on the one who perseveres under trial. Papyrus 23 was found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and is dated to the 3rd century.
