jm_p23_10.d: The other side of Papyrus 23, with James 1:10-12. It holds the words about the rich person who will pass away like a flower of the field and the blessing on the one who perseveres under trial. Papyrus 23 was found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and is dated to the 3rd century.

jm_p20_recto.f: Princeton, Ms AM 4117 - P.Oxy. IX 1171 (Papyrus 20) recto James 2,19–3, 2.jpg
jm_p20_recto.c: One side of Papyrus 20, a leaf from a codex of James found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and dated to the 3rd century (now in Princeton University Library). This side has James 2:19-3:2, from the end of the argument that faith without works is dead to the first warning about teachers.
jm_p20_recto.d: One side of Papyrus 20, a leaf from a codex of James found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and dated to the 3rd century (now in Princeton University Library). This side has James 2:19-3:2, from the end of the argument that faith without works is dead to the first warning about teachers.

jm_p20_verso.f: Princeton, Ms AM 4117 - P.Oxy. IX 1171 (Papyrus 20) verso James 3, 3–9.jpg
jm_p20_verso.c: The back of the Papyrus 20 leaf, now in Princeton University Library. It has James 3:3-9, the passage about the bit in a horse's mouth, the ship's rudder and the tongue that no one can tame.
jm_p20_verso.d: The back of the Papyrus 20 leaf, now in Princeton University Library. It has James 3:3-9, the passage about the bit in a horse's mouth, the ship's rudder and the tongue that no one can tame.

jm_ossuary.c: A limestone ossuary, or bone box, of the kind used in Jerusalem before AD 70. Its Aramaic inscription is read as: James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus. It was announced in 2002 and has no known findspot. In 2003 an Israeli committee judged the inscription a modern forgery, though other experts disagreed. Names like these were common, and the box cannot be tied to the James who wrote the letter.
jm_ossuary.d: A limestone ossuary, or bone box, of the kind used in Jerusalem before AD 70. Its Aramaic inscription is read as: James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus. It was announced in 2002 and has no known findspot. In 2003 an Israeli committee judged the inscription a modern forgery, though other experts disagreed. Names like these were common, and the box cannot be tied to the James who wrote the letter.
jm_ossuary.a: Paradiso. The James ossuary was on display at the Royal Ontario Museum from November 15, 2002 to January 5, 2003.

jm_mesad.c: A pottery fragment from the 7th century BC, found in 1960 at a Judean fortress near Yavne-Yam on the coast and now in the Israel Museum. In it a field worker complains to the commander that an official took his garment after he finished his harvesting, and asks for it back. It is some six centuries older than James, but it shows a harvester appealing for justice, as the workmen do in James 5:4.
jm_mesad.d: A pottery fragment from the 7th century BC, found in 1960 at a Judean fortress near Yavne-Yam on the coast and now in the Israel Museum. In it a field worker complains to the commander that an official took his garment after he finished his harvesting, and asks for it back. It is some six centuries older than James, but it shows a harvester appealing for justice, as the workmen do in James 5:4.

jm_gezer.c: A small limestone tablet from Gezer, found in 1908, from about the 10th century BC (now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums). It lists the farm tasks of the year in order, from the ingathering and planting to the barley harvest, pruning and summer fruit. James 5:7 pictures a farmer who waits for the fall and spring rains, the rhythm that such a calendar records.
jm_gezer.d: A small limestone tablet from Gezer, found in 1908, from about the 10th century BC (now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums). It lists the farm tasks of the year in order, from the ingathering and planting to the barley harvest, pruning and summer fruit. jm_ring.f: Gold ring with glass cameo in bezel MET GR674.jpg
jm_ring.c: A gold ring with a glass cameo set in the bezel, made in Cyprus in the 1st or 2nd century AD (Metropolitan Museum of Art). In Rome a gold finger ring showed rank and wealth, and Pliny the Elder writes about who had the right to wear one. James 2:2 pictures a visitor "wearing a gold ring and fine clothes."
jm_ring.d: A gold ring with a glass cameo set in the bezel, made in Cyprus in the 1st or 2nd century AD (Metropolitan Museum of Art). In Rome a gold finger ring showed rank and wealth, and Pliny the Elder writes about who had the right to wear one. James 2:2 pictures a visitor "wearing a gold ring and fine clothes."

jm_ring2.c: A Roman ring of gold-plated bronze with a blue agate set in the bezel and engraved with the goddess Fortuna, from the late 2nd or early 3rd century AD (Vidy Roman Museum, Switzerland). It is later than James, but shows that people also wore cheaper rings that looked like gold.
jm_ring2.n: A Roman ring with an engraved stone
jm_ring2.d: A Roman ring of gold-plated bronze with a blue agate set in the bezel and engraved with the goddess Fortuna, from the late 2nd or early 3rd century AD (Vidy Roman Museum, Switzerland). It is later than James, but shows that people also wore cheaper rings that looked like gold.

jm_bit.c: A bronze horse bit of the 4th or 3rd century BC (Metropolitan Museum of Art). A small piece of metal in the horse's mouth steers the whole animal, which is the first picture James uses for the tongue (3:3).
jm_bit.d: A bronze horse bit of the 4th or 3rd century BC (Metropolitan Museum of Art). A small piece of metal in the horse's mouth steers the whole animal, which is the first picture James uses for the tongue (3:3).

jm_rudder.f: Rudder of a Roman Boat (RG Museum Koeln, Germany).JPG
jm_rudder.c: The stern-mounted steering oar of a Roman Rhine boat of the 1st century AD, now in the Römisch-Germanisches Museum in Cologne. Ancient ships were steered with oars like this one. James 3:4 says that big ships driven by strong winds are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined.
jm_rudder.d: The stern-mounted steering oar of a Roman Rhine boat of the 1st century AD, now in the Römisch-Germanisches Museum in Cologne. Ancient ships were steered with oars like this one. James 3:4 says that big ships driven by strong winds are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined.

jm_hinnom.f: 95945 jerusalem new bridge over the ben hinnom valley PikiWiki Israel.jpg
jm_hinnom.c: The Hinnom Valley south of the Old City of Jerusalem, with a modern bridge. Its Hebrew name gives the Greek word Gehenna, which James 3:6 uses when he says the tongue "is itself set on fire by hell." In the Old Testament the valley was linked with child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31-32), and in the Gospels Jesus uses Gehenna for the place of judgment.
jm_hinnom.d: The Hinnom Valley south of the Old City of Jerusalem, with a modern bridge. Its Hebrew name gives the Greek word Gehenna, which James 3:6 uses when he says the tongue "is itself set on fire by hell." In the Old Testament the valley was linked with child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31-32), and in the Gospels Jesus uses Gehenna for the place of judgment.

jm_masada.c: Casemate room 1109 in the wall of Masada, where a Hebrew scroll of the Wisdom of Ben Sira (Sirach) was found. The book was written about 180 BC. Its teaching on trials, speech and wisdom is close to topics in James, though James never quotes it by name.
jm_masada.n: Where the Ben Sira scroll was found
jm_masada.d: Casemate room 1109 in the wall of Masada, where a Hebrew scroll of the Wisdom of Ben Sira (Sirach) was found. The book was written about 180 BC. Its teaching on trials, speech and wisdom is close to topics in James, though James never quotes it by name.

jm_olive_press.c: An ancient olive press at the Agios Georgios site beside the Ledra City Archaeological Museum in Nicosia, Cyprus. Olive oil was used for food, for light and for treating wounds (Luke 10:34). James 5:14 tells the elders to pray over the sick person and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.
jm_olive_press.d: An ancient olive press at the Agios Georgios site beside the Ledra City Archaeological Museum in Nicosia, Cyprus. Olive oil was used for food, for light and for treating wounds (Luke 10:34). James 5:14 tells the elders to pray over the sick person and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.

jm_elijah_dura.c: A wall painting from the synagogue at Dura-Europos in Syria, catalogued on Commons as Elijah on Mount Carmel. It dates from the 3rd century AD and shows how Elijah's story was told in a Jewish setting. James 5:17-18 says that Elijah was a man just like us, and that his prayers shut the sky and then opened it.
jm_elijah_dura.d: A wall painting from the synagogue at Dura-Europos in Syria, catalogued on Commons as Elijah on Mount Carmel. It dates from the 3rd century AD and shows how Elijah's story was told in a Jewish setting. James 5:17-18 says that Elijah was a man just like us, and that his prayers shut the sky and then opened it.
jm_elijah_dura.a: Unknown artist (3rd century AD), public domain

jm_rahab.f: Tissot The Harlot of Jericho and the Two Spies.jpg
jm_rahab.c: The Harlot of Jericho and the Two Spies, a gouache by James Tissot or a follower, painted about 1896-1902 (Jewish Museum, New York). Joshua 2 tells how Rahab hid the Israelite spies in Jericho. James 2:25 asks whether even Rahab the prostitute was not justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route.
jm_rahab.a: James Tissot or a follower (about 1896-1902), public domain

jm_elijah_tissot.f: Tissot Drawing 340 Elijah from Mount Carmel sees a cloud 1 Kings 18 44 for Brunoff 312 Élie sur le Mont Carmel voit un nuage.jpg
jm_elijah_tissot.c: Elijah on Mount Carmel sees a small cloud rising from the sea (1 Kings 18:44), in a pen-and-ink sketch by James Tissot, 1901. It is a modern artist's picture, not a record from the time. James 5:18 says that Elijah prayed again, "the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops."

jm_job.c: Job and His Friends, painted by Ilya Repin in 1869. James 5:11 points to Job as an example of those who persevered, and to the outcome that the Lord gave him, for the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.

jm_anemone.c: Crown anemones in bloom at Tal Shachar, Israel. Wild flowers cover the hills in the winter rains and are soon dried up by the heat of the sun. James does not name a plant, but he pictures the rich person passing away like a flower of the field, which the scorching sun withers (1:10-11). Isaiah 40:6-8 uses a similar picture.

jm_stjames.f: Entrance to the Cathedral of Saint James in the Armenian Quarter of Jerusalem.jpg
jm_stjames.c: The entrance of the Cathedral of St James in the Armenian Quarter of Jerusalem. The church honors two apostles named James, the son of Zebedee and James the brother of the Lord. The building is mostly from the 12th century, so it is a memorial of the tradition and not evidence from the first century. James the brother of Jesus led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9).
jm_stjames.a: John S Y Lee, CC BY 2.0

jm_moriah.c: The Temple Mount in Jerusalem with the Dome of the Rock. According to 2 Chronicles 3:1 Solomon built the temple on Mount Moriah, and Jewish tradition connects this with the place where Abraham was told to offer Isaac (Genesis 22:2). James 2:21 asks whether Abraham was not justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar.

jm_fire.c: A fire in the Carmel forest near Isfiya, Israel, on the first day of the fire in December 2010. A dry Mediterranean forest can burn very quickly. James 3:5 says that a small spark sets a great forest ablaze, and compares it to the tongue.
jm_fire.a: רונית בן צבי בת משפחה, CC BY-SA 3.0

jm_muhraqa.f: Panorama of Western Galilee from atop Mount Carmel (20830397795).jpg
jm_muhraqa.c: The view from the rooftop lookout of the Muhraqa Carmelite monastery on Mount Carmel, with Haifa at the far left and Megiddo to the right. Muhraqa, a name that means the burning place, is the traditional place of Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18). The Bible does not name the exact spot on the long Carmel ridge. James 5:17-18 recalls Elijah's prayers for drought and for rain.

jm_c4.f: Antioch on the Orontes, Antakya, Turkey (35863345530).jpg
jm_c4.c: Antakya in Turkey, the modern city on the site of ancient Antioch on the Orontes, a large city of Roman Syria with many Jews. James does not say where his readers lived, and Antioch is only one suggestion. In 4:13 he pictures merchants who plan to go to a city, spend a year there and make a profit.

jm_ship.c: A Roman fresco of a merchant ship named the Isis Giminiana, now in the Vatican Museums (about AD 200-250). It is later than James, but it shows a cargo ship of the kind that carried traders around the Mediterranean. James 4:13 pictures merchants who say they will go to a city, spend a year there and make a profit.
jm_ship.d: A Roman fresco of a merchant ship named the Isis Giminiana, now in the Vatican Museums (about AD 200-250). It is later than James, but it shows a cargo ship of the kind that carried traders around the Mediterranean. James 4:13 pictures merchants who say they will go to a city, spend a year there and make a profit.

jm_mirror.f: Greek Bronze Mirror Box, Corinth, 350-325 BC (28221243421).jpg
jm_mirror.c: A Greek bronze mirror box from Corinth (350-325 BC), now in the Louvre. Mirrors were polished metal and gave a less clear image than modern glass. In James 1:23-24 a man looks at his face in a mirror and then goes away and forgets what he looked like, a picture of one who hears the word and does not do it.
jm_mirror.d: A Greek bronze mirror box from Corinth (350-325 BC), now in the Louvre. Mirrors were polished metal and gave a less clear image than modern glass. In James 1:23-24 a man looks at his face in a mirror and then goes away and forgets what he looked like, a picture of one who hears the word and does not do it.

jm_theodotus.c: A Greek inscription found in Jerusalem in 1913. It records that a priest named Theodotus built a synagogue for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments, with a guesthouse for visitors. Most scholars date it before AD 70. James 2:2 calls the gathering a synagogue (translated "meeting" in many Bibles).
jm_theodotus.d: A Greek inscription found in Jerusalem in 1913. It records that a priest named Theodotus built a synagogue for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments, with a guesthouse for visitors. Most scholars date it before AD 70. James 2:2 calls the gathering a synagogue (translated "meeting" in many Bibles).

jm_isaac.c: The Sacrifice of Isaac, by Caravaggio, painted about 1598. James 2:21-22 says Abraham was justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar, and that his faith was working together with his actions.

jm_jericho.c: Tell es-Sultan, the mound of ancient Jericho. Rahab lived in a house on the city wall (Joshua 2:15). Excavators disagree about what the city looked like at the time of Joshua. James 2:25 names Rahab as one who was justified by her actions.
jm_jericho.d: Tell es-Sultan, the mound of ancient Jericho. Rahab lived in a house on the city wall (Joshua 2:15). Excavators disagree about what the city looked like at the time of Joshua. James 2:25 names Rahab as one who was justified by her actions.

jm_reaper.f: Vincent van Gogh - Wheatfield with a reaper - Google Art Project.jpg
jm_reaper.c: Wheatfield with a Reaper, painted by Vincent van Gogh in September 1889. It is a modern picture of the work James has in mind in 5:4, where the wages withheld from the workmen who mowed the fields cry out against the rich, and the cries of the harvesters reach the Lord of Hosts.

jm_ostia.c: The synagogue at Ostia, the port of Rome. What stands today was rebuilt in the 4th century, though the first building may go back to the 1st. It shows that Jewish communities lived in cities all around the Mediterranean, the Dispersion to which James writes (1:1).
jm_ostia.d: The synagogue at Ostia, the port of Rome. What stands today was rebuilt in the 4th century, though the first building may go back to the 1st. It shows that Jewish communities lived in cities all around the Mediterranean, the Dispersion to which James writes (1:1).

p1_p72_a.c: A leaf of Papyrus 72, a papyrus codex from Egypt of the 3rd or 4th century (the Bodmer papyri), with the text of 1 Peter 2:7-17. This stretch of the letter has the stone that the builders rejected, the chosen people and the command to honor the king. It is the earliest surviving copy of 1 Peter.
p1_p72_a.d: A leaf of Papyrus 72, a papyrus codex from Egypt of the 3rd or 4th century (the Bodmer papyri), with the text of 1 Peter 2:7-17. This stretch of the letter has the stone that the builders rejected, the chosen people and the command to honor the king. It is the earliest surviving copy of 1 Peter.
p1_p72_a.a: Unknown scribe (3rd or 4th century), public domain

p1_p72_b.f: Vatican, Apostolic Library Ms Papyrus Bodmer VIII 2 (Papyrus 72) Ending of 1 Peter - Beginning of 2 Peter.jpg
p1_p72_b.c: A leaf of Papyrus 72 with the end of 1 Peter, including the closing greetings of 5:13-14, and the beginning of 2 Peter (Papyrus Bodmer VIII, Vatican Library). The scribe copied the two letters of Peter together.
p1_p72_b.d: A leaf of Papyrus 72 with the end of 1 Peter, including the closing greetings of 5:13-14, and the beginning of 2 Peter (Papyrus Bodmer VIII, Vatican Library). The scribe copied the two letters of Peter together.
p1_p72_b.a: Unknown scribe (3rd or 4th century), public domain

p1_stater.c: A gold coin (stater) of Lydia, about 560-546 BC, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Sardis, the Lydian capital in what became Roman Asia, was famous for its gold, and excavations there found 6th-century BC workshops where gold was separated from silver. Peter says that proven faith is more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire (1:7).
p1_stater.d: A gold coin (stater) of Lydia, about 560-546 BC, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Sardis, the Lydian capital in what became Roman Asia, was famous for its gold, and excavations there found 6th-century BC workshops where gold was separated from silver. Peter says that proven faith is more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire (1:7).

p1_bust.c: A marble bust of a Roman woman, about AD 80, in the Glyptothek in Munich. Tall hairstyles built up with curls and added hair were fashionable at court and beyond in the Flavian period, a little after Peter wrote. Peter tells wives that their beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes (3:3).
p1_bust.n: A Roman woman of the Flavian period
p1_bust.d: A marble bust of a Roman woman, about AD 80, in the Glyptothek in Munich. Tall hairstyles built up with curls and added hair were fashionable at court and beyond in the Flavian period, a little after Peter wrote. Peter tells wives that their beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes (3:3).
p1_bust.a: Photo released into the public domain

p1_tablet.c: Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, known as the Flood Tablet, from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, 7th century BC (British Museum). It tells of a man who builds a boat to save his family and living creatures from a flood. Scholars compare it with Genesis 6-9. Peter mentions only Noah and the eight souls who were saved through water (3:20).
p1_tablet.d: Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, known as the Flood Tablet, from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, 7th century BC (British Museum). It tells of a man who builds a boat to save his family and living creatures from a flood. Scholars compare it with Genesis 6-9. Peter mentions only Noah and the eight souls who were saved through water (3:20).

p1_wreath.f: Fragment of an ancient Greek gold wreath.jpg
p1_wreath.c: Fragment of a Greek gold laurel wreath of the 4th or 3rd century BC in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Victors and honored people wore wreaths, which were usually made of leaves that soon withered. Peter promises the elders, when the Chief Shepherd appears, the crown of glory that will never fade away (5:4).
p1_wreath.d: Fragment of a Greek gold laurel wreath of the 4th or 3rd century BC in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Victors and honored people wore wreaths, which were usually made of leaves that soon withered. Peter promises the elders, when the Chief Shepherd appears, the crown of glory that will never fade away (5:4).

p1_lion.f: Mosaic of a lion in the Musée National du Bardo in Tunis (3rd century AD).jpg
p1_lion.c: A Roman mosaic of a lion, 3rd century AD, in the Bardo Museum in Tunis. Lions were well known to Romans from the arena, and the Bible uses the lion as a picture of enemies (Psalm 22:13; 2 Timothy 4:17). Peter says the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (5:8).
p1_lion.d: A Roman mosaic of a lion, 3rd century AD, in the Bardo Museum in Tunis. Lions were well known to Romans from the arena, and the Bible uses the lion as a picture of enemies (Psalm 22:13; 2 Timothy 4:17). Peter says the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (5:8).

p1_goodshep.c: The Good Shepherd carrying a sheep, painted in the Catacomb of Priscilla in Rome in the second half of the 3rd century (a copy published by Joseph Wilpert in 1903). Peter calls Christ the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls (2:25) and the Chief Shepherd (5:4).
p1_goodshep.a: Joseph Wilpert (1903 copy of a 3rd-century painting), public domain

p1_noah.f: 1846 Noah's Ark oil on canvas 66 x 76.2 cm Philadelphia Museum of Art.jpg
p1_noah.c: Noah's Ark, painted by the American folk artist Edward Hicks in 1846 (Philadelphia Museum of Art). Peter says that in the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water (3:20).

p1_torches.c: Torches of Nero, painted by Henryk Siemiradzki in 1876. It imagines what Tacitus describes in his Annals (15.44): after the fire of Rome in AD 64 Nero blamed the Christians and put some to death at night as lamps. The scene is a 19th-century picture, not evidence.

p1_ankara.f: Ankara Hacı Bayram Mosque Exterior and Augustus Temple in 2011 04.jpg
p1_ankara.c: The Hacı Bayram Mosque in Ankara, with the Temple of Augustus and Rome beside it. Ankara is the modern city on the site of ancient Ancyra, a leading city of Galatia, one of the provinces Peter names (1:1). Peter names no town, so Ancyra is only an example of the kind of city his readers lived in.

p1_cappadocia.c: The Göreme Valley in Cappadocia, in central Turkey, with its rock formations of volcanic tuff. Cappadocia is one of the five provinces in 1:1. Peter does not say where in these provinces his readers lived.

p1_zion.c: The Dormition Abbey on Mount Zion, the southwest hill of Jerusalem that Christians have called Zion since early centuries. In the Old Testament, Zion is Jerusalem and especially the temple hill, and that is the Zion of Isaiah 28:16, which Peter quotes in 2:6.

p1_ararat.f: Mount Ararat, Two volcanic cones, Ararat Plain, Armenia.jpg
p1_ararat.c: Mount Ararat, with Great and Little Ararat, seen across the Ararat plain in Armenia. Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat, the region the Assyrians called Urartu. The volcano now called Ararat is one traditional candidate, but the Bible names a range of mountains and not this peak.

p1_obelisk.f: Obelisk via della Concilliazione Piazza San Pietro Vatican City.jpg
p1_obelisk.c: The obelisk in St Peter's Square, Vatican City. It was brought from Egypt under Caligula, stood in the circus of Gaius and Nero on the Vatican plain, and was moved to its present place in 1586. Tacitus says Nero put Christians to death in his gardens and circus after the fire of AD 64. Church tradition says Peter died in Rome under Nero, and his letter ends with greetings from Babylon (5:13).

p1_res.f: The Temple of Augustus and Rome with the Res Gestae Divi Augusti ("Deeds of the Divine Augustus") inscribed on the walls of the cella, Ancyra, Ankara (Turkey) (26068591006).jpg
p1_res.c: The Temple of Augustus and Rome at Ankara (ancient Ancyra), the leading city of the province of Galatia. The emperor's own account of his deeds, the Res Gestae, is inscribed on its walls in Latin and Greek. Peter writes to people in Galatia and four other provinces (1:1) and tells them to honor the king (2:17).
p1_res.n: The Temple of Augustus at Ancyra
p1_res.d: The Temple of Augustus and Rome at Ankara (ancient Ancyra), the leading city of the province of Galatia. The emperor's own account of his deeds, the Res Gestae, is inscribed on its walls in Latin and Greek. Peter writes to people in Galatia and four other provinces (1:1) and tells them to honor the king (2:17).

p1_isaiah.c: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (about 125-100 BC). Peter quotes Isaiah in 1:24-25, where all flesh is like grass and the word of the Lord lasts, and in 2:6-8, where a stone is laid in Zion.
p1_isaiah.d: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (about 125-100 BC). Peter quotes Isaiah in 1:24-25, where all flesh is like grass and the word of the Lord lasts, and in 2:6-8, where a stone is laid in Zion.

p1_sinai.c: Jebel Musa in the Sinai, the traditional Mount Sinai (Horeb). At Sinai God called Israel a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exodus 19:6). Peter says of the church that you are a royal priesthood, a holy nation (2:9). The exact site of Sinai is not certain.
p1_sinai.d: Jebel Musa in the Sinai, the traditional Mount Sinai (Horeb). At Sinai God called Israel a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exodus 19:6). Peter says of the church that you are a royal priesthood, a holy nation (2:9). The exact site of Sinai is not certain.

p1_west.c: Herodian stones of the Temple Mount's western retaining wall in Jerusalem. Peter calls Christ a living stone and believers living stones being built into a spiritual house (2:4-5). The stones of the Temple were famous (Mark 13:1), and the Temple was destroyed in AD 70.
p1_west.d: Herodian stones of the Temple Mount's western retaining wall in Jerusalem. Peter calls Christ a living stone and believers living stones being built into a spiritual house (2:4-5). The stones of the Temple were famous (Mark 13:1), and the Temple was destroyed in AD 70.

p1_collar.f: Inscribed bronze slave collar (Rome MNR 65043; CIL XV 7194).jpg
p1_collar.c: An inscribed bronze collar of a runaway slave, Museo Nazionale Romano, Rome. Such collars date mostly to the 4th century, but they show what slavery was like in the Roman world. Peter writes to household slaves and points them to Christ, who suffered and did not pay back (2:18-23).
p1_collar.d: An inscribed bronze collar of a runaway slave, Museo Nazionale Romano, Rome. Such collars date mostly to the 4th century, but they show what slavery was like in the Roman world. Peter writes to household slaves and points them to Christ, who suffered and did not pay back (2:18-23).

p1_nero.f: MBALyon2018 - Expo Claude - Aureus de Neron 54 ap J-C.jpg
p1_nero.c: A gold aureus struck in AD 54 for the new emperor Nero. Church tradition places Peter's death in Rome under Nero. Peter tells his readers to honor the king (2:17).
p1_nero.d: A gold aureus struck in AD 54 for the new emperor Nero. Church tradition places Peter's death in Rome under Nero. Peter tells his readers to honor the king (2:17).

p1_pliny.c: A statue of Pliny the Younger on the façade of Como cathedral, carved in the late 15th century. About AD 112 Pliny, governor of Bithynia and Pontus (two of the provinces Peter names), wrote to the emperor Trajan about people brought before him as Christians (Letters 10.96).
p1_pliny.n: Statue of Pliny the Younger, Como
p1_pliny.d: A statue of Pliny the Younger on the façade of Como cathedral, carved in the late 15th century. About AD 112 Pliny, governor of Bithynia and Pontus (two of the provinces Peter names), wrote to the emperor Trajan about people brought before him as Christians (Letters 10.96).

p1_dura.f: Christ Healing the Paralytic - Dura-Europos circa 232.jpg
p1_dura.c: Christ healing the paralytic, painted in the baptistery of the house church at Dura-Europos in Syria in the 3rd century (before the city fell in AD 256). It is the oldest known Christian baptistery and shows baptism as the early church practiced it. Peter ties baptism to Noah and to the resurrection of Jesus Christ (3:20-21).
p1_dura.d: Christ healing the paralytic, painted in the baptistery of the house church at Dura-Europos in Syria in the 3rd century (before the city fell in AD 256). It is the oldest known Christian baptistery and shows baptism as the early church practiced it. Peter ties baptism to Noah and to the resurrection of Jesus Christ (3:20-21).
p1_dura.a: Yale University Art Gallery, public domain

p1_forum.c: The Roman Forum, the center of the city of Rome. Peter's letter ends with greetings from the church in Babylon (5:13), and most readers take Babylon as a code name for Rome.

p1_babylon.c: Roman tower of the Babylon fortress in Old Cairo, Egypt. A few readers have thought Peter's Babylon (5:13) was this Egyptian site, but the fortress is later than Peter and the ancient writers who comment took Babylon to mean Rome.
p1_babylon.d: Roman tower of the Babylon fortress in Old Cairo, Egypt. A few readers have thought Peter's Babylon (5:13) was this Egyptian site, but the fortress is later than Peter and the ancient writers who comment took Babylon to mean Rome.

p1_banquet.f: Fresco showing guests at a banquet, from the House of the Triclinium in Pompeii, AD 40-79, National Archaeological Museum of Naples (49197773156).jpg
p1_banquet.c: A fresco of a dinner party from the House of the Triclinium at Pompeii (AD 40-79, National Archaeological Museum, Naples). Guests recline on couches while slaves serve them. Peter's readers had once joined in drunkenness and carousing, and their old friends were surprised when they stopped (4:3-4).
p1_banquet.d: A fresco of a dinner party from the House of the Triclinium at Pompeii (AD 40-79, National Archaeological Museum, Naples). Guests recline on couches while slaves serve them. Peter's readers had once joined in drunkenness and carousing, and their old friends were surprised when they stopped (4:3-4).

p1_corner.c: The Corner Stone, a watercolor by James Tissot (about 1886-94, Brooklyn Museum). Peter quotes Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 28:16 about the stone that the builders rejected, which became the cornerstone (2:6-7).

p2_p72_open.f: Vatican, Apostolic Library Ms Papyrus Bodmer VIII 2 (Papyrus 72) Ending of 1 Peter - Beginning of 2 Peter.jpg
p2_p72_open.c: A leaf of Papyrus 72 (Papyrus Bodmer VIII, Vatican Library) with the end of 1 Peter and the opening of 2 Peter. The scribe copied the two letters together, and this papyrus book from Egypt of the 3rd or 4th century is the earliest surviving copy of 2 Peter (1:1).
p2_p72_open.d: A leaf of Papyrus 72 (Papyrus Bodmer VIII, Vatican Library) with the end of 1 Peter and the opening of 2 Peter. The scribe copied the two letters together, and this papyrus book from Egypt of the 3rd or 4th century is the earliest surviving copy of 2 Peter (1:1).
p2_p72_open.a: Unknown scribe (3rd or 4th century), public domain

p2_p72_end.f: Vatican, Apostolic Library Ms Papyrus Bodmer VIII 2 (Papyrus 72) Ending of 2 Peter.jpg
p2_p72_end.c: A leaf of Papyrus 72 (Papyrus Bodmer VIII, Vatican Library) with the closing part of 2 Peter. Origen, Eusebius and Jerome say that some doubted the letter, yet it was being copied in Egypt by the 3rd or 4th century.
p2_p72_end.d: A leaf of Papyrus 72 (Papyrus Bodmer VIII, Vatican Library) with the closing part of 2 Peter. Origen, Eusebius and Jerome say that some doubted the letter, yet it was being copied in Egypt by the 3rd or 4th century.
p2_p72_end.a: Unknown scribe (3rd or 4th century), public domain

p2_lamp.f: Lamp - 1st century B.C.–4th century A.D. - Getty collection 83.AQ.377.525.jpg
p2_lamp.c: A clay oil lamp of the 1st century BC to the 4th century AD in the Getty collection. A lamp like this gave a small, steady light in a dark room. Peter says the prophetic word is like a lamp shining in a dark place until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts (1:19).
p2_lamp.d: A clay oil lamp of the 1st century BC to the 4th century AD in the Getty collection. A lamp like this gave a small, steady light in a dark room. Peter says the prophetic word is like a lamp shining in a dark place until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts (1:19).
p2_lamp.a: J. Paul Getty Museum, open content

p2_tent.c: A Bedouin camp at Wadi Rum in Jordan, with a tent of woven cloth. A tent is a light shelter that can be taken down and carried away. Peter speaks of putting off his own tent soon (1:13-14), a picture Paul also used for the body (2 Corinthians 5:1).
p2_tent.d: A Bedouin camp at Wadi Rum in Jordan, with a tent of woven cloth. A tent is a light shelter that can be taken down and carried away. Peter speaks of putting off his own tent soon (1:13-14), a picture Paul also used for the body (2 Corinthians 5:1).

p2_tabor.c: The Church of the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor. Peter says he and the others heard the voice from heaven when they were with Jesus on the holy mountain (1:16-18). He does not name the mountain, and many readers think of Tabor or of Mount Hermon.

p2_hermon.c: Snow-capped Mount Hermon, north of Caesarea Philippi. Matthew 17:1 puts the Transfiguration six days after Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi, so some readers place it on or near Hermon. The letter says only the holy mountain (1:18).

p2_dtrans.c: The Transfiguration, by Gustave Doré (1866). Peter recalls this scene as the moment when the apostles saw Christ’s majesty and heard the voice from heaven (1:16-18).

p2_obelisk.f: Obelisk via della Concilliazione Piazza San Pietro Vatican City.jpg
p2_obelisk.c: The obelisk in St Peter’s Square, Vatican City. It stood in the circus of Gaius and Nero on the Vatican plain, where church tradition places the death of Peter under Nero. The writer says he will soon put off his tent, as the Lord had made clear to him (1:14).

p2_deiralla.c: A modern transcription of part of the Deir ’Alla wall text, about 800 BC, which begins as the book of Balaam son of Beor, a seer. This picture shows the typeset letters, not the plaster itself. Peter says the false teachers follow the way of Balaam son of Beor (2:15).
p2_deiralla.d: A modern transcription of part of the Deir ’Alla wall text, about 800 BC, which begins as the book of Balaam son of Beor, a seer. This picture shows the typeset letters, not the plaster itself. Peter says the false teachers follow the way of Balaam son of Beor (2:15).

p2_tell.c: Tell Deir ’Alla in the Jordan valley, where an expedition in 1967 found plaster fragments with the name of Balaam son of Beor. Numbers 22-24 tells of Balaam, whom Peter names in 2:15-16.

p2_charnel.f: Bab edh-Dhra cemetery Early Bronze Age III charnel house.jpg
p2_charnel.c: A mud-brick building for bones in the great Early Bronze Age cemetery at Bab edh-Dhra, east of the Dead Sea. The town beside it is one of the candidate sites for Sodom, which Peter says God reduced to ashes as an example (2:6). No inscription there names Sodom.
p2_charnel.d: A mud-brick building for bones in the great Early Bronze Age cemetery at Bab edh-Dhra, east of the Dead Sea. The town beside it is one of the candidate sites for Sodom, which Peter says God reduced to ashes as an example (2:6). No inscription there names Sodom.

p2_babgate.f: Bab edh-Dhra gate overlooking south end dead sea 2014.jpg
p2_babgate.c: The town gate at Bab edh-Dhra, looking toward the south end of the Dead Sea. Bab edh-Dhra is one proposed site for Sodom (2:6), but the Bible does not say where the cities stood, and other places are also proposed.

p2_sodom.f: Mount Sodom, Dead Sea Outlook, Israel 03.jpg
p2_sodom.c: Mount Sodom, a ridge of salt on the southwest shore of the Dead Sea. The name is old, but it does not show that Sodom stood here. Peter says God condemned Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly (2:6).

p2_balaam.c: Balaam and the Ass, by Rembrandt (1626). Numbers 22 tells how the donkey saw the angel of the LORD and spoke. Peter says Balaam was rebuked by a donkey that spoke with a man’s voice (2:15-16).

p2_ararat.f: Mount Ararat, Two volcanic cones, Ararat Plain, Armenia.jpg
p2_ararat.c: Mount Ararat, with Great and Little Ararat, seen across the Ararat plain in Armenia. Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Peter recalls that God preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, when the flood came on the ungodly world (2:5; 3:6). The Bible names a range of mountains and not this peak.

p2_noah.f: 1846 Noah's Ark oil on canvas 66 x 76.2 cm Philadelphia Museum of Art.jpg
p2_noah.c: Noah’s Ark, painted by the American folk artist Edward Hicks in 1846 (Philadelphia Museum of Art). Peter says God preserved Noah with seven others when he brought the flood on the ungodly world (2:5).

p2_tablet.c: Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, known as the Flood Tablet, from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, 7th century BC (British Museum). It tells of a man who builds a boat to save his family and living creatures from a flood. Scholars compare it with Genesis 6-9. Peter says only that God preserved Noah and brought the flood on the ungodly world (2:5; 3:6).
p2_tablet.d: Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, known as the Flood Tablet, from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, 7th century BC (British Museum). It tells of a man who builds a boat to save his family and living creatures from a flood. Scholars compare it with Genesis 6-9. Peter says only that God preserved Noah and brought the flood on the ungodly world (2:5; 3:6).

p2_dog.c: A black-and-white mosaic of a dog at the door of a house in Pompeii, with the Latin warning cave canem, beware of the dog. Dogs guarded Roman houses. Peter ends chapter 2 with two sayings about animals: a dog returns to its vomit (Proverbs 26:11), and a washed sow goes back to wallowing in the mud (2:22).
p2_dog.d: A black-and-white mosaic of a dog at the door of a house in Pompeii, with the Latin warning cave canem, beware of the dog. Dogs guarded Roman houses. Peter ends chapter 2 with two sayings about animals: a dog returns to its vomit (Proverbs 26:11), and a washed sow goes back to wallowing in the mud (2:22).

p2_isaiah.c: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (about 125-100 BC), which holds the whole book of Isaiah. Peter’s new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells (3:13) recall Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22, so the passage he knew was already in scrolls like this one.
p2_isaiah.d: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (about 125-100 BC), which holds the whole book of Isaiah. Peter’s new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells (3:13) recall Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22, so the passage he knew was already in scrolls like this one.

p2_p46.c: A folio of Papyrus 46, a papyrus book of Paul’s letters usually dated to about AD 200, though some scholars place it earlier. Peter calls Paul our beloved brother and says his letters, like the rest of the Scriptures, are twisted by the ignorant and unstable (3:15-16).
p2_p46.d: A folio of Papyrus 46, a papyrus book of Paul’s letters usually dated to about AD 200, though some scholars place it earlier. Peter calls Paul our beloved brother and says his letters, like the rest of the Scriptures, are twisted by the ignorant and unstable (3:15-16).

j1_p9.f: Cambridge MA, Harvard Houghton Library MS Gr SM3736 - P. Oxy. III 402 (Papyrus 9) recto 1 John, 4, 11–12.jpg
j1_p9.c: Papyrus 9 (P. Oxy. III 402), a single leaf from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, now at Harvard’s Houghton Library, usually dated to the 3rd century. It has 1 John 4:11-12 and 14-17, which includes the words that God is love (4:16). It is one of the earliest surviving pieces of the letter.
j1_p9.d: Papyrus 9 (P. Oxy. III 402), a single leaf from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, now at Harvard’s Houghton Library, usually dated to the 3rd century. It has 1 John 4:11-12 and 14-17, which includes the words that God is love (4:16). It is one of the earliest surviving pieces of the letter.

j1_p52.f: Manchester, John Rylands Library Ms Greek P 457 (Papyrus 52) recto John 18, 31-33.jpg
j1_p52.c: Papyrus 52 in the John Rylands Library, Manchester: a scrap of papyrus with John 18:31-33 on one side and 18:37-38 on the other, usually dated to the 2nd century. It is the oldest known piece of the Gospel of John, the book that 1 John so often echoes.
j1_p52.d: Papyrus 52 in the John Rylands Library, Manchester: a scrap of papyrus with John 18:31-33 on one side and 18:37-38 on the other, usually dated to the 2nd century. It is the oldest known piece of the Gospel of John, the book that 1 John so often echoes.

j1_p66.c: A page of Papyrus 66, a papyrus book that holds large parts of the Gospel of John and is usually dated to about AD 200. The letter shares much of the Gospel’s wording, such as light, life, abiding and the new commandment, and 1 John 5:13 restates the purpose given in John 20:31.
j1_p66.d: A page of Papyrus 66, a papyrus book that holds large parts of the Gospel of John and is usually dated to about AD 200. The letter shares much of the Gospel’s wording, such as light, life, abiding and the new commandment, and 1 John 5:13 restates the purpose given in John 20:31.

j1_murat.c: The Muratorian Fragment, a Latin list of New Testament books found in the Ambrosian Library at Milan. The copy is of the 8th century, and the list is usually dated to the late 2nd century, though some scholars argue for the 4th. While speaking of John’s Gospel it recalls the opening words of 1 John about what the writer has seen and heard.
j1_murat.d: The Muratorian Fragment, a Latin list of New Testament books found in the Ambrosian Library at Milan. The copy is of the 8th century, and the list is usually dated to the late 2nd century, though some scholars argue for the 4th. While speaking of John’s Gospel it recalls the opening words of 1 John about what the writer has seen and heard.

j1_didache.c: A strip from the Codex Hierosolymitanus (copied in AD 1056), the only complete Greek copy of the Didache, with its title lines. The Didache is an early church manual. Its chapters 11-13 tell how to test apostles and prophets who travel from town to town, a problem close to the one in 1 John 4:1.
j1_didache.d: A strip from the Codex Hierosolymitanus (copied in AD 1056), the only complete Greek copy of the Didache, with its title lines. The Didache is an early church manual. Its chapters 11-13 tell how to test apostles and prophets who travel from town to town, a problem close to the one in 1 John 4:1.

j1_basilica.f: Basilica of St. John in Ephesus 01.jpg
j1_basilica.c: The ruins of the Basilica of St John on Ayasuluk Hill, Selçuk, beside ancient Ephesus. The church was built under the emperor Justinian in the 6th century over an earlier shrine. Church tradition says the apostle John spent his last years at Ephesus and was buried here. The letter itself names no place.

j1_basilica2.f: Basilica of St. John in Ephesus 04.jpg
j1_basilica2.c: Columns and arches in the Basilica of St John at Ephesus. Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus about AD 190, wrote that John, who leaned on the Lord’s breast, lay at rest in Ephesus (quoted in Eusebius, Church History 3.31; 5.24).

j1_tomb.f: Tomb of Saint John the Apostle.jpg
j1_tomb.c: The traditional tomb of John the apostle inside the ruins of the Basilica at Ephesus. The shrine is marked by a slab, and the tradition goes back at least to Polycrates about AD 190. The letter does not say who wrote it or where.

j1_sebastoi.c: The ruins of the Temple of the Sebastoi, also called the Temple of Domitian, at Ephesus. It was dedicated about AD 89-90 to the emperor Domitian and his family, and it earned the city its first title as keeper of an imperial temple. Idols in 1 John 5:21 would have included such worship as well as the old gods of the city.

j1_sebastoi2.c: The terrace and foundations of the Temple of the Sebastoi at Ephesus. The temple stood above the city center and was the first of the city’s imperial temples.

j1_domitian.f: Bust of Domitianus in Musei Capitolini.jpg
j1_domitian.c: A marble bust of the emperor Domitian (reigned AD 81-96) in the Capitoline Museums, Rome. Church writers from Irenaeus on place John’s old age at Ephesus in the reign of Domitian, when emperor worship was strong in Asia. 1 John does not name any ruler.
j1_domitian.d: A marble bust of the emperor Domitian (reigned AD 81-96) in the Capitoline Museums, Rome. Church writers from Irenaeus on place John’s old age at Ephesus in the reign of Domitian, when emperor worship was strong in Asia. 1 John does not name any ruler.

j1_comma.f: Cod. Montfortianus p 434 r 1 John 5 Comma.jpg
j1_comma.c: A page of Codex Montfortianus (Trinity College, Dublin), a Greek manuscript copied about 1520 that has the extra words in 1 John 5:7-8 about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in heaven. The words are not in the early Greek manuscripts, and the Berean Standard Bible leaves them out. They were printed in Erasmus’s third edition (1522).
j1_comma.d: A page of Codex Montfortianus (Trinity College, Dublin), a Greek manuscript copied about 1520 that has the extra words in 1 John 5:7-8 about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in heaven. The words are not in the early Greek manuscripts, and the Berean Standard Bible leaves them out. They were printed in Erasmus’s third edition (1522).

j1_thomas.c: The Incredulity of Saint Thomas, by Caravaggio (1601-02). John 20:27 has Jesus invite Thomas to touch his wounds. The prologue of 1 John says the writers heard, saw with their eyes, looked at and touched the Word of life (1:1).

j1_light.f: Hunt, William Homan - The Light of the World - 1853-54.jpg
j1_light.c: The Light of the World, by William Holman Hunt (1853-54). The painting shows Christ at a closed door with a lantern (Revelation 3:20). Jesus calls himself the light of the world in John 8:12, and 1 John 1:5 says that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.

j1_polycarp.c: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, in a mosaic in the church of Sant’Apollinare Nuovo, Ravenna (completed about AD 526). Irenaeus says that as a boy he heard Polycarp tell of his talks with John. Polycarp’s own letter to the Philippians (7) repeats the test of 1 John 4:2-3, without naming the letter.
j1_polycarp.a: Master of Sant’Apollinare Nuovo (about AD 526), public domain

j1_patmos.c: The Cave of the Apocalypse on the island of Patmos, where tradition says John saw the visions of Revelation. Revelation 1:9 says John was on Patmos, and the church writers from Irenaeus on place his time at Ephesus in the reign of Domitian. 1 John does not name its author.

j2_sin_end.f: End of 1 John and beginning of 2 John in Sinaiticus.jpg
j2_sin_end.c: A page of Codex Sinaiticus, a Greek Bible copied in the 4th century AD, with the end of 1 John (5:5-21) and the first seven verses of 2 John. Sinaiticus places 2 John, 3 John and Jude after 1 John, in the years when Eusebius still listed 2 and 3 John among the disputed books.
j2_sin_end.n: 1 John 5 and 2 John 1 in Codex Sinaiticus
j2_sin_end.d: A page of Codex Sinaiticus, a Greek Bible copied in the 4th century AD, with the end of 1 John (5:5-21) and the first seven verses of 2 John. Sinaiticus places 2 John, 3 John and Jude after 1 John, in the years when Eusebius still listed 2 and 3 John among the disputed books.

j2_sin_23.f: 2 John, 3 John, and Jude in Sinaiticus.jpg
j2_sin_23.c: A page of Codex Sinaiticus (4th century AD) with 2 John, 3 John and Jude. The two short letters of the elder sit side by side, as they do in most later Bibles.
j2_sin_23.n: 2 John, 3 John and Jude in Codex Sinaiticus
j2_sin_23.d: A page of Codex Sinaiticus (4th century AD) with 2 John, 3 John and Jude. The two short letters of the elder sit side by side, as they do in most later Bibles.

j2_irenaeus.c: The title page of the first printed edition of Irenaeus’s Against Heresies, edited by Erasmus and printed by Johannes Froben at Basel in 1526. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, quotes 2 John 7-8 (3.16.8) and 2 John 10-11 (1.16.3) as the words of John, the Lord’s disciple. The work survives mostly in an old Latin translation.
j2_irenaeus.d: The title page of the first printed edition of Irenaeus’s Against Heresies, edited by Erasmus and printed by Johannes Froben at Basel in 1526. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, quotes 2 John 7-8 (3.16.8) and 2 John 10-11 (1.16.3) as the words of John, the Lord’s disciple. The work survives mostly in an old Latin translation.
j2_irenaeus.a: Erasmus and Johannes Froben (Basel, 1526), public domain

j2_eusebius.f: Eusebius of Caesarea and Ammonius of Alexandria Rabbula Gospels Icon.jpg
j2_eusebius.c: A 6th-century portrait of Eusebius of Caesarea (with Ammonius of Alexandria) from the Rabbula Gospels, a Syriac Gospel book. In his Church History (3.25) Eusebius lists 1 John among the books accepted everywhere and 2 and 3 John among the disputed ones.
j2_eusebius.d: A 6th-century portrait of Eusebius of Caesarea (with Ammonius of Alexandria) from the Rabbula Gospels, a Syriac Gospel book. In his Church History (3.25) Eusebius lists 1 John among the books accepted everywhere and 2 and 3 John among the disputed ones.

j2_peshitta.f: Peshitta464 (The S.S. Teacher's Edition-The Holy Bible - Plate XIII).jpg
j2_peshitta.c: A section of British Library Add. MS 14425, a copy of the Peshitta, the Syriac Bible, whose scribe says it was written at Amida in AD 464. This piece has Exodus 13:14-16. The Peshitta at first held only James, 1 Peter and 1 John among the General Letters, and 2 John came into Syriac Bibles in later translations.
j2_peshitta.n: The Peshitta, British Library Add. MS 14425
j2_peshitta.d: A section of British Library Add. MS 14425, a copy of the Peshitta, the Syriac Bible, whose scribe says it was written at Amida in AD 464. This piece has Exodus 13:14-16. The Peshitta at first held only James, 1 Peter and 1 John among the General Letters, and 2 John came into Syriac Bibles in later translations.

j2_inkwell.f: Terracotta inkwell and bronze stylus MET DP121128.jpg
j2_inkwell.c: A Roman terracotta inkwell with a bronze stylus, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Ink was a black mix of soot and gum, written with a cut reed pen on papyrus; the stylus was for wax tablets. The writer of 2 John would rather not use “paper and ink” (verse 12) but speak face to face.
j2_inkwell.d: A Roman terracotta inkwell with a bronze stylus, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Ink was a black mix of soot and gum, written with a cut reed pen on papyrus; the stylus was for wax tablets. The writer of 2 John would rather not use “paper and ink” (verse 12) but speak face to face.

j3_apion.c: A papyrus letter of the 2nd century AD in the Egyptian Museum and Papyrus Collection, Berlin (P. 7950). Apion, a recruit in the Roman fleet at Misenum in Italy, writes home to his father Epimachus in Egypt. After the greeting he prays that his father is well, as the elder prays for the health of Gaius in 3 John 2, and he ends with greetings to people at home.
j3_apion.d: A papyrus letter of the 2nd century AD in the Egyptian Museum and Papyrus Collection, Berlin (P. 7950). Apion, a recruit in the Roman fleet at Misenum in Italy, writes home to his father Epimachus in Egypt. After the greeting he prays that his father is well, as the elder prays for the health of Gaius in 3 John 2, and he ends with greetings to people at home.
j3_apion.a: Sandra Steiß (scan), Ägyptisches Museum und Papyrussammlung Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0

j3_reedpen.f: Writing pen made of obliquely cut reed, reed - Museo Egizio, Turin P 668 p01.jpg
j3_reedpen.c: A writing pen cut from a reed, from Roman Egypt (1st to 2nd century AD), in the Museo Egizio, Turin. The “pen” of 3 John 13 is the Greek kalamos, a reed like this one, cut at a slant and dipped in black ink.
j3_reedpen.n: A reed pen from Roman Egypt
j3_reedpen.d: A writing pen cut from a reed, from Roman Egypt (1st to 2nd century AD), in the Museo Egizio, Turin. The “pen” of 3 John 13 is the Greek kalamos, a reed like this one, cut at a slant and dipped in black ink.

j3_pergamum.c: The steep theater on the acropolis of Pergamum (Bergama, Turkey). A church list of about AD 380, the Apostolic Constitutions, names a Gaius as bishop of Pergamum. The tradition is late and cannot be checked, and 3 John does not say where its Gaius lived.
j3_pergamum.d: The steep theater on the acropolis of Pergamum (Bergama, Turkey). A church list of about AD 380, the Apostolic Constitutions, names a Gaius as bishop of Pergamum. The tradition is late and cannot be checked, and 3 John does not say where its Gaius lived.

j3_philadelphia.c: Brick piers of the Byzantine Church of St John at Alaşehir, Turkey, the ancient Philadelphia. The church was built centuries after the New Testament. The Apostolic Constitutions (about AD 380) name a Demetrius as bishop of Philadelphia, a late tradition that may or may not mean the Demetrius of 3 John 12.
j3_philadelphia.d: Brick piers of the Byzantine Church of St John at Alaşehir, Turkey, the ancient Philadelphia. The church was built centuries after the New Testament. The Apostolic Constitutions (about AD 380) name a Demetrius as bishop of Philadelphia, a late tradition that may or may not mean the Demetrius of 3 John 12.

j3_kafr_hawr.c: The village of Kafr Hawr below Mount Hermon in Syria, photographed by Félix Bonfils in the late 19th century. A Greek inscription found here was set up by a man who called himself a slave of the Syrian goddess and who collected money for her on his journeys. The brothers of 3 John 7 took nothing from the pagans they preached to.
j3_kafr_hawr.n: Kafr Hawr (Kefr Hawar), near Mount Hermon
j3_kafr_hawr.d: The village of Kafr Hawr below Mount Hermon in Syria, photographed by Félix Bonfils in the late 19th century. A Greek inscription found here was set up by a man who called himself a slave of the Syrian goddess and who collected money for her on his journeys. The brothers of 3 John 7 took nothing from the pagans they preached to.
j3_kafr_hawr.a: Félix Bonfils (British Library EAP644/1/37), public domain

j3_caupona.c: The caupona of Philippus at Pompeii, buried in AD 79. A caupona sold food and wine, and many also let rooms. Roman writers often speak of inns as dirty and rough, which is one reason travelers looked for friends to stay with. Gaius opened his home to traveling brothers (3 John 5-8).
j3_caupona.d: The caupona of Philippus at Pompeii, buried in AD 79. A caupona sold food and wine, and many also let rooms. Roman writers often speak of inns as dirty and rough, which is one reason travelers looked for friends to stay with. Gaius opened his home to traveling brothers (3 John 5-8).

jd_p78.f: Oxford, Sackler Library MS P.Oxy. XXXIV 2684 (Papyrus 78) verso Jude 1, 4-5; 1, 7-8.jpg
jd_p78.c: Papyrus 78 (P.Oxy. XXXIV 2684), a small folded sheet from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt with Jude 4-5 and 7-8 in Greek, copied in the 3rd or 4th century. Its small size and wide shape suggest it was carried as a charm. With Papyrus 72 it is one of the two oldest copies of Jude.
jd_p78.n: Papyrus 78: Jude on a tiny charm
jd_p78.d: Papyrus 78 (P.Oxy. XXXIV 2684), a small folded sheet from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt with Jude 4-5 and 7-8 in Greek, copied in the 3rd or 4th century. Its small size and wide shape suggest it was carried as a charm. With Papyrus 72 it is one of the two oldest copies of Jude.
jd_p78.a: Sackler Library, Oxford (3rd-4th century), public domain

jd_alex.c: The closing lines of Jude in Codex Alexandrinus, a Greek Bible of the 5th century now in the British Library, with the scribe’s decorated end title for the letter. Alexandrinus is one of the old copies that read “Jesus” in Jude 5.
jd_alex.n: The end of Jude in Codex Alexandrinus
jd_alex.d: The closing lines of Jude in Codex Alexandrinus, a Greek Bible of the 5th century now in the British Library, with the scribe’s decorated end title for the letter. Alexandrinus is one of the old copies that read “Jesus” in Jude 5.

jd_enoch_geez.f: Etiopia, libro di enoch (in ge'ez), xviii secolo (bnf).jpg
jd_enoch_geez.c: An 18th-century copy of the Book of Enoch in Ge‘ez, the old church language of Ethiopia, from the Bibliothèque nationale de France. The whole book survives only in this language, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts it as Scripture. Jude 14-15 quotes its opening vision.
jd_enoch_geez.n: The Book of Enoch in Ge‘ez
jd_enoch_geez.d: An 18th-century copy of the Book of Enoch in Ge‘ez, the old church language of Ethiopia, from the Bibliothèque nationale de France. The whole book survives only in this language, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts it as Scripture. Jude 14-15 quotes its opening vision.

jd_4q201.c: Pieces of 4Q201, the oldest of the Aramaic copies of the Book of Enoch found in Cave 4 at Qumran, written in the first half of the 2nd century BC. It has parts of the opening chapters, the Book of the Watchers. The copies from Qumran show that the book Jude quotes was read in the land of Israel long before his time.
jd_4q201.n: An Aramaic copy of Enoch from Qumran (4Q201)
jd_4q201.d: Pieces of 4Q201, the oldest of the Aramaic copies of the Book of Enoch found in Cave 4 at Qumran, written in the first half of the 2nd century BC. It has parts of the opening chapters, the Book of the Watchers. The copies from Qumran show that the book Jude quotes was read in the land of Israel long before his time.
jd_4q201.a: Dead Sea Scrolls, 4Q201 (2nd century BC), public domain

jd_blake_enoch.c: Enoch, a lithograph of 1807 by William Blake, his only known work in that medium. Blake shows the patriarch seated among figures of the arts. Genesis says only that Enoch walked with God and that God took him; a large body of later Jewish writing was set under his name, and Jude 14 calls him “the seventh from Adam.”
jd_blake_enoch.d: Enoch, a lithograph of 1807 by William Blake, his only known work in that medium. Blake shows the patriarch seated among figures of the arts. Genesis says only that Enoch walked with God and that God took him; a large body of later Jewish writing was set under his name, and Jude 14 calls him “the seventh from Adam.”

jd_signorelli.f: Signorelli, Luca - Moses's Testament and Death - 1481-82.jpg
jd_signorelli.c: The Testament and Death of Moses, a fresco of about 1482 in the Sistine Chapel, by Luca Signorelli with Bartolomeo della Gatta. Moses reads the law, hands his staff to Joshua, is shown the promised land from Mount Nebo by an angel, and is mourned at the upper left. Jude 9 refers to a Jewish story about what happened to his body afterward.
jd_signorelli.n: Signorelli, The Testament and Death of Moses
jd_signorelli.d: The Testament and Death of Moses, a fresco of about 1482 in the Sistine Chapel, by Luca Signorelli with Bartolomeo della Gatta. Moses reads the law, hands his staff to Joshua, is shown the promised land from Mount Nebo by an angel, and is mourned at the upper left. Jude 9 refers to a Jewish story about what happened to his body afterward.

jd_korah.f: Botticcelli, Sandro - The Punishment of Korah and the Stoning of Moses and Aaron - 1481-82.jpg
jd_korah.c: The Punishment of Korah, Dathan and Abiram, a fresco of 1481-82 by Sandro Botticelli in the Sistine Chapel. In the center Moses calls down judgment on the rebels as their incense is refused; at the left the ground opens under them (Numbers 16). Jude 11 says the intruders “have perished in Korah’s rebellion.”
jd_korah.d: The Punishment of Korah, Dathan and Abiram, a fresco of 1481-82 by Sandro Botticelli in the Sistine Chapel. In the center Moses calls down judgment on the rebels as their incense is refused; at the left the ground opens under them (Numbers 16). Jude 11 says the intruders “have perished in Korah’s rebellion.”

jd_martin_sodom.c: The Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, painted by John Martin in 1852, now in the Laing Art Gallery, Newcastle. Lot and his daughters flee at the right while his wife looks back. Jude 7 says the cities “are on display as an example.”
jd_martin_sodom.n: John Martin, The Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (1852)
jd_martin_sodom.d: The Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, painted by John Martin in 1852, now in the Laing Art Gallery, Newcastle. Lot and his daughters flee at the right while his wife looks back. Jude 7 says the cities “are on display as an example.”

jd_agape.f: Catacombe di Priscilla, Rome - Fresco of a Christian Agape feast - Fractio panis - Greek chapel - 2nd - 4th century.jpg
jd_agape.c: A wall painting in the Greek Chapel of the Catacomb of Priscilla in Rome, of the 2nd to 4th century, known as the Fractio Panis, “the breaking of the bread.” Seven people sit at a table with a cup, fish and baskets of bread. It may show the Lord’s Supper, a church meal or a meal for the dead; scholars differ. Jude 12 speaks of the church’s “love feasts.”
jd_agape.n: A shared meal in the Catacomb of Priscilla
jd_agape.d: A wall painting in the Greek Chapel of the Catacomb of Priscilla in Rome, of the 2nd to 4th century, known as the Fractio Panis, “the breaking of the bread.” Seven people sit at a table with a cup, fish and baskets of bread. It may show the Lord’s Supper, a church meal or a meal for the dead; scholars differ. Jude 12 speaks of the church’s “love feasts.”
jd_agape.a: Catacomb of Priscilla, Rome (2nd-4th century), public domain

jd_nebo_church.f: Memorial Church of Moses, Mount Nebo, Jordan (40633713832).jpg
jd_nebo_church.c: The Memorial Church of Moses on the summit of Mount Nebo in Jordan. Christians built here in the 4th century to mark the place where Moses saw the promised land and died (Deuteronomy 34). No grave is shown, since Deuteronomy says that no one knows it. Jude 9 uses a Jewish story about the body of Moses.
jd_nebo_church.n: The Memorial Church of Moses, Mount Nebo
jd_nebo_church.d: The Memorial Church of Moses on the summit of Mount Nebo in Jordan. Christians built here in the 4th century to mark the place where Moses saw the promised land and died (Deuteronomy 34). No grave is shown, since Deuteronomy says that no one knows it. Jude 9 uses a Jewish story about the body of Moses.

jd_nebo_view.f: Overhead view from Mount Nebo of the Dead Sea and Jordan Valley area.jpg
jd_nebo_view.c: The view west from Mount Nebo: the north end of the Dead Sea at the left, the Jordan valley, and Jericho beyond. Deuteronomy 34 says the Lord showed Moses the whole land from here before he died.
jd_nebo_view.d: The view west from Mount Nebo: the north end of the Dead Sea at the left, the Jordan valley, and Jericho beyond. Deuteronomy 34 says the Lord showed Moses the whole land from here before he died.

rv_patmos_mon.c: The fortified Monastery of St John the Theologian on the hilltop of Patmos, founded by the monk Christodoulos in 1088. John says he was on Patmos “because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (Revelation 1:9).
rv_patmos_mon.n: The Monastery of St John, Patmos
rv_patmos_mon.d: The fortified Monastery of St John the Theologian on the hilltop of Patmos, founded by the monk Christodoulos in 1088. John says he was on Patmos “because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (Revelation 1:9).

rv_velazquez.f: Diego Velázquez - St John the Evangelist at Patmos - WGA24356.jpg
rv_velazquez.c: St John the Evangelist on the Island of Patmos, painted by Diego Velázquez about 1618 (National Gallery, London). John writes as he looks up at the vision of the woman clothed with the sun in chapter 12.
rv_velazquez.d: St John the Evangelist on the Island of Patmos, painted by Diego Velázquez about 1618 (National Gallery, London). John writes as he looks up at the vision of the woman clothed with the sun in chapter 12.

rv_smyrna.c: The remains of the Roman agora of Smyrna in modern Izmir, rebuilt after an earthquake in AD 178. The letter to Smyrna (Revelation 2:8-11) speaks of poverty, slander and coming prison.
rv_smyrna.d: The remains of the Roman agora of Smyrna in modern Izmir, rebuilt after an earthquake in AD 178. The letter to Smyrna (Revelation 2:8-11) speaks of poverty, slander and coming prison.

rv_pergamon_altar.c: The Great Altar of Pergamum, built in the 2nd century BC and rebuilt in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. It is one of the suggestions for “where the throne of Satan sits” in Revelation 2:13; others point to the temple of the emperor or the governor’s court.
rv_pergamon_altar.d: The Great Altar of Pergamum, built in the 2nd century BC and rebuilt in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. It is one of the suggestions for “where the throne of Satan sits” in Revelation 2:13; others point to the temple of the emperor or the governor’s court.

rv_thyatira.c: Columns in the small excavated area of ancient Thyatira, in the center of modern Akhisar, Turkey. The letter to Thyatira is the longest of the seven (Revelation 2:18-29).
rv_thyatira.d: Columns in the small excavated area of ancient Thyatira, in the center of modern Akhisar, Turkey. The letter to Thyatira is the longest of the seven (Revelation 2:18-29).

rv_sardis_artemis.c: The great temple of Artemis at Sardis, below the acropolis that was twice captured by surprise. Christ warns the church, “If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief” (Revelation 3:3).
rv_sardis_artemis.n: The temple of Artemis at Sardis
rv_sardis_artemis.d: The great temple of Artemis at Sardis, below the acropolis that was twice captured by surprise. Christ warns the church, “If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief” (Revelation 3:3).

rv_sardis_syn.f: Sardis Synagogue, late 3rd century AD, Sardis, Lydia, Turkey (19331773400).jpg
rv_sardis_syn.c: The large synagogue at Sardis, built into part of the city’s bath and gymnasium complex and used from the late 3rd century AD. It shows a strong and settled Jewish community in a city of the seven churches, later than John’s time.
rv_sardis_syn.d: The large synagogue at Sardis, built into part of the city’s bath and gymnasium complex and used from the late 3rd century AD. It shows a strong and settled Jewish community in a city of the seven churches, later than John’s time.

rv_domitian_temple.c: The platform of the temple of the emperors at Ephesus, dedicated about AD 89-90 in the reign of Domitian. Most scholars date Revelation to his reign. The worship of the emperors stands behind the beast and its image in Revelation 13.
rv_domitian_temple.n: The Temple of Domitian at Ephesus
rv_domitian_temple.d: The platform of the temple of the emperors at Ephesus, dedicated about AD 89-90 in the reign of Domitian. Most scholars date Revelation to his reign. The worship of the emperors stands behind the beast and its image in Revelation 13.

rv_domitia_coin.c: A silver denarius of the empress Domitia, struck under Domitian about AD 82-83. The reverse shows their dead infant son, called divine, seated on a globe with seven stars around him. Christ in Revelation 1:16 holds seven stars in his right hand.
rv_domitia_coin.n: Domitia’s coin: the emperor’s son among seven stars
rv_domitia_coin.d: A silver denarius of the empress Domitia, struck under Domitian about AD 82-83. The reverse shows their dead infant son, called divine, seated on a globe with seven stars around him. Christ in Revelation 1:16 holds seven stars in his right hand.

rv_nero.c: A portrait of the emperor Nero (ruled AD 54-68) in the Capitoline Museums, Rome, restored in the 17th century. Nero persecuted the Christians of Rome in AD 64. The numbers 666 and 616 both fit his name written in Hebrew letters, and rumors after his death said he would return.
rv_nero.d: A portrait of the emperor Nero (ruled AD 54-68) in the Capitoline Museums, Rome, restored in the 17th century. Nero persecuted the Christians of Rome in AD 64. The numbers 666 and 616 both fit his name written in Hebrew letters, and rumors after his death said he would return.

rv_p115.c: Papyrus 115 (P. Oxy. LXVI 4499), pieces of a copy of Revelation from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, of the late 3rd or early 4th century, now in Oxford. At Revelation 13:18 it gives the number of the beast as 616.
rv_p115.d: Papyrus 115 (P. Oxy. LXVI 4499), pieces of a copy of Revelation from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, of the late 3rd or early 4th century, now in Oxford. At Revelation 13:18 it gives the number of the beast as 616.

rv_p47.c: A page of Papyrus 47 (Chester Beatty III), the oldest substantial copy of Revelation, written in the 3rd century, now in the Chester Beatty Library, Dublin. This page holds Revelation 13:16-14:4, including the number of the beast, which it gives as 666.
rv_p47.d: A page of Papyrus 47 (Chester Beatty III), the oldest substantial copy of Revelation, written in the 3rd century, now in the Chester Beatty Library, Dublin. This page holds Revelation 13:16-14:4, including the number of the beast, which it gives as 666.

rv_megiddo.c: The mound of ancient Megiddo above the Jezreel valley in northern Israel, a fortress that guarded the main road and saw many battles. “Armageddon” in Revelation 16:16 is usually taken as Har Megiddo, “the mountain of Megiddo.”
rv_megiddo.d: The mound of ancient Megiddo above the Jezreel valley in northern Israel, a fortress that guarded the main road and saw many battles. “Armageddon” in Revelation 16:16 is usually taken as Har Megiddo, “the mountain of Megiddo.”

rv_babylon.c: Rebuilt walls among the ruins of Babylon on the Euphrates, south of Baghdad. The city that destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC had been reduced to a small town long before John’s day, and its name became a byword for a proud and godless power (Revelation 14:8; 17-18).
rv_babylon.d: Rebuilt walls among the ruins of Babylon on the Euphrates, south of Baghdad. The city that destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC had been reduced to a small town long before John’s day, and its name became a byword for a proud and godless power (Revelation 14:8; 17-18).
rv_babylon.a: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin, CC BY-SA 4.0

rv_ishtar.c: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon, built by Nebuchadnezzar II about 575 BC, rebuilt from its glazed bricks in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin. It shows the splendor of the city whose name Revelation gives to “Babylon the great.”
rv_ishtar.d: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon, built by Nebuchadnezzar II about 575 BC, rebuilt from its glazed bricks in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin. It shows the splendor of the city whose name Revelation gives to “Babylon the great.”

rv_euphrates.c: The Euphrates River below Dura-Europos in Syria, a frontier town fought over by Rome and Parthia. The sixth trumpet and the sixth bowl both turn to the Euphrates, the edge of the Roman world (Revelation 9:14; 16:12).
rv_euphrates.d: The Euphrates River below Dura-Europos in Syria, a frontier town fought over by Rome and Parthia. The sixth trumpet and the sixth bowl both turn to the Euphrates, the edge of the Roman world (Revelation 9:14; 16:12).

rv_portus.f: Portus - Claudius first harbour and hexagonal basin extension under Trajan.jpg
rv_portus.c: A plan of Portus, the great harbor built by Claudius near Ostia and enlarged by Trajan with a six-sided basin. Through it came the grain and luxuries of the empire, the trade the merchants and seafarers mourn in Revelation 18:11-19.
rv_portus.d: A plan of Portus, the great harbor built by Claudius near Ostia and enlarged by Trajan with a six-sided basin. Through it came the grain and luxuries of the empire, the trade the merchants and seafarers mourn in Revelation 18:11-19.

rv_durer_horsemen.f: Albrecht Dürer, The Four Horsemen, 1498, NGA 142352.jpg
rv_durer_horsemen.c: The Four Horsemen, a woodcut from Albrecht Dürer’s Apocalypse of 1498. The riders on the white, red, black and pale horses of Revelation 6:1-8 ride down people of every rank.
rv_durer_horsemen.d: The Four Horsemen, a woodcut from Albrecht Dürer’s Apocalypse of 1498. The riders on the white, red, black and pale horses of Revelation 6:1-8 ride down people of every rank.
rv_durer_horsemen.a: Albrecht Dürer (1498), National Gallery of Art, Washington, CC0

rv_durer_trumpets.f: Albrecht Dürer, The Seven Angels with the Trumpets, probably c. 1496-1498, NGA 850.jpg
rv_durer_trumpets.c: The Seven Angels with the Trumpets, from Dürer’s Apocalypse: the angels receive their trumpets before God while an angel offers incense at the altar and the first plagues fall on the earth (Revelation 8).
rv_durer_trumpets.n: Dürer, The Seven Angels with the Trumpets
rv_durer_trumpets.d: The Seven Angels with the Trumpets, from Dürer’s Apocalypse: the angels receive their trumpets before God while an angel offers incense at the altar and the first plagues fall on the earth (Revelation 8).
rv_durer_trumpets.a: Albrecht Dürer (1498), National Gallery of Art, Washington, CC0

rv_durer_book.f: Albrecht Dürer, Saint John Devouring the Book, 1498, NGA 142357.jpg
rv_durer_book.c: Saint John Devouring the Book, from Dürer’s Apocalypse: the mighty angel with legs like pillars of fire gives John the little scroll to eat (Revelation 10).
rv_durer_book.n: Dürer, St John Devouring the Book
rv_durer_book.d: Saint John Devouring the Book, from Dürer’s Apocalypse: the mighty angel with legs like pillars of fire gives John the little scroll to eat (Revelation 10).
rv_durer_book.a: Albrecht Dürer (1498), National Gallery of Art, Washington, CC0

rv_durer_woman.f: Albrecht Dürer, The Apocalyptic Woman, 1498, NGA 142358.jpg
rv_durer_woman.c: The Apocalyptic Woman, from Dürer’s Apocalypse: the woman clothed with the sun and crowned with twelve stars, given eagle’s wings, while the seven-headed dragon waits (Revelation 12).
rv_durer_woman.n: Dürer, The Woman Clothed with the Sun
rv_durer_woman.d: The Apocalyptic Woman, from Dürer’s Apocalypse: the woman clothed with the sun and crowned with twelve stars, given eagle’s wings, while the seven-headed dragon waits (Revelation 12).
rv_durer_woman.a: Albrecht Dürer (1498), National Gallery of Art, Washington, CC0

rv_durer_michael.f: Albrecht Dürer, Saint Michael Fighting the Dragon, 1498, NGA 142359.jpg
rv_durer_michael.c: Saint Michael Fighting the Dragon, from Dürer’s Apocalypse: Michael and his angels fight the dragon in the sky above a quiet landscape (Revelation 12:7-9).
rv_durer_michael.n: Dürer, St Michael Fighting the Dragon
rv_durer_michael.d: Saint Michael Fighting the Dragon, from Dürer’s Apocalypse: Michael and his angels fight the dragon in the sky above a quiet landscape (Revelation 12:7-9).
rv_durer_michael.a: Albrecht Dürer (1498), National Gallery of Art, Washington, CC0

rv_durer_babylon.f: Albrecht Dürer, The Babylonian Whore, probably c. 1496-1498, NGA 6684.jpg
rv_durer_babylon.c: The Babylonian Whore, from Dürer’s Apocalypse: the woman on the seven-headed beast holds out her golden cup while the city burns behind her and the rider Faithful and True appears in the sky (Revelation 17-19).

rv_durer_key.f: Albrecht Dürer, The Angel with the Key to the Bottomless Pit, probably c. 1496-1498, NGA 6685.jpg
rv_durer_key.c: The Angel with the Key to the Bottomless Pit, from Dürer’s Apocalypse: the angel locks the dragon in the Abyss, while another angel shows John the new Jerusalem (Revelation 20:1-3; 21:9-10).

rv_ghent.f: Ghent Altarpiece - Adoration of the Mystic Lamb.jpg
rv_ghent.c: The Adoration of the Mystic Lamb, the central panel of the Ghent Altarpiece by Jan and Hubert van Eyck, finished in 1432. Martyrs, prophets, apostles and saints gather around the Lamb on the altar, in the spirit of Revelation 5 and 7.

rv_san_vitale.f: Basilica of San Vitale - Lamb of God mosaic.jpg
rv_san_vitale.c: The Lamb of God in a starry wreath held by four angels, in the vault of the presbytery of San Vitale, Ravenna, built about AD 547. Revelation’s main name for Christ is the Lamb who was slain (5:6).

rv_pudenziana.c: The apse mosaic of Santa Pudenziana in Rome, of about AD 400, one of the oldest in the city. Christ is enthroned among the apostles before a heavenly city, with the four living creatures of Revelation 4 in the sky above.

rv_angers.c: Part of the Apocalypse Tapestry in the castle of Angers, France, woven about 1377-1382 and still the largest medieval tapestry in existence. Its scenes follow the visions of Revelation one by one.

rv_last_judgment.c: The Last Judgment by Michelangelo, painted on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel in 1536-1541. Christ judges the dead, who rise from the earth, a picture of the great white throne of Revelation 20:11-15.
